decisions.what: Build the app in plain browser JavaScript with no framework and no build step. The files that sit in the repository are the exact files the browser downloads — nothing is compiled, packaged or transformed on the way out.
decisions.why: Nothing to keep alive. There is no toolchain that can rot, no build server, no versions to upgrade. Anyone (including a future auditor or a different AI) can open a file and read exactly what runs. The deploy workflow is 18 lines and explicitly turns the build off. IMPORTANT HONESTY NOTE: this reasoning is reconstructed from the code and the deploy configuration — no document anywhere actually records WHY this was chosen. It is an inherited decision. That is precisely the kind of thing that gets re-litigated, so it is worth Kunal writing the 'why' down once.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out React, Vue, Angular, Svelte or any framework rewrite. Rules out TypeScript, npm packaging, bundlers and a CI build stage. Rules out 'just npm install that library' — every third-party file has to be deliberately copied into the repo (see F-14). Also means the app can be opened straight off a disk in an emergency.
decisions.whoDecided: inherited (original build, March 2026) — never formally recorded

decisions.what: The app is one screen that swaps its content in place (a single-page app), and the great majority of it lives in one very large file, index.html — 6,637 lines, about 1 megabyte. Four smaller companion files were split out over time: db.js (the local database), sync.js (talking to the cloud), phase2.js (transfers between stores) and records.js (the shared record history).
decisions.why: It started as one file and grew. The splits that did happen were carved off when a piece became big and self-contained enough to stand alone. Keeping it in one file means there is never a question about load order or which copy of a function is live.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out assuming any file is small enough to rewrite wholesale. It carries a standing working rule that has bitten repeatedly: because one giant file can contain the same function defined twice, and the LAST definition wins, you must always search for duplicates after editing a method — a fix has more than once landed on a dead copy while the live one stayed broken.

decisions.why: No app-store accounts, no review queues, no release approvals, no per-platform builds. An update is a file upload; every device picks it up on next load. For a six-salon internal tool the app-store route would add cost and weeks of delay for nothing.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out native iOS/Android apps, and rules out anything that only works in a native app (push notifications to a locked phone, barcode hardware integration via a native SDK, background processing while the app is closed).

decisions.what: Everything happens on the device first. When a staff member logs a movement it is written to the phone or PC immediately and the screen updates instantly; sending it to the cloud happens afterwards, in the background. The app never makes anyone wait for the internet.
decisions.why: Salon Wi-Fi is unreliable and staff are logging stock between clients. A tool that spins while it waits for a server does not get used. Technically this is enforced by a deliberate design choice recorded in the code: the function that reads data stays instant (synchronous) and the database write is fired off in the background, specifically so that the 140-plus places in the app that read data did not have to be rewritten to wait.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out any design where a screen waits on the cloud before it will show a number, and rules out server-rendered pages. It is also the reason F-17 exists — you cannot put a cloud permission check in front of ordinary stock logging without breaking this.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude (Phase 3), consistent with Kunal's offline-first requirement

decisions.what: Two different ways of writing to the local database, chosen per table. History tables that only ever grow (movements, deletions, transfers) get one new row appended at a time. Small reference tables (products, stores, users — under about 200 rows each) are simply wiped and rewritten whole.
decisions.why: Appending scales to a hundred thousand movements without lag; rewriting a two-hundred-row product list costs nothing and is far simpler than tracking individual changes. Using the wrong one either way is a performance or a complexity trap. Wiping-and-rewriting EVERYTHING is reserved for three specific moments only: the one-time migration, first-run seeding, and merging a cloud pull.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out clear-and-rewrite on the movement ledger (it would not survive the row counts). Rules out per-row change tracking on the little reference tables (needless complexity).
decisions.whoDecided: Claude (recorded in code as 'Hybrid write strategy — Option C')

decisions.what: Move the device's storage from the browser's simple key-value store (localStorage) to a proper on-device database (IndexedDB, accessed through a small library called Dexie). Old devices migrate once, automatically, on first launch — and the old copy is kept as a safety net rather than deleted.
decisions.why: localStorage holds everything as one single lump of text with a hard size cap and no way to query it, so a growing movement history would eventually simply stop fitting. IndexedDB is a real database with indexes. The migration deliberately refuses to boot an empty app if the copy fails — it stops and serves the still-intact old data instead, because a silent 'all your stock is now zero' is the worst possible outcome.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out going back to a single stored blob, and rules out any 'just clear the browser data to fix it' advice — that is now a data-loss instruction, not a reset.

decisions.what: Stock levels are never stored anywhere. Every stock number you see is added up on the spot from the complete history of movements: everything that came in, minus everything that went out.
decisions.why: A stored number can drift out of step with the records behind it — someone edits one and not the other and the books quietly stop agreeing with reality. If the number is always derived, that class of error cannot exist: the history IS the truth, and any figure can be re-explained by pointing at the rows that produced it. This is the single most load-bearing idea in the whole app.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a 'current stock' column anywhere. Rules out 'just set the count to 40' — a correction has to be entered as a movement that explains itself. Rules out deleting old movements to save space (see F-22 — you must snapshot the balance first). And it is the reason the ledger grows forever, which is what forces F-20, F-21 and F-22.
decisions.whoDecided: inherited (original build) — reaffirmed at every architecture review since

decisions.what: Nothing in the movement history is ever edited or erased. A deletion is recorded as a NEW row that points at the row it cancels (a 'tombstone'); a correction is a new movement, not a rewrite.
decisions.why: The cloud sync only ever looks forward — it asks 'what rows are newer than the last one I saw'. A row that was quietly changed in place would never be noticed by any device again. Append-only is also what makes the history auditable: you can see that something was cancelled, by whom and when, rather than finding a gap.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out editing rows in place, anywhere. CRITICAL OPERATIONAL CONSEQUENCE, and it is written down in only two places: NOBODY may ever edit or delete rows directly in the SharePoint list by hand. Devices would never see the change and would silently disagree with the cloud forever. Every change goes through the app.
decisions.whoDecided: inherited, formalised as a mandatory condition of the pull upgrade

decisions.what: The cloud side is built entirely from Microsoft 365 pieces the business already pays for — SharePoint lists hold the data, Azure Logic Apps act as the middleman — rather than a custom-built server with its own database.
decisions.why: Cost, and having nothing extra to run. SharePoint comes with the M365 Business subscription the business already has; Logic Apps are billed per run and sit inside the free allowance at this volume; the website hosting is a free tier. Total running cost is effectively zero. There is no server to patch, no database to back up, no hosting bill that grows.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a conventional web backend (a Node/.NET server, a SQL or Cosmos database, Dataverse). It also imposes SharePoint's limits on the whole design — most importantly the 5,000-item query ceiling that drives F-20, F-21 and F-22 — and Logic Apps' limits, most importantly that they cannot do pattern-matching on text (see F-23).
decisions.whoDecided: Kunal (Phase 3 — 'M365 migration' over four working days)

decisions.what: Store devices never talk to SharePoint directly. Every request goes through a Logic App, which is the only thing allowed to touch the data. The Azure Function (the small piece of real code in the cloud) is likewise called only by Logic Apps, never by the browser.
decisions.why: It keeps one door instead of many. All the checking, de-duplicating and permission work can be done in one place, and a device only ever holds a key to the door — not to the data itself. It is also enforced technically: the app's security policy only permits connections to Logic App addresses, and there is not a single reference to the Function's address anywhere in the client code (verified today: zero matches across all five client files).
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out giving a device a SharePoint login. Rules out the browser calling the Azure Function directly. Anything new the app needs from the cloud has to be added as a Logic App endpoint — that is the only shape allowed.

decisions.what: The devices staff use are Windows PCs, iPhones and Android phones. NOT iPads.
decisions.why: It is what the salons actually have. This is flagged in three separate documents because it has been got wrong repeatedly and it changes real decisions — screen layouts, touch targets, and how much memory the app can assume it has (a low-end phone is the tightest constraint in the app, and it is the reason the history has to be kept bounded — see F-22).

decisions.what: Every outside file the app uses is copied into the project and served from our own address. Nothing is loaded from a third-party content network at run time. The browser security policy was then tightened to forbid outside sources entirely — with one deliberate exception kept.

The upgrade path was deliberately kept open by using the same message format, so moving to per-device registration later does not mean rebuilding it.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out Microsoft sign-in for this generation of the app. Rules out the earlier shortcut of treating a Head Office device as equivalent to a Director — Kunal explicitly rejected that: a Director is not Head Office. decisions.what: Not every action is put behind a personal login check in the cloud. Ordinary stock logging stays device-local and offline-capable; only Director-level actions (approving a stock take, resolving or cancelling a transfer, recording a delivery, adjustments) require the person to be verified online at the moment they act.

The ledger's protection instead comes from being append-only and fully audited, plus each store only receiving its own data. NOTE: whether the Director-online rule was actually built as described is one of the register's open contradictions — the design says yes, the build record says the intent was noted but enforcement exists only on two paths. Worth confirming before launch, because it decides what Kunal and Shahin can do in a store with poor signal.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'require login for every action' as a security answer. It means the honest description of any audit trail is 'this came from an authenticated account on an authenticated store device' — never 'this person personally did it'.

decisions.what: Transfers, deliveries and stock takes travel between devices as an append-only stream of small steps — 'transfer sent', 'transfer received', 'discrepancy flagged', 'Director resolved' — held in ONE general-purpose list. Each device rebuilds the current state of a transfer by replaying its steps in order.
decisions.why: The exact same idea that already works for stock (F-8), applied to records. The alternative — sending the whole transfer document each time somebody changes it — is unsafe when two shops edit the same transfer while offline: one simply overwrites the other. Steps cannot overwrite each other. Both auditors independently landed on one general list rather than one per record type; one called append-only 'more correct'. Per-type lists were rejected as roughly three times the build for no safety gain, since the line items inside a transfer would still need packing into text anyway.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out one SharePoint list per record type. Rules out 'last person to save wins'. Rules out sending whole record documents over the wire. And it fixed the single biggest gap in the app: before this, a transfer created on one shop's device was invisible on the other shop's device — the stock moved but the paperwork did not.
decisions.whoDecided: Kunal, after an architecture review by both auditors (recorded as decision D1)

decisions.what: Stock and paperwork travel in two separate streams that must never be confused. Stock movements go in the movement ledger; lifecycle steps go in the record-steps list; a lifecycle step NEVER moves stock by itself. When an action does both, the stock rows are sent FIRST and the step is only sent once those rows are confirmed accepted.
decisions.why: This is the core safety rule of the whole record-sync design, and both auditors independently flagged its absence as the number-one gap. If a step could move stock, the same receipt arriving twice would credit the stock twice. By keeping them separate and ordered, a step that arrives without its stock rows shows visibly as 'pending' or 'mismatched' rather than silently inventing inventory.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out any shortcut where receiving a transfer 'just adds the stock' as part of the paperwork. The list of expected stock rows attached to each step later became load-bearing for two further pieces of work (the permission checks and the per-store data separation), so changing it now would break three things at once.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, after both auditors flagged the gap; folded into the Chunk 4 build

decisions.what: When a device asks the cloud for history it now walks the list by row number rather than by timestamp. Built in June, proven against 20,048 rows, reviewed by both auditors — and NEVER INSTALLED.
decisions.why: SharePoint refuses any query that matches more than about 5,000 items, no matter how it is indexed. Asking 'give me everything since date X' hits that wall the moment the ledger passes 5,000 rows, and the request simply fails. Walking by row number uses the list's built-in numbering, which has no such limit. Day-to-day syncing of a handful of new rows is fine today — the case that breaks is a BRAND NEW DEVICE, or one that has been off for a long time, asking to catch up. THIS IS A DATED RISK: the ledger reaches the ceiling around October 2026, and onboarding a new franchisee means onboarding new devices — exactly the case that breaks. There is also a trap: the app already sends the new-style request, and the live cloud endpoint cannot understand it, so the cloud change must go out before or with the app.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out ever paging cloud data by timestamp again. Rules out 'add an index to fix it' — proven not to work past 5,000. Depends absolutely on F-9 (nothing edited in place), because walking forward by row number can never look back at a row it has already passed.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude designed; both auditors approved; Kunal has not yet scheduled the install

decisions.what: SharePoint indexes must be created at the moment a list is created, while it is still empty, and tracked deliberately in one manifest. You cannot add one later.
decisions.why: Two hard platform limits, both discovered the hard way. SharePoint refuses to add an index to a list that already holds more than 5,000 items, and it allows only about twenty indexed columns per list. So getting this wrong at go-live is unfixable without rebuilding the list. A separate, expensive correction is recorded here too: an earlier belief that indexes could be set through the Microsoft Graph interface was proven WRONG — that only sets a cosmetic flag; a real index needs a different method and only works while the list is small.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'we'll index it if it gets slow'. Rules out casually indexing extra columns (each one slows writes and burns the twenty-column budget). It also constrains the ORDER of the go-live steps: the live lists must be created with their full index set before any data lands in them. STALE RECORD: AZURE-CHUNK1-INDEXING.md still carries the disproven Graph claim under a 'done and verified' heading, with no correction.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, after both auditors' Chunk 1 review; correction ground-truthed 2026-06-23

decisions.what: The answer to an ever-growing history is: take an opening-balance snapshot per product per store at a cutoff point, then move the older movements to a separate archive list. Devices seed their stock numbers from the snapshot and only apply movements since. The cutoff is set by SharePoint row number, NOT by date.
decisions.why: Because stock is the sum of every movement ever made (F-8), you can never simply delete old rows. The tighter limit is not the cloud — it is a low-end store phone, which downloads the whole history and adds it up in memory; that starts to hurt at tens of thousands of rows. The snapshot bounds both. The cutoff is by row number rather than date for a subtle but important reason: a movement entered late or backdated from an offline phone gets a NEW, higher row number, so it lands after the cutoff and is still counted. A date-based cutoff would silently swallow it. Kunal was offered 'design now, build later' and chose to BUILD IT NOW so everything ships together.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out deleting old movements to save space. Rules out a date-based archive cutoff. Rules out assuming a device always holds the complete history — reports that reach back past the cutoff must either fetch archived rows or say plainly that they cannot cover the range.
decisions.whoDecided: Kunal chose to build now (recorded as decision D8-0), against Claude's recommendation to defer

decisions.what: Do the cloud-side checking inside the Logic Apps themselves wherever possible, rather than writing custom code. Logic Apps cannot do pattern-matching on text, so a technique was devised that achieves the same result using length comparison plus explicit blocks on the handful of dangerous characters. A small Azure Function was nonetheless added later, when genuine code was unavoidable.
decisions.why: Fewer moving parts, nothing extra to deploy or pay for. Both auditors reviewed the workaround and agreed it was equivalent to the pattern-matching it replaces. The Function exception was accepted for money validation, where the checking genuinely needed real code — Kunal chose it, and it was the auditor's preferred option. That Function App now hosts ten routes and has become a real, permanent part of the architecture, so the original 'no Function' stance should be read as 'no Function for simple validation', not as a standing ban.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out expecting pattern-matching to work in a Logic App — it does not exist there, and the workaround must be reused verbatim rather than reinvented. Standing risk: the same technique is now copied in two places (the ledger and the record steps); changing it in one silently makes them disagree.
decisions.whoDecided: Both auditors chose the Logic-App-only route for validation; Kunal chose the Function for money checking

decisions.what: Permission checks that run in the browser are NOT security. They stop mistakes and catch regressions; they do not stop a determined person. Anyone with the browser's developer tools open can change their own role, their store, the local data, the backup file and the messages sent to the cloud. This is written into the always-loaded project brief as a permanent rule.
decisions.why: An honest statement of what the app actually enforces, so that no audit report and no plan is ever built on a false sense of protection. It was accepted deliberately for a trusted internal alpha — known staff, no customer data, no payments. IMPORTANT UPDATE: the rule as written says authentication, permissions, store enforcement and audit logging MUST all move to the cloud before any broader rollout. Kunal's ruling on 2026-08-01 changes that condition: staff are not a hostile-user threat, so security hardening may follow release. The honest description of what the app enforces is unchanged; the deadline attached to it is not.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out describing browser-side role checks as 'secure' in any report, ever. Rules out relying on the app hiding a screen to keep a number private — hiding is not the same as not sending. That distinction is exactly why per-store data separation had to be built server-side. NOTE: the rule points readers at a backlog file whose path does not exist in the repo (the real file is in the untracked audit-artifacts folder) — a broken reference in the one document loaded into every session.

Risk-ordering unblocks the things that are actually wrong now.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out resuming the Account Access security items ahead of the money and data-leak queue. Rules out treating 'it's only a security item' as a reason to defer a data leak — a leak is a leak regardless of which chunk it came from. Also rules out the old absolute rollout gate (F-25).

decisions.what: Build ONE living feature-and-decision register, kept current, that doubles as training material for staff and Head Office — and build it BEFORE the Cockburn pricing work and the Southlands ownership work.
decisions.why: There are about a hundred documents at the top of the project and every one is a snapshot of a past moment; none is a record of what is true now. Decisions get silently re-argued because nobody can find the original reasoning. Kunal is not a developer and should not have to personally remember rulings made months ago. Doing it before the pricing and ownership work means that work starts from a correct picture rather than adding to the pile.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out adding another dated snapshot document. Rules out separate 'technical docs' and 'staff training' — it is one artefact serving both. IMPORTANT PLACEMENT WARNING: the existing partial attempt lives in audit-artifacts/, which is excluded from version control (.gitignore:10) — it exists on this machine only and would vanish with it. The living register must be a TRACKED file at the top of the project.
decisions.source: Kunal's session ruling, 2026-08-01; the partial precursor is at C:\Users\joshi\repos\bob-stock\audit-artifacts\MASTER-DECISION-REGISTER.md (built 2026-07-30)

decisions.what: Claude writes the specs, the Logic App definitions and the client code, but cannot click in the Azure portal or change SharePoint. Kunal applies every cloud change himself, with the Azure command-line tool available on this machine for scripted steps.
decisions.why: It was identified up front as the real bottleneck — 'the first thing to settle, because without it the cloud work cannot land'. Three options were on the table: the command-line tool, Kunal driving the portal against exact written steps, or an outside Azure developer. In practice it settled on the first two. It matters because every cloud change costs Kunal's own hands-on time, which is the scarcest resource on the project — one apply plan alone is estimated at around twenty-two hours of it.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out assuming a cloud change can just be made. Every cloud step must be written as exact, checkable instructions, and the time cost of applying it must be counted in the plan — not treated as free.
decisions.when: raised 2026-06-22; settled through the chunk builds
decisions.source: C:\Users\joshi\repos\bob-stock\AZURE-PHASE-SCOPE.md:72-79; CLAUDE.md:263-264 ('He runs every cloud apply himself')

decisions.what: Product and store information flows DOWN to devices as a versioned catalogue published from the cloud, and the decision on how it gets republished was: a deliberate manual publish by a Director, not an automatic trigger whenever someone edits a SharePoint list.
decisions.why: Predictability. An automatic republish fires on every stray edit, including half-finished ones, and pushes them to every device immediately. A manual publish means somebody decides the catalogue is ready. Recorded as decision D3, with Claude's stated lean toward manual first and automation later; built as Director-only.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out auto-publishing on every list change. STALE RECORD: AZURE-CHUNK6-SCOPE.md records this as decided at line 109 and, thirty lines later, as 'the one OPEN decision for Kunal' — the same file contradicts itself. The open version should be deleted.

decisions.what: Every piece of server-phase work follows the same ten steps in order: write the scope, have outside auditors attack the scope BEFORE any code exists, map what already works, build the whole wave in one go on the test environment, prove it locally, run the full local break-it sweep, write the review pack, ground-truth every finding, fix them all in one batch, then loop until both auditors pass. Any change to this process gets WRITTEN INTO the process document, not just agreed in a chat.
decisions.why: Before this, work was reviewed only after it was built, which made every design defect cost a whole wave to unwind instead of a paragraph. Ratifying it in one document stops each session inventing its own order of work. The write-it-down clause exists because a process agreed only in conversation is invisible to the next session.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out ad-hoc 'just build it and review after'; rules out reviewing code before the design has been attacked; rules out changing the process by agreeing something in chat and leaving the document behind (this rule has now been broken twice — see PROC one-cutover entry).

decisions.what: The roles are fixed and do not rotate. Claude is the ONLY one who writes code. GPT/Codex and Antigravity (AGY) are outside auditors who report findings and never touch a file. Kunal owns the project: he routes the audits, makes the gating calls and personally runs every cloud change.
decisions.why: An auditor that edits is no longer independent, and on one occasion an agentic auditor trampled an uncommitted test file in the live working tree (Wave H). Keeping one hand on the code and two independent sets of eyes on it is what makes the findings worth anything.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out letting an auditor apply its own fix; rules out a second engineer or an agentic file-editing auditor; rules out Claude deploying anything itself.

decisions.what: Auditors are used TWICE on every piece of work, not once: first on the written design before a single line of code exists, and again after the wave is built and locally proven.
decisions.why: A defect found in a spec costs a paragraph to fix; the same defect found after building costs a whole wave. Item 5's history is the proof — three review rounds, all on a spec, each one finding real defects that would otherwise have been built.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating auditors as a final rubber stamp; rules out starting to build while the spec review is still out.

decisions.what: Discover before you touch: before changing anything that already works, map how it currently behaves and make sure a test covers that behaviour FIRST. No behaviour change without a covering test already in place.
decisions.why: Changing shipped behaviour with no test around it means nobody finds out it broke until a user does. This came out of real incidents where an unrelated fix silently disabled an existing safeguard.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'small safe edit, no test needed'; rules out writing the covering test after the change.
decisions.whoDecided: inherited (audit framework P-12), ratified into the chunk process

decisions.what: Mode A build: Claude builds the entire wave autonomously — client and cloud together — on the STAGING environment only, committing nothing. Kunal reviews once, at the end of the wave.
decisions.why: Kunal is not a developer and reviewing every intermediate step costs him time without buying safety. Reviewing one finished, self-consistent wave is both cheaper for him and a better review. Staging-only means a half-finished wave can never reach the real business data.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out step-by-step approval during a wave; rules out touching the live app or live cloud mid-wave; rules out committing work before the wave review.

decisions.what: Every change must come with two things: a test proving the new behaviour, AND a deliberate sabotage of the code proving that test actually catches the break. Then the full test suite must be green, the sabotage run clean, and real end-to-end checks must be driven against the ACTUAL staging cloud — never against a mock.
decisions.why: A test you have never seen fail is not a test. And a mocked cloud passes even when the real deployed cloud answers with something completely different — that has happened here and only a real-cloud run caught it.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out shipping a change covered only by a test that has never been proven to bite; rules out proving a cloud contract with a mocked harness.
decisions.whoDecided: Kunal / inherited from the audit framework

decisions.what: The complete break-it sweep (every sabotage ever written, all waves since the beginning) runs on Claude's machine only, in the foreground. It is NEVER handed to an auditor. Auditors get the finished log as evidence and may spot-check individual items.
decisions.why: Each sabotage spins up a full browser test run; the complete set is impractical on an auditor's machine — GPT once churned for 12+ hours and AGY errored out, and to an auditor a 90-process run looks like a hang. Running it in the foreground matters because the sweep spawns child processes that survive a kill and keep mutating the live working tree.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out asking an auditor to run the full sweep or the gate-mutation suite; rules out backgrounding the sweep; rules out recovering from a bad sweep with 'git checkout' instead of the .sabotage-bak restore.

decisions.what: External auditors must EXECUTE the client test harness themselves every wave — the test suite, the scoped sabotage set for that wave, and real probes against the staging cloud. They may not accept Claude's reported numbers. They report only what they observed.
decisions.why: Through the early Azure phase the auditors reviewed exported artifacts and trusted Claude's numbers; GPT said outright 'I did not touch cloud resources or run scripts'. That is a review, not an audit. The client harness needs no password and no cloud access, so there is no excuse for not re-running it.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a read-only 'artifact review' being called an audit; rules out an auditor reporting a verdict without printed numbers from their own run.

decisions.what: Every finding is ground-truthed by actually running the scenario before anything is fixed — including findings that look obviously correct, and including a deliberate attempt to REFUTE them. False positives are written up with the evidence, not fixed.
decisions.why: Fixing a finding that is not real adds risk for nothing, and auditors do produce mis-rated and occasionally invented findings (Gemini fabricated a CVE; AGY once mis-rated a client-only view hint as a P1 data leak). Refuting is also how the good findings get sharper.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out fixing on an auditor's say-so; rules out dismissing a finding without running it; rules out trusting any auditor's severity rating unverified.

decisions.what: When an audit comes back with findings, ALL confirmed findings get fixed in one batch. No cherry-picking. Each fix gets its own test plus its own sabotage, then everything is re-proven and a re-verify note goes back to the auditors.
decisions.why: Kunal's explicit preference — partial fixes leave the same round open and guarantee another round. Batching also means the re-audit tests one coherent state instead of a moving target.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out picking the easy findings and deferring the rest; rules out fixing without adding the covering test and its sabotage.

decisions.what: CONVERGENCE RULE: a chunk is not clean until BOTH auditors independently come back clean on the SAME revision — re-running the tests, the scoped sabotage set and the real cloud, not just eyeballing the diff. Not one auditor. Not 'the gate is green'. Both. Then the chunk goes on HOLD.
decisions.why: Every single Codex round on this project has found something real, and on the item-5 round AGY found the only genuine counter-example after Codex had examined the same question and reported nothing. Stopping at one pass would have shipped that defect. Requiring the SAME revision stops a stale 'pass' from an earlier snapshot being counted.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out declaring a chunk done on one auditor's PASS; rules out counting a green test suite as convergence; rules out counting two passes taken against different versions of the code.

decisions.what: BOTH auditors get the SAME complete brief. Questions are never split between them by which auditor is 'better' at that topic.
decisions.why: Claude proposed splitting questions by strength to cut AGY's turnaround (AGY runs 3-5x slower than Codex). Kunal overruled it, and the same day's evidence proved him right: Codex was given question 1, examined it and reported 'no counter-example found'; AGY, asked the same question, FOUND one — the only genuine counter-example to the property the whole design rests on. Under the split that defect would have shipped. Redundancy only works because it is redundant; splitting removes the second pair of eyes from exactly the question where the first pair was wrong. AGY's slower turnaround costs waiting time only — they already run in parallel — which is cheap next to a missed defect.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out topic-splitting briefs, 'AGY-only' or 'Codex-only' question sets, and any turnaround optimisation that reduces the number of independent looks at a question.

decisions.what: Gemini is retired as an auditor. The auditors are GPT/Codex and Antigravity (AGY), and nobody else.
decisions.why: Gemini fabricated findings — an invented security vulnerability and two hallucinated 'critical' issues in one wave. An auditor that invents findings costs more time than it saves, because every finding then has to be disproved.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the old 'every significant step goes to Gemini before executing' rule; rules out reinstating a third auditor without a fresh decision; rules out using an agentic file-editing model as an auditor.
decisions.source: HANDOVER.md:222; CLAUDE.md:261-264 (supersession banner); registered as CUT-11 in audit-artifacts/MASTER-DECISION-REGISTER.md:541-547

decisions.what: The auditor quality tiering was REVISED: AGY is no longer treated as the junior. They are not better and worse, they are differently shaped — AGY is sharper on what the Azure platform actually does at runtime, Codex is sharper on whether the paperwork and the gates hold together.
decisions.why: In one round AGY found the only genuine counter-example AND spotted that a proposed correction would produce a wiring shape Azure refuses to save, while Codex found the document defects, the gates that were checking nothing, and the unreproducible audit package. The old line ('AGY mid, thin on product reasoning') did not survive that evidence.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out discounting an AGY verdict as second-tier, and rules out the practice of 'AGY verdict discounted' seen in earlier fold records. NOTE: HANDOVER.md:223-224 still carries the OLD tiering wording in the same file, twenty lines above the revision.

decisions.what: An auditor hand-off is a SHORT cover note that points at a pack file committed in the repo (PASTE-TO-AUDITORS-*.md). The pack contents are never dumped into a chat message. This is the default — Kunal should not have to ask for it.
decisions.why: The pack has to be a fixed, citable artifact tied to a specific commit, otherwise the auditor and the engineer are looking at different text. It also keeps Kunal's routing job to a copy-paste.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out pasting a full brief into chat; rules out an auditor working from an uncommitted or working-tree-only document.

decisions.what: Every brief must contain, explicitly: a numbered prioritised file list with exact paths; a DO-NOT-READ line; where ground truth actually is (the committed captures, not the spec — where they disagree the capture wins and that disagreement IS the finding); a DO-NOT-RUN line naming what not to execute and why; one or two numbered questions, one pass each; a hard time box (~90 minutes, report what you have); and neutral quality-assurance language throughout.
decisions.why: Rounds die in setup, not in auditing. AGY once burned a whole night on a loose brief with four jobs in it, and there are ~100 markdown files at the repo root for an unguided reader to wander into. Neutral language is required because OpenAI's safety filter has blocked audits mid-run over offensive-security wording — twice with the trigger words sitting in the linked spec, not the brief.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'read the spec and the captures' as a file list; rules out multi-job briefs; rules out treating the spec as ground truth over a real captured definition; rules out any offensive-security wording in the brief OR in anything it links to.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude (banked from incidents), endorsed by Kunal

decisions.what: Before any brief is sent, run node audit-artifacts/check-auditor-pack.js against it. It verifies the cited commit exists AND is on the remote, that every file the brief names is present at that commit, and that the brief's content claims hold there.
decisions.why: One hand-off went out wrong three times in a row — a commit that never existed, a commit whose spec still carried wording an auditor had already refused twice, and files named as ground truth that were gitignored and absent from the commit. The gate catches all three in about a second. It checks the COMMIT, not the working tree, because the tree was correct all three times.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out sending a brief without the pre-flight check; rules out citing an unpushed commit; rules out claiming a file is ground truth when it is gitignored.

decisions.what: Auditor hygiene, each rule earned by a specific incident: cite a PUSHED commit; auditors work from their OWN fresh copy with dependencies copied in, never Claude's working tree; round 2 and later need a fresh copy plus a printed staleness proof; never describe a file you have not opened; sabotage runs capped at 5 concurrent so both auditors can run at once; every cloud test id prefixed gpt_ / agy_; functional probes only, NO load tests against the shared SharePoint connection.
decisions.why: Each one comes from something that actually went wrong: an auditor trampled an uncommitted test file in the live tree; gitignored dependencies meant nothing could run; 'the fix is missing' BLOCKs turned out to be stale snapshots; AGY once fabricated a cloud expression from a file that did not exist; unprefixed test ids made one auditor's rows look like the other's duplicates; and the staging cloud shares one connection with the LIVE cloud, so a load test can throttle real sync.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out auditors sharing Claude's working tree; rules out un-namespaced cloud test data; rules out load/volume testing on staging; rules out accepting a 'missing fix' report without a staleness proof.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude (banked from incidents), ratified into the process doc

decisions.what: Paper reviews, spec reviews and local-only audits go to BOTH auditors at the same time. Only audits that share the staging cloud are run one at a time.
decisions.why: Parallel is faster and there is nothing to collide over when the work is reading documents or running a credential-free local harness. Cloud audits are serialised because two auditors writing to the same staging lists produce each other's false duplicates.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out serialising every audit by default and doubling convergence time for no reason.

decisions.what: At the end of the phase, once every chunk is on HOLD, a 6-way BLIND audit runs: six auditors with no knowledge of what was fixed, against a de-primed copy of the code. Deliberately, there is no full blind audit before that final one.
decisions.why: Primed auditors confirm what they are told is fixed instead of attacking it — the single most-confirmed bug in the project's history (tombstone egress, found four times) lived in code GPT had already called 'clean', and every primed round afterwards confirmed it clean instead of re-attacking. Blind auditors catch the siblings a primed sweep misses. Holding it to the end is Kunal's call: an earlier full blind audit would only re-flag the items already known to be open.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating a primed 'clean' verdict as evidence the code is solid; rules out running the expensive blind audit early; rules out skipping the blind round because the primed rounds all passed.

decisions.what: ONE single commit and deployment at the end of the whole server phase, only with Kunal's explicit OK — never before. This rule still governs everything except the two named exceptions below.
decisions.why: A string of small risky deploys is more dangerous than one carefully audited cutover, and the app is not in use, so there is no pressure to ship in pieces. Kunal personally runs every cloud change.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out per-fix auto-deploy (the old CLAUDE.md §7 model); rules out merging the working branch to main early; rules out anyone but Kunal running a cloud apply. WARNING: the governing process document still states the rule with no exceptions and has not been amended, in breach of its own line 4.
decisions.supersededBy: CUT-2 (franchise wizard split out, 2026-07-29) and CUT-3 (Contract 2 parked, 2026-07-29) — the rule now has two named exceptions and still governs everything else

decisions.what: The franchise wizard is NOT part of the single cutover. It ships afterwards as its own smaller, separately-audited deploy.
decisions.why: It is a director-only screen that no staff member ever opens. The one-cutover rule exists to avoid a string of risky deploys, not to hold the entire launch behind a screen nobody using the app will touch. Consequence: the ~Sep-Oct 2026 new franchisee no longer gates the launch — the documented scripted onboarding runbook covers that one franchisee and the wizard serves the next.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out blocking launch on the org-structure/wizard work; rules out reading the absolute 'no device gets the app until ALL chunks are done' gate as still binding.

decisions.what: Contract 2 (the correction route, which lets a director fix a mistake in a stock record) is PARKED and will ship as its own later, separately-audited deploy. Parking was verified safe: nothing already applied to staging depends on it, and there is no correction screen in the app, so no user loses something they had.
decisions.why: It is the least-finished thing in the project — 17 confirmed defects and 7 blocking gaps on its delivery path, never deployed, never run — while everything else is built and audited. Kunal's direction for when it IS built is Option A: corrections must reach the shop floor, not just the books, which makes it bigger, not smaller — a further reason not to build it under time pressure. Stated cost of parking: it also parks the ability to produce any buy-back settlement for a departing franchisee.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out folding C2 back into the main cutover; rules out a books-only correction design; rules out treating a buy-back settlement as available before C2 ships. Parking is only safe if six carried obligations are honoured (HANDOVER.md:424-467) — obligation 1 is verified NOT DONE.

decisions.what: Item 5 (server-side ingest validation) is PARKED as of 2026-08-01 and must NOT be resumed until four preconditions are ALL met: the edit file complete at 58 of 58 actions with real definitions and replacement values, four validator holes closed each with a self-test seen to fire, coverage stated as a measured number rather than an adjective, and the enforcement switch re-derived so that a MISSING switch means OFF.
decisions.why: Three audit rounds, three BLOCKs, both auditors every time — and resuming early is exactly what produced those three rounds. It is applied last anyway (sessions 7-9) and nothing in sessions 1-6 needs it, so it is not worth being the bottleneck. The generalisable lesson: the recurring defect was never a missing check, it was CLAIMING something was covered or authoritative before it was — two consecutive rounds were lost to precisely that.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out resuming item 5 on partial credit; rules out describing anything as 'authoritative', 'covered' or 'done' without a measured number behind it.

decisions.what: Stop hand-patching prose: any property that a machine can check must live as DATA with a validator, not as English in a document. Where the prose and the data disagree, the data wins and defects get fixed in the data.
decisions.why: Two consecutive audit rounds found corrections stated at the top of a spec that never reached the instructions below, plus shapes the cloud platform cannot accept. Hand-patching the prose introduced NEW defects both times — one correction created a circular dependency, another was stated twice and applied never. When the same defects were seeded into the new validator it caught all four auditor findings plus a fifth nobody had flagged.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out correcting a machine-checkable defect by editing the document; rules out treating an English spec as the source of truth for anything a script could verify.

decisions.what: THE OVERRIDE that beats every other process rule: on this project the wins have never come from more thinking. They came from mechanical gates that bite and from external adversarial review. If you are about to propose more parallel agents where a check would do the job, build the check instead. A gate you have never seen fail is not a gate.
decisions.why: Repeatedly demonstrated: the contract harness and the gate-mutation suite caught things careful reasoning did not, and Codex once slipped 15 of 16 deliberate corruptions past three 'clean' gates. Extra reasoning capacity does not buy a gate, and is never a substitute for one.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out spending on parallel orchestration when a mechanical check would settle the question; rules out trusting a gate that has never been mutation-tested.

decisions.what: Effort-mode protocol. Default is HIGH and if HIGH is right, say nothing and just work. If the mode should CHANGE, say so as its own message and then STOP and wait — never state the recommendation and start the work in the same message.
decisions.why: Kunal is paying for this and cannot tell from a task description whether parallel orchestration will earn its cost, so he must be told. And in his own words: 'If you inform me and start working, how am I supposed to change it?' — a recommendation delivered alongside the finished work is decorative. Announcing the mode on every task when nothing changes is just noise.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out silently spending on a heavy workflow; rules out announcing the mode every single task; rules out bundling the recommendation with the work it applies to. Only three situations earn the heavy mode: refuting a claim from several angles, genuinely independent parallel sweeps, and comparing rival designs. Never for one script, document edits, an already-decided edit list, auditor messages, commits or conversation.

decisions.what: Nothing deploys without Kunal's explicit OK, and he runs every cloud apply personally. Show changes before applying them; confirm before committing or deploying.
decisions.why: He is the owner, the cloud is the real business's data, and stability is his stated top priority. Keeping his hands on the apply step is the last backstop between an audited plan and the live business.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out Claude running an Azure apply; rules out committing or pushing without asking; rules out silent edits.

decisions.what: Bank ideas, do not build them. A new feature idea goes into a backlog file the same day it is raised, and is built only when Kunal explicitly says to build it.
decisions.why: Feature ideas raised mid-wave derail the wave and get lost if they only live in chat. Writing them down the same day means nothing is forgotten and nothing is started by accident.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out starting work on an idea the moment it is mentioned; rules out leaving an idea only in a chat transcript.

decisions.what: How Kunal wants to be communicated with: plain English first, always, before any code detail. Relaxed conversational tone, not an audit report. Challenge weak ideas rather than agreeing. Reassure proactively about stability, and clearly distinguish 'hardening an isolated new file' from 'touching the live app'.
decisions.why: He is a business owner, not a developer, and cannot read a diff. Audit churn has made him anxious about the app's stability before, so the distinction between churn on new isolated work and risk to the live app has to be spelled out rather than assumed.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out leading with code or jargon; rules out audit-report formality in conversation; rules out agreeing with a weak idea to be agreeable.

decisions.what: Shared vocabulary: PHASE contains CHUNKS, chunks contain WAVES (which nest), and each audit pass is a ROUND. 'Slice' is commit vocabulary only and means a small increment with a mechanical gate after it — described as the single most valuable habit on the project.
decisions.why: Sessions were using the same words for different sized things. And slicing exists because building a large artifact against an unverified contract produced 20 wrong function calls at once — small increments with a gate after each catch that on the first one.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out building a large artifact in one go against a contract nobody has verified.

decisions.what: Before any hand-off or any claim that work has been 'pushed', verify it: check that HEAD is attached to a branch and compare the remote's commit with the local one. A quiet 'Everything up-to-date' from git proves nothing.
decisions.why: On 2026-07-31 three commits of real work sat on a detached HEAD while the branch stayed put, so every push was a no-op that reported success — and the branch's own newer commits made the auditor brief look like the work had been reverted. It was caught only because the auditor-pack gate checks that the cited commit is on the remote, and it wasn't.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating a successful-looking 'git push' as proof the work is on the remote.

decisions.what: Every lesson learned goes back into the audit framework (it only ever grows, never shrinks), and a row is appended to the project log after every shipped change.
decisions.why: The framework's value is cumulative — each incident that produced a rule is why the rule is trusted. Without banking, the same mistake is rediscovered by the next session.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out deleting or quietly narrowing an existing framework rule; rules out shipping a change without logging it.

decisions.what: The current audit verdict vocabulary is PASS / PASS-with-notes / BLOCK, with numbered findings and a concrete sequence of steps for each finding.
decisions.why: It gives a clean convergence test — a chunk converges when both auditors return PASS or PASS-with-notes on the same revision — and 'with-notes' lets an auditor pass without swallowing a real but non-blocking observation.
decisions.rulesOut: Supersedes the June 2026 process-audit proposal of BLOCKING PARTIAL / FULL SIGN-OFF / FULL SIGN-OFF FAILED statuses (EXTERNAL-AUDIT-PROCESS-AUDIT-GPT-CODEX-2026-06-05.md:49) — that taxonomy was never adopted in the Azure phase and appears in no current pack.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude / auditor-driven, in the pack template

decisions.what: ROLLOUT GATE: no store device — including franchisee stores — receives the app until ALL chunks are done and audited.
decisions.why: Written as a hard gate at the time to stop a partial rollout reaching stores before the server-side protections existed.
decisions.rulesOut: DANGER: this is still written in capitals as an absolute gate in three documents, none of which carry a supersession banner. A future reader could reasonably block the entire launch on it. It must not be treated as current.
decisions.supersededBy: CUT-2 and CUT-3 — the org-structure/wizard work and Contract 2 are both explicitly NOT built at launch, so 'all chunks done' can no longer be the gate

decisions.what: The backlog is re-sorted by RISK, not by chunk order. Staff are not technically inclined and are not a hostile-user threat, so SECURITY HARDENING may follow release — but DATA LEAKS, LOGIC/MONEY defects and FEATURE GAPS may NOT be deferred.
decisions.why: Six salons, known people, internal use only — there is no hostile user to defend against before launch. Meanwhile the security work (Account Access items 5-11, the correction route, most of the last month) has been blocking a queue of money and data-leak defects that need none of it. This inverts the old priority order.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out resuming the security-hardening work ahead of the money and data-leak queue; rules out deferring anything in the data-leak, money-logic or feature-gap categories on the grounds that it is 'not security'.
decisions.source: HANDOVER.md:12-26 and :166-168; and Kunal's ruling of 2026-08-01

decisions.what: A single living FEATURE + DECISION REGISTER is to be built and kept current, doubling as training material for staff and Head Office. It is being built BEFORE the Cockburn pricing work and the Southlands ownership work.
decisions.why: There are ~100 markdown files at the repo root and every one is a snapshot of a past moment, not a record of current truth. Kunal is not a developer and is tired of having to personally remember decisions made months ago. Decisions get silently re-litigated because nobody can find the reasoning. Building it first means the pricing and ownership work is done against a known state rather than a guess.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out continuing to record decisions only in per-wave snapshot documents; rules out starting the Cockburn pricing or Southlands ownership work first.
decisions.source: Kunal's ruling of 2026-08-01; the partial prior attempt is audit-artifacts/MASTER-DECISION-REGISTER.md (built 2026-07-30, and gitignored)

decisions.what: Before ANY server-side change is made, build a completely separate practice copy of the cloud (its own SharePoint list, its own copies of the Logic Apps) and do all development and testing there. Live is never the test bed.
decisions.why: Up to that point no audit had ever exercised the real cloud path, and there was no way to test a change to the way the app talks to SharePoint without risking the real stock ledger. A write-isolated sandbox lets a change be proven against the REAL plumbing (same connector, same field formats) rather than a mock that can drift.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'just try it on live and watch'. Rules out proving a server change with a mock or a local stub only — every chunk from 2 onward must show a real staging round-trip before it is called done.

decisions.what: On staging, only small functional tests are allowed — never load tests or bulk seeding.
decisions.why: The staging Logic Apps share ONE SharePoint connection with the live ones. Heavy seeding by an auditor can throttle that shared connection and cause real failures on the live app. Also, every auditor's test rows must be prefixed (gpt_ / agy_) because the staging lists enforce unique keys, so unprefixed ids surface as the other auditor's false 'duplicate'.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out asking an auditor to run a volume/performance test on staging. Rules out treating staging as fully isolated — it is isolated for DATA, not for capacity.

decisions.what: The columns the sync depends on must be indexed on a SharePoint list BEFORE that list grows past about 5,000 rows — indexes cannot be added afterwards. Only index columns that are actually filtered or sorted on server-side; every index costs write speed and there is a cap of about 20 per list.
decisions.why: SharePoint physically refuses to add an index once a list passes the threshold, so getting this wrong at list-creation time is permanent. This is the reason index planning is a named, tracked activity rather than an afterthought.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'we'll add the index when it starts to hurt'. Rules out indexing columns speculatively. Makes list creation ORDER a cutover-critical step.

decisions.what: Setting the 'indexed' flag through the Microsoft Graph API does NOT create a real, usable index — it only sets a cosmetic marker. A real index can only be built through SharePoint's own REST/admin path, and only while the list is still small.
decisions.why: Proven by test: a Graph-flagged list still choked past 5,000 rows, while a list indexed the proper way while empty returned results cleanly. The original Chunk-1 write-up claimed the Graph method worked and is still sitting in the repo under a 'done + verified' heading with no correction on it.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out using Graph to index the LIVE lists at cutover — it would look done and silently not be. Any future 'we indexed it' claim must say HOW.
decisions.supersededBy: AZURE-INDEX-MANIFEST.md:18 supersedes the original claim in AZURE-CHUNK1-INDEXING.md:13

decisions.what: Even a real index cannot page through a result set bigger than 5,000 rows. The only thing that can is walking the list by its built-in row number (the ID cursor). So the ledger download was rebuilt to page by row ID instead of by timestamp.
decisions.why: This is the architectural reason the whole pull-hardening upgrade exists. SharePoint throttles any query whose MATCHED set exceeds ~5,000 regardless of indexing, which meant a brand-new device, or a device that had been offline a long time, would simply be unable to catch up once the live ledger passed 5,000 rows. Row ID is the primary key, always ordered, always available, and needs no custom index.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'add more indexes' as the answer to scale. Rules out the old timestamp-based download cursor. Rules out any future server query designed to return more than 5,000 matching rows.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude + both auditors (Codex APPROVE-WITH-CONDITIONS, AGY APPROVE)

decisions.what: Four safety rules ride with the ID-cursor download: (1) each cycle freezes a top row number at the start so new rows arriving mid-download cannot extend the walk forever; (2) each cycle re-reads the last 100 rows it already had, because SharePoint can make row 101 visible before row 100 and a naive cursor would skip 100 forever; (3) the saved position only moves forward once EVERY page has been safely stored; (4) a page that does not move the position forward aborts the cycle rather than quietly advancing.
decisions.why: Each of these is a silent-data-loss hole found by an auditor. The 100-row look-back is deliberately tied to the push concurrency of 50 (it is 2x that) — raise the push concurrency or add a bulk writer without raising the look-back first and the download starts missing rows.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out changing push concurrency in isolation. Rules out any 'stop and advance' shortcut on a bad page.
decisions.whoDecided: auditor-driven (Codex Q1/Q4 + AGY #1), ratified after fixes

decisions.what: When the download switched to the new method, the server was built to accept BOTH the old and the new request shape, chosen automatically per request — not swapped over in one go.
decisions.why: An atomic swap would have trapped any device still running old cached code: it would send no row-id, the server would default to row 0, and the device would loop on page one forever, burning battery and Azure cost. The dual contract lets old devices keep working right through the cutover.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a same-URL hard cutover for any endpoint devices cache. Establishes the pattern for every later endpoint change.
decisions.whoDecided: auditor-driven (Codex P1 + AGY critical, the #1 blocker of that round)

decisions.what: Standing operational rule for the LIVE system: never edit or delete rows directly in the SharePoint list. Corrections must be made through the app, which appends a new row.
decisions.why: The download only ever walks forward by row number, so it can never see a change made to a row it has already passed. A direct edit or delete is invisible to every device that already synced past it. This is why deletions in the app are recorded as brand-new 'tombstone' rows rather than by removing anything.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out fixing a bad row by hand in SharePoint. Rules out any future cloud code that UPDATEs or DELETEs a StockTransactions row in place.

decisions.what: Every stock row arriving from a device is re-checked by the server against the same rules the app applies, before it is written. The cloud does not trust the device.
decisions.why: Before this, any device (or anyone who had extracted a sync URL) could write any quantity, any type, any store, any product — including deliberately hostile text — straight into the ledger with no check at all. Client-side checks are a convenience control only (the permanent P-13 rule), so the wall has to be on the server.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out relying on the app's own validation as the only gate. Rules out adding a new cloud write path without a matching server-side check.

decisions.what: The server must tell the truth about what it actually saved. It returns exactly which rows were accepted, which were duplicates, which were permanently rejected, and which failed temporarily — and it refuses the whole batch (saving nothing) if those four numbers do not add up to the number of rows sent.
decisions.why: The old server returned 'processed: N' where N was simply the number of rows SENT, not the number stored. A row that failed to insert was still reported as fine, the device marked it as synced, and the movement was silently lost forever. This was the single most dangerous gap found, and both auditors insisted it be fixed in the same change as the validation rather than after.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out any endpoint that returns a bare 'ok'. Every write endpoint built since (record steps, catalogue) reuses this same four-bucket honest contract — that is now the house standard.

decisions.what: A rejected row goes to a durable cloud quarantine list AND is reported back to the device, which keeps it, flags it to an admin, and stops trying to re-send it. Rejected is permanent; failed is retried.
decisions.why: Kunal's rule was 'quarantine, never silently drop'. Splitting permanent rejections from temporary failures matters: a genuinely bad row retried forever is a loop, and a temporary network failure treated as a permanent rejection is a lost movement. An auditor blocked the first version precisely because only the device-side half existed, with no durable cloud record.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out dropping a bad row. Rules out one undifferentiated 'error' bucket.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude + both auditors (AGY BLOCK on the missing cloud sink)

decisions.what: If the product/store catalogue cannot be read at all, the server skips only the catalogue check (and says so loudly in its reply); but if the catalogue loads and the store or product is genuinely unknown, the row is REJECTED.
decisions.why: A configuration hiccup must not block the entire ledger — but a real unknown store or product is exactly the thing the check exists to catch. Failing open on a real miss would silently disable the control forever with nobody noticing.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out blanket fail-open. Rules out blanket fail-closed on catalogue reads. Note the deliberate contrast with the auth check (C5-4), which fails CLOSED.

decisions.what: Duplicate protection moved from 'look first, then insert' to letting SharePoint itself enforce that the transaction id is unique, and treating its rejection as 'already saved'.
decisions.why: The old check-then-insert had a race (two devices could both check, both find nothing, both insert) and did one extra database lookup per row at 50-at-a-time, risking throttling. Letting the database enforce uniqueness is atomic and removes both problems at once. Folded into Chunk 2 rather than kept separate because it is the same code path.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out GET-then-insert dedup anywhere. Carries a hard precondition: the live list must be proven free of duplicate/blank transaction ids BEFORE the unique constraint is switched on (see open questions).

decisions.what: Logic Apps have no pattern-matching (no regex), so the server's id safety check was rebuilt out of plain string operations that produce EXACTLY the same allowed characters as the app's own rule. No separate Azure Function was added for this.
decisions.why: A looser server rule would accept ids like 'abc.def' that the app itself would quarantine on the way back down — the server and the app would disagree, which is just a different flavour of silent data loss. The server must reject every id the app would. Eight specific 'not dangerous but client-unsafe' ids were made a formal acceptance bar to prove the equivalence.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a narrow 'block the dangerous characters' list. Rules out adding a Function to Chunk 2. Any future server-side id check must match the app's rule exactly, not approximately.

decisions.what: Chunk 2 checks the SHAPE of data only. Who is allowed to write what (roles, stores, permissions) was deliberately kept out and pushed to Chunk 5.
decisions.why: Mixing shape validation with permission checks in one Logic App would have made both harder to reason about and audit. Keeping the boundary explicit also stopped anyone describing Chunk 2 as 'securing' the push, which it does not — it stops malformed data, not a hostile authorised device.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out describing ingest validation as a security control. Rules out sneaking permission logic into the validation workflow.

decisions.what: There is no standalone Chunk 3. The double-receive problem was folded into Chunk 4. And the business rule was locked: if two devices receive the same transfer with the SAME quantity, it is silently de-duplicated; if they receive it with DIFFERENT quantities, it becomes a conflict that a Director must resolve by choosing which count is correct.
decisions.why: Kunal explicitly rejected 'whichever device syncs first wins', which was the engineering lean. A genuine disagreement about how much stock arrived is a business question, not a race to be settled by network timing. Making the Director choose needs cross-device record visibility and a resolution screen — which is exactly what Chunk 4 was building, so the two had to be built together.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out first-sync-wins on receive quantities. Rules out building receive-idempotency as a standalone piece. Note: the old Q1-Q6 'leans' further down that same file, including the first-sync-wins lean at line 37, are now overruled and should not be read as live.

decisions.what: Transfers, deliveries and stock-takes sync between devices as an append-only list of LIFE-EVENTS ('sent', 'received', 'flagged', 'resolved', 'counted', 'approved'), each one a permanent entry that is never edited. Each device replays those entries to rebuild the full record. One generic list for all three types — not a separate list per type, and not a mutable record that gets overwritten.
decisions.why: Records mutate through their life, which is the opposite of the stock ledger. Storing them as mutable blobs means two offline devices overwrite each other and there is no way to tell who was right. Making every step its own permanent entry removes the 'who overwrote whom' race entirely and reuses the sync machinery already proven on the ledger. Both auditors independently converged on a generic list; one picked append-only outright and the other called it 'more correct'.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out one SharePoint list per record type (about 3x the build, plus schema churn). Rules out last-writer-wins on a whole-record blob. Rules out editing a synced record in place.
decisions.whoDecided: Kunal, after GPT + AGY architectural review

decisions.what: Stock numbers and record details are TWO SEPARATE streams. A record step never adds or removes stock — the stock effect always rides the existing ledger. They are linked by the transfer/record id.
decisions.why: This is the core safety invariant of the whole design. It means the new metadata stream physically cannot corrupt stock counts, and the proven ledger sync and validation are reused unchanged. Both auditors endorsed it as safer than putting lifecycle information into the stock ledger.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out ever computing stock from record steps. Rules out putting quantities in a step that the app would then trust.

decisions.what: Two different anti-duplicate keys doing two different jobs: the LEDGER key is fixed per transfer+store+product so a second receive can never double the stock; the STEP key deliberately includes a per-attempt marker so BOTH devices' receives survive and the disagreement stays visible. The attempt marker is created once and stored, so a crash-and-retry on the same device replays the same key rather than inventing a phantom second receive.
decisions.why: If both keys were fixed, the second receive would vanish and the quantity disagreement would be invisible — the exact thing Kunal decided must reach a Director. If the step key were a fresh random each time, one device tapping receive twice after a crash would look like two different people disagreeing. Both auditors changed the original design specifically to make the attempt marker stable and persisted.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a single shared idempotency key. Rules out a fresh random key per tap. Rules out keying on device id alone.

decisions.what: A record must never show a stock effect that did not actually land. The stock rows are sent FIRST and the matching record step is held back until those rows are confirmed saved; each step carries the list of ledger rows it expects, and shows as 'stock pending' or 'stock mismatch' until they are confirmed present.
decisions.why: This was the #1 gap both auditors flagged: a 'received' transfer whose stock rows had been rejected by validation would show a green tick to staff while the stock never moved. The first build got this half-right — it computed the state but still displayed the record as completed — and an auditor blocked it.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out sending a record step before its stock. Rules out showing a completed record on unconfirmed stock.

decisions.what: A transfer DRAFT is private to the device that made it and never syncs. The first thing other devices see is the 'submit' — the moment the transfer is actually sent.
decisions.why: Drafts are work-in-progress; propagating half-finished ones would be noise, and it matches the existing model where stock is deducted on submit, not on draft.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out cross-device draft collaboration on transfers.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude (realised in code, flagged to auditors)

decisions.what: Old records already sitting on devices are pushed up automatically, once, the first time the new code runs — never behind a button a person has to remember to press. If two devices hold genuinely different versions of the same record, that is flagged as a conflict, not silently resolved by whoever got there first.
decisions.why: Kunal's reasoning on the button was blunt: 'no one will remember'. There is no real production data yet, so at launch this is effectively a no-op — the machinery exists as a safety net so no record on a device is ever stranded. The conflict-not-first-writer-wins half was an auditor requirement, and the first build got it wrong (it deduplicated on the id and never compared the contents) until an auditor caught it.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a manual 'upload my old records' button. Rules out silent first-writer-wins on divergent history.

decisions.what: The server checks the OUTSIDE of a record step (safe ids, known record and step types, size limits, and — new for deliveries — that money values are sane, positive, capped and to 2 decimal places). It does NOT re-implement the app's business rules on the inside of the step.
decisions.why: The server is a shape and safety backstop, not a second copy of the app. Over-validating the inside would reject legitimate shapes as the app evolves, and Logic Apps have no pattern matching anyway. Delivery money is the first money to reach the cloud, which is why the money check that was deliberately deferred from Chunk 2 lands here. Kunal chose to do the money check in a small Azure Function rather than in the Logic App.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out full domain re-validation server-side. Note the money check FAILS OPEN if the Function is unreachable (the app's own check is the backstop) — deliberately the opposite of the auth check.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude + auditors (D4-G, D4-K); Function choice by Kunal

decisions.what: New delivery and stock-take ids get a random suffix so two devices can never mint the same id. Existing local ids are left alone.
decisions.why: Delivery and stock-take ids were plain millisecond timestamps. The moment those records started syncing, two devices creating a record in the same millisecond would collide and one record would overwrite the other. Rewriting existing ids was rejected because it would break their links to ledger rows.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out timestamp-only ids for anything that syncs. Rules out retroactively renumbering existing records.

decisions.what: The two empty 'Transfers' and 'StockTakes' SharePoint lists left over from an earlier attempt are to be DELETED unused at phase cleanup, along with the dead V1 Logic Apps and a stray duplicate column — not repurposed.
decisions.why: They were scaffolded with a mutable-blob shape that the append-only design explicitly rejected, and were never wired to anything. Deleting them only after cutover verification and after confirming zero live references was an auditor condition.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out reusing those lists. NOTE: the index manifest (AZURE-INDEX-MANIFEST.md:26) still says they will be 'replaced/repurposed' — that line is stale and contradicts this decision.

decisions.what: Three kinds of key: one per store (held by that store's devices), the head-office key, and a DIRECTOR key held only by Kunal and Shahin on their four personal devices. The Director key works on its own and covers every store — a Director device holds no store key at all.
decisions.why: Kunal rejected the earlier shortcut of treating head-office devices as if they were Directors: head-office staff must NOT be able to perform Director actions. Directors work from personal devices across all stores, which matches the app's existing director role, so tying the Director key to one store would fight the real workflow (both auditors agreed). Accepted risk, written down: Kunal and Shahin SHARE the key, so a leak means full write control of every store until it is rotated, and there is no way to tell which of the two acted.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'head office device = Director'. Rules out binding the Director key to a store. Rules out Microsoft/Entra logins for this generation of the app (cost, shared store logins, offline-first). Rules out per-device registration for now — kept as a documented later upgrade on the same wire format.
decisions.whoDecided: Kunal (rejecting the round-1 design), ratified by both auditors

decisions.what: The server never stores a key. It stores a scrambled fingerprint of it, made with a per-row random value plus one secret 'pepper' that lives ONLY in the Azure Function's settings — never in SharePoint, never in the app, never in the repo. Rotation mints a new version and keeps accepting the old one until a grace date so offline devices are not locked out.
decisions.why: If the credential list itself leaks, the keys must still be useless. Keeping the pepper out of SharePoint means reading the whole credential list is not enough to forge anything. Dual-accept rotation from day one was an auditor requirement — without it, rotating a key strands any device that was offline at the time along with its unsynced movements.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out storing keys anywhere in readable form. Rules out a hard rotation cut-off with no grace window.

decisions.what: A named list of operations requires the Director key, not just a store key: stock adjustments (including stock-take approvals), recording or editing deliveries, approving/rejecting stock-takes, resolving or cancelling transfers, and cost changes. Ordinary movement deletion is deliberately NOT on the list.
decisions.why: These are the operations that move money or override someone else's count. Everything else only needs the store key, so day-to-day staff work is unaffected. Future cloud writes are born Director-gated by default: catalogue publishing, user management, supplier admin and pricing.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a store device performing a Director action. Rules out inferring 'this is a delivery' from free-text notes — delivery gating goes structurally through the record-step link, never through reading a reason field.
decisions.whoDecided: Kunal + both auditors (D2c, after a GPT counter and two amendments)

decisions.what: Key checking is done in one batched call to the Azure Function, which returns only yes/no and never any fingerprint material. If any required key is wrong — or the checking service is unreachable — the request is REFUSED.
decisions.why: Deliberately the opposite of the money check, which fails open. Money has a backstop in the app; authentication IS the wall, so 'we couldn't check' must mean 'no'. Batched into one call because a request can present two keys and two sequential calls would double the latency and cost and create awkward half-failures. It was proven by pulling the pepper out live and confirming the push then returned 401.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out fail-open on auth. Rules out the server ever handing back hash material (which would make it a password-guessing oracle). Rules out per-credential sequential verify calls.
