decisions.what: Checking an overall rule about a group of rows is NOT a substitute for checking each individual row that a request points at. The transfer gate had to be rebuilt to look up EVERY ledger row a step references and confirm each one belongs to that transfer and to one of its two stores.
decisions.why: The first fix checked only rows already TAGGED with the transfer id. An auditor then smuggled in an UNTAGGED foreign row and had it accepted — the same hole a second time. This is the single most repeated lesson on this project: an aggregate invariant misses anything outside the grouping key. A genuinely missing row is treated as 'try again later', never as 'fine'.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out satisfying a per-item requirement with a grouped check. Rules out treating a missing referenced row as confirmation.
decisions.whoDecided: auditor-driven (GPT blocked twice on the same fix family), ground-truthed and fixed by Claude

decisions.what: Authentication was rolled out in two phases: first the server ADVERTISES that keys will be required and devices ship the ability to send them; only at the final cutover does the server start enforcing. Every refusal returns a self-explaining message so even an old cached copy of the app can tell the user why.
decisions.why: The bootstrap paradox — if you turn enforcement on before every device has a key, every device is locked out at once with no way to be told why. An auditor raised this as a counter in round 1 and it was adopted.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out flipping enforcement on in one step. Rules out a bare 401 with no explanation.

decisions.what: The keys travel inside the request body, not in an HTTP header as the written spec said.
decisions.why: A custom header triggers an extra browser pre-flight request whose handling in Logic Apps is a deployment risk; body fields avoid it entirely and the whole body is already hidden from the run history. Functionally the same gate. Both auditors reviewed and accepted the deviation.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out anyone 'correcting' the code back to a header on the strength of the spec. The scope document still says header and has no correction banner on it.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude (build deviation), accepted by both auditors
decisions.supersededBy: AZURE-CHUNK5-WAVE-REVIEW.md:50-52 supersedes the header wording in AZURE-CHUNK5-SCOPE.md

decisions.what: Chunk 5 gives every authenticated store the ability to read the WHOLE company ledger. Real row-level privacy between stores was scheduled as Chunk 10, which has since been built and converged.
decisions.why: The caveat was accepted at the time on the explicit condition that it was scheduled as a launch blocker, not left open-ended — franchisees exist before launch, so 'one compromised store key can read the whole ledger' could not be allowed to survive to release.
decisions.rulesOut: The Chunk-5 scope AND the Chunk-5 wave review both still present the whole-ledger-read caveat and the single-store write rule as current, with no forward pointer. Do not quote either as today's behaviour.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude + auditors (D4), superseded by the Chunk 10 build
decisions.supersededBy: Chunk 10 store isolation (converged 2026-07-09)

decisions.what: Real rate limiting was deferred from Chunk 5 to Chunk 7. Chunk 7 was then built and shipped with no rate-limiting item in it at all.
decisions.why: The deferral was agreed by both auditors on the basis that batch size caps and reject logging would hold in the meantime. The target chunk then silently evaporated — this is a decision that lost its landing place rather than one that was reversed.
decisions.rulesOut: Nothing yet — that is the problem. It is neither built nor formally accepted.
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK5-SCOPE.md:107, :211 vs AZURE-CHUNK7-SCOPE.md and AZURE-CHUNK7-WAVE-REVIEW.md (zero mentions — verified by search)

decisions.what: Original rule: no store device, including franchisee stores, receives the app until every chunk 5 through 10 is finished and audited.
decisions.why: Set when the security chunks were the critical path and the intent was one single safe cutover. It has since been overtaken: on 2026-07-29 Kunal split the franchise wizard out of the cutover and parked the Contract-2 correction route as its own later deploy, and on 2026-08-01 he re-sorted the backlog BY RISK — security hardening may follow release, but data leaks, money/logic defects and feature gaps may not be deferred.
decisions.rulesOut: No longer rules anything out — but the absolute wording still sits in the Chunk-5 scope with no banner, and reads as a live launch gate.
decisions.supersededBy: HANDOVER.md:505-512 (wizard split out) and the 2026-08-01 risk-sorted backlog decision

decisions.what: Catalogue changes reach the stores when a Director presses a 'Review & Publish' button — not automatically on every edit. The screen shows how many unpublished changes there are, a preview of exactly what will change, and when it was last published.
decisions.why: Kunal is the main editor and edits are infrequent. Auto-publish would push a mistyped price company-wide the instant it was typed. 'Make my changes, then publish' matches how the work is actually done. Auto-publish stays available as a later change if the button becomes a nuisance.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out publish-on-every-keystroke. Rules out publishing without a preview.
decisions.whoDecided: Kunal (Claude lean, both auditors agreed) — D3

decisions.what: A publish sends ONLY the rows that actually changed, each stamped with the version it was based on. The server merges them one row at a time and rejects a row whose server copy has moved on since. Publishing a full snapshot of the local catalogue is forbidden.
decisions.why: Merging by id alone still loses data two ways: two publishes reading the same starting point both write the whole file and one wins; and a device publishing its FULL local snapshot silently overwrites rows it never touched but which someone else has since updated. An auditor then proved a worse version of this live — a publish that was correctly REJECTED by the server still reported the row as 'accepted', so the app cleared it and the edit vanished. The fix retries the read-merge-write until it genuinely lands and reports success only after it has persisted.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out whole-blob replacement. Rules out trusting an 'accepted' list that was produced before the write persisted.
decisions.whoDecided: auditor-driven (GPT, the stronger of the two), adopted + hardened after a P1 block

decisions.what: THE COST STRIP. What BOB pays for a product is removed entirely from the shared catalogue that everyone receives. Cost is served through a separate, guarded channel available only to Directors and to corporate (company-owned) stores. A franchisee's device never receives it and keeps its own cost, which the franchisee enters themselves.
decisions.why: Kunal's business rule is that a franchisee's cost is genuinely different — they buy at the price head office charges them — so one company-wide cost is simply wrong for them and must never overwrite theirs. But BOTH auditors countered the original plan of 'send the cost and have franchisee devices ignore it': that is a privacy LEAK, because a franchisee can read the shared file directly and extract BOB's costs and margins. The rule that came out of it is now a general principle on this project: security and privacy rules must be enforced by the server; a client-side 'ignore' is not enforcement. A related hole was found and closed in the same round — the config endpoint was quietly handing the whole cost file to a franchise key.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out putting cost in the shared catalogue at all. Rules out client-side 'ignore the field' as a privacy control. Also fixes what happens when a store changes hands: corporate-to-franchise stops central cost and prompts a local cost review; franchise-to-corporate starts receiving it.
decisions.whoDecided: Kunal (business rule) + both auditors (COUNTER on the mechanism), adopted

decisions.what: Only the Director key may publish catalogue changes to the cloud. Widening it to the head-office store key later is a small, reversible, one-endpoint change with no data migration.
decisions.why: The two auditors split on this. The deciding factor was who actually does product data entry: if it is Kunal and Shahin, Director-only is fine; if it is warehouse staff, they need a path. Kunal chose to start tight. The trade-off written down: head-office-originated catalogue edits stay local and unpublished until a Director re-enters and publishes them.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a store key publishing catalogue changes. WARNING: the same file at :139-149 still presents this as 'the one OPEN decision for Kunal' — it is decided; the open version is stale.

decisions.what: The catalogue version number is owned by the server and only ever goes up. A device may never set it.
decisions.why: It is the signal every device uses to decide whether to take a new catalogue. If a device could mint it, one bad device could either freeze everyone's catalogue or force endless re-downloads.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out client-supplied version numbers on any published payload.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, stated to auditors (D-VERSION), no dissent

decisions.what: The rule 'you cannot deactivate a product or category that still has stock' stays enforced in the app only, NOT on the server.
decisions.why: Deliberately owned and documented. It is a tidiness rule, not a security rule: the only person who could bypass it is a trusted Director using developer tools, the effect (hiding something) is reversible and loses no data, and enforcing it server-side would mean summing the whole ledger on every publish — a permanent runtime cost on a shared connection for negligible benefit. The principle it established: security and privacy rules MUST be server-side; a Director-only, reversible tidiness rule may be client-side. Flagged for revisit only if per-account permissions let less-trusted roles deactivate.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out re-raising this as a server-side gap. Gives a written test for where a rule belongs. The revisit trigger (Chunk 9 per-account auth) has now happened — see open questions.
decisions.whoDecided: Kunal + Claude, after a GPT counter; both auditors accepted

decisions.what: Chunk 7 splits in two: the app-side hardening and small carried code items were built now; ALL secret rotation and relocation (deploy token, function secrets to Key Vault, rotating the sync URLs) was deferred to a single security pass executed as the last step before the live cutover.
decisions.why: You rotate a secret AT the boundary you are protecting against — right before the app leaves single-owner alpha. Everything was on staging and uncommitted, so rotating early would just mean rotating again at cutover. Kunal specifically chose to include the deploy token in the deferred pass rather than doing it early, accepting that it sits in the private repo until then.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out ad-hoc secret rotation mid-build. Creates a hard dependency: the cutover security checklist MUST be executed, or none of it happens.

decisions.what: Chart.js, Dexie and the three Google fonts were downloaded into the app itself, and the browser security policy was tightened to drop all three outside internet addresses. Inline scripts and inline styles were deliberately KEPT allowed.
decisions.why: Removing outside dependencies removes a whole class of supply-chain risk and makes the app fully self-contained. But both auditors countered the original plan to go fully strict: the app uses inline scripts, inline onclick handlers and inline styles throughout, so a strict policy would simply break the rendering. A proper nonce-based policy is a separate future refactor, not this chunk. Both auditors byte-verified the downloaded copies against the originals.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out loading anything from a third-party address. Rules out an auditor flagging 'unsafe-inline' as an unowned finding — it is a documented, both-auditor-endorsed decision.
decisions.whoDecided: Kunal (D7-3) + both auditors (COUNTER on keeping inline)

decisions.what: Only the Latin character set of the fonts was bundled — 10 files instead of Google's 54.
decisions.why: Appropriate for a Western Australian English app. But both auditors banked a launch-gating condition: if ANY staff member, store or product name uses non-Latin characters, the font set must be regenerated before launch or those names will not render properly.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out adding a non-Latin name without regenerating the fonts. This is a launch condition hiding inside what looks like a cosmetic choice.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, condition added by both auditors

decisions.what: Categories and product types can no longer be hard-deleted. 'Delete' now means 'deactivate' — the row stays, publishes normally, disappears from the pick-lists for new items, but its label still shows on historical records that point at it. The server refuses to attach a new product to a deactivated category.
decisions.why: Hard deletes never propagated to other devices at all (the sync only ever adds or updates, it never removes), so a category deleted on the office PC lived on forever on every store phone. Converting delete to deactivate makes the change actually travel. Keeping the label visible means old records do not suddenly display blanks.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out hard deletion of catalogue reference data. Rules out expecting a removal to sync.
decisions.whoDecided: Kunal (D7-4, both auditors agreed) + GPT's inactive-semantics detail

decisions.what: On top of checking that a referenced stock row belongs to the right transfer and store, the server now also checks that the row is the right KIND for that step (a 'submit' may only point at a transfer-out, a 'receive' at a transfer-in, and so on).
decisions.why: Carried forward from the Chunk-5 audit as agreed hardening. The original shorthand for this map was wrong — a legitimate resolve ALSO produces transfer-in rows for flagged settlements and returns, not only adjustments. Both auditors corrected it against the actual code before it was built.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a context-correct but semantically wrong row being accepted.
decisions.whoDecided: auditor-driven (both, carried from the C5 review)

decisions.what: Ledger archival is BUILT NOW and ships in the single cutover — Kunal overruled the engineering recommendation to design it now and build it later.
decisions.why: Claude's lean was to design it, get it audit-approved, then prioritise the two real pre-launch blockers and build archival later as an add-on, because the growth ceiling was months away. Kunal chose to have everything done and audited before launch in one deploy rather than a string of later deploys.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating archival as post-launch work. Note: the growth reasoning that framed the urgency is now void — the app is not in use and nobody is logging transactions (HANDOVER.md:528-535) — but the build-now decision stands and the work is done.
decisions.whoDecided: Kunal (D8-0, choosing Option A over Claude's lean B)

decisions.what: You can never simply delete old movements, because stock is the SUM of every movement ever made. Old movements are only removed after their balance has been captured in an immutable snapshot: work out the balance per store and product, prove it, save it, copy the movements to an archive list, verify the copy, and only then remove them from the live list.
decisions.why: This is the founding invariant of the whole chunk. Deleting a movement without snapshotting first silently changes the stock number. Everything else in Chunk 8 exists to make that sequence provably safe.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out ever pruning the ledger by date or age alone. Rules out storing a current stock level anywhere as the authority.

decisions.what: THE CRUX: the archival cut-off point is the SharePoint row number, not a business date. A movement that was entered late or offline for an old date gets a NEW higher row number, so it lands on the 'keep' side and is counted — never silently swallowed by the archive.
decisions.why: Both auditors independently identified date-based cut-off as a data-loss bug. A movement dated last month but synced today would fall on the archived side of a date boundary, after the snapshot had already been computed without it — the stock would be quietly wrong and there would be no trace. Row numbers only ever go up, so a late arrival can never fall behind the line. The business date is still kept on the row for reporting.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out any date-based archival boundary. This decision is cited BY LINE NUMBER from the org-structure work, so editing above line 87 of the Chunk-8 scope silently breaks that reference.
decisions.whoDecided: auditor-driven (both raised it; the crux fix), adopted

decisions.what: Archiving runs when the live ledger reaches about 5,000 rows OR six months have passed, whichever comes FIRST. Archived movements move to a separate archive list, not a flag on the existing one.
decisions.why: Kunal picked a hybrid over both auditors' suggestions (one wanted annual, the other a rolling 12 months). The 5,000 trigger is the SharePoint threshold itself, so it is a genuine safety valve that self-paces to how busy the business is; the six-month cap gives a predictable rhythm aligned to end-of-financial-year reporting. LOAD-BEARING: the 5,000 trigger is the only thing keeping the archive run's single-page read safe — the run reads at most 5,000 rows in one go and refuses if there are more. Paging past that was documented but never built.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out relaxing the cadence without first building paging into the archive run. Rules out an archived-flag-on-the-same-list design.

decisions.what: A device must NEVER see a half-finished archive run — an old snapshot alongside a shrunk live ledger would show wrong stock. The run holds a lock, and the new snapshot version is published LAST, after the archive copy is durable and verified.
decisions.why: Both auditors independently rated this the highest severity item in the chunk. A device catching the system mid-run would compute stock from a snapshot that does not cover the rows that have already been removed.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out publishing the snapshot before the archive is verified. Rules out running archival without a lock.

decisions.what: Before anything is archived, the run must prove it changes no stock number: every store-and-product pair must add up identically before and after (including products with no recent movement), and the archive copy must match the source by both count and content fingerprint. On ANY mismatch it publishes nothing, archives nothing and leaves the live ledger untouched. A device with unsynced local movements does not switch to the snapshot until they have drained.
decisions.why: Kunal's top stated priority is robustness. An auditor countered the original migration gate as 'too thin' — balance-neutrality alone was not enough without freezing writes, covering zero-movement products, and hashing both copies. A later round found the hash proved only that the same ROWS were there, not that their CONTENTS were intact, and it was upgraded to a content hash that the run re-reads and re-checks before it publishes or deletes anything.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out an archive run that 'mostly' balances. Rules out identity-only verification.
decisions.whoDecided: auditor-driven (GPT COUNTER on D8-5, then GPT-2 at the code audit)

decisions.what: Any report whose date range reaches back into archived history must either load the archive or refuse with a clear 'archive required' message. It must never quietly return a smaller number. When a Director does load the archive, those rows are spliced into the working data so EVERY report and export sees them, rather than each report being wired up individually.
decisions.why: Kunal's requirement was explicit: reports and charts — including the end-of-financial-year report that spans the archive boundary — must stay available. A silent under-count in a sales or wastage report is worse than an error message, because nobody notices. An auditor then found that about ten report and CSV paths read the raw data directly and would have bypassed any per-report wiring, so the overlay approach was adopted instead.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a silent under-count. Rules out wiring archive awareness report-by-report.
decisions.whoDecided: Kunal (requirement) + both auditors (fail-closed, P1) + AGY-2 fix

decisions.what: Archiving touches the stock ledger ONLY. A completed old transfer whose stock rows have been archived must still show as confirmed, not regress to 'stock pending'. Whether an archived row counts as confirmed is decided by a real per-row archive index, not by comparing dates.
decisions.why: Without this, archiving would make every old completed transfer suddenly look unfinished. The first build used a date shortcut — if the step was older than the cut-off, assume its rows were archived — and an auditor showed this falsely cleared rows that had NEVER landed, breaking the Chunk-4 guarantee that a record never claims a stock effect that did not happen. This is the same aggregate-instead-of-per-item trap as C5-5, one chunk later.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a date heuristic standing in for per-row proof. Rules out archiving record steps alongside ledger rows.
decisions.whoDecided: auditor-driven (both, P1; then GPT-1 at the code audit)

decisions.what: Uniqueness of transaction ids must be checked across BOTH the live and the archive lists. A movement that has already been folded into a published snapshot can no longer be deleted in the app. Accepted residual, written down: a deletion arriving in a LATER archive cycle for an already-snapshotted movement cannot retroactively correct that snapshot — this is managed by habit (do not delete long-archived movements) rather than by code.
decisions.why: Once a movement is inside a snapshot balance, deleting it would need the snapshot recomputed, which is not something a store device can do. Blocking the delete is honest; allowing it would create a phantom deletion that changes nothing. The residual is money-affecting and is recorded in exactly one place, in a document that has no external-audit section on it.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out checking uniqueness against the live list alone. Rules out deleting an archived movement through the app.
decisions.whoDecided: auditor-driven (both, P1; AGY-3 for the delete block)
decisions.when: 2026-07-06, delete-block added at the code audit

decisions.what: Reading archived movements requires either the Director key or the head-office store key. A franchisee cannot pull other stores' archived history.
decisions.why: The archive carries every store's historical movements in one place, so it is exactly the kind of thing store-level privacy is meant to protect. Restricting it to Director/head-office was the interim gate; proper franchise scoping over the archive was noted as a Chunk-10 concern.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a franchise store key reading the archive.

decisions.what: Logins belong to a ROLE AND A PLACE, not to a person. Each store gets two accounts — a shared shop-floor account and a store-manager account — plus territory manager, franchisee, Head Office and Director accounts. Around 15-40 accounts in total. Staff still TYPE their name on each movement, but that name is a label, not a login.
decisions.why: Staff cannot be logging in and out all day on a shared shop-floor device, and Kunal did not want to administer a password for every individual. Accountability comes from the append-only movement history, not from personal passwords.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out individual staff logins and any per-person staff directory. Rules out ever claiming in a report or an audit that 'person X personally did this' — the honest wording is 'authenticated as account X from device/store Y'. Also rules out designs that need a device to hold a roster of people (it only ever needs its own one account).

decisions.what: Staff accounts stay app-managed. No Microsoft 365 / Entra / MSAL logins for the Stock App.
decisions.why: Kunal's hard constraint: no per-user licences, no new monthly cost. The existing Function + Logic App + SharePoint plumbing can do server-side password checking for free.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'just use Microsoft logins' as an answer to any future auth problem — including single sign-on, Microsoft-hosted password resets, and email/SMS reset infrastructure.

decisions.what: Two separate locks, both of which must open for a sensitive action: the DEVICE must be an authorised device (Chunk 5 key), AND the PERSON must be a verified account (Chunk 9 proof).
decisions.why: A device key alone cannot tell Kunal apart from a staff member holding Kunal's unlocked phone. A person login alone would leave an unknown device talking to the cloud. Keeping both means a stolen password is useless without an authorised device and vice-versa.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out replacing the device keys with a person login, and rules out treating a person login on its own as authorisation. It is also why the store-scoping in Chunk 10 could be hung on the device credential rather than on the person.

decisions.what: The password travels only twice: when you log in, and when the app re-asks for it before a sensitive action. After that the server hands back a short-lived signed 'pass' (12 hours for a session, 5 minutes for a specific sensitive action) and it is the pass, not the password, that rides along with each request.
decisions.why: Sending the password with every sensitive request means it sits in memory and in more places than necessary. A short-lived pass, tied to the device it was issued on, cannot be replayed from another device and dies instantly when a password is reset.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the original design of attaching the password to each sensitive request. Rules out long-lived tokens, cross-device reuse of a pass, and any grace period after a password change.
decisions.whoDecided: Codex audit finding, adopted by Kunal

decisions.what: The person check applies ONLY to the admin actions that already need internet — publishing the catalogue, reading corporate costs, running or pulling the archive, and user administration. Everyday shop-floor work (logging stock in and out, receiving, counting) needs the device key only. User administration is Director-only; Head Office can look but not change.
decisions.why: The app is offline-first and staff must be able to work with no signal. The sensitive actions were already online-only, so requiring a cloud person-check there costs nothing operationally.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out putting person authentication in front of everyday stock movements — that would break offline working, which is non-negotiable. Rules out Head Office creating or resetting accounts.

decisions.what: The staff/account list is delivered privately and trimmed to what each device needs. Director and Head Office devices see all active accounts; a store or franchise device sees only accounts connected to its own store. It is never published in the open catalogue payload that every device downloads.
decisions.why: Both external auditors independently rejected the original plan (publish the directory inside the shared catalogue) as a privacy leak — a franchise device would learn every other store's staff and roles.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out putting the account list into the shared master_data catalogue. Rules out any design that needs a full company account list on a store device.

decisions.what: Five wrong passwords locks the account for 15 minutes, then 30, 60, 120. A Director can unlock early. Crucially, a lockout must be VISIBLE: the user-admin screen shows who is locked and how many failures, and one email goes out per lockout event (not per attempt).
decisions.why: Kunal: 'I need to know this has happened to someone, so if it is malicious I can do something about it.' A silent lockout tells him nothing.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out silent lockouts, and rules out an email per failed attempt (which would let someone email-bomb the business by typing wrong passwords in a loop).

decisions.what: The device is checked FIRST, and a failed password only counts against an account if the device was entitled to try that account in the first place. A store device can only attempt its own store's account or its own users — it can never reach a Director account, so it can never lock Kunal out. Directors themselves can still be locked (a stolen Director device gets five tries). If BOTH Directors are locked, the recovery is a manual SharePoint edit using the Microsoft 365 admin account.
decisions.why: Without this, anyone holding any store device could deliberately lock the owner out of his own admin screens by spamming wrong passwords. Fixing it with a blanket 'Directors never lock' would have handed a stolen Director device unlimited guesses. Checking the device first solves both.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a Director exemption from lockout. Rules out counting failed attempts before the device has been authenticated.
decisions.whoDecided: Auditor-driven (Antigravity + Codex), reconciled; the internal deep audit then found it had NOT actually been built and fixed it

decisions.what: Kunal sets and keeps every password. No self-service password choosing, no forced password change on first login. Minimum length 8, or 10 for the two Director accounts. Auditors are told to treat 'the owner knows all passwords' as an accepted business decision, not a finding.
decisions.why: Kunal's words: 'I always know everyone's passwords.' It is a small business with shared shop-floor devices; recovering a forgotten staff password must not need infrastructure.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out self-service resets, must-change-on-first-login flows, and email/SMS reset plumbing. Rules out any audit report claiming password secrecy from the Directors, or claiming personal non-repudiation.

decisions.what: The PIN is left exactly as it was — the 10-minute idle unlock and the 24-hour stock-take code both stay. Instead, the app re-asks for the PASSWORD (checked by the server) immediately before the most sensitive actions: publishing the catalogue, running the archive, user administration, and backup export/import.
decisions.why: The only PIN flow actually used in the business is the 24-hour stock-take code that covers a manager being away, and it already works. Redesigning it would have been churn. The walk-away risk it used to carry is now covered by the password re-prompt instead.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a PIN redesign in Chunk 9, and rules out using the PIN to gate anything sensitive.
decisions.supersededBy: AA-PIN-SERVER (the Account Access chunk turns the 24h PIN into a server-issued grant, adds PIN-to-receive, and makes 'Clear PIN' an instant kill switch)

decisions.what: The 24-hour PIN stops being a local check on the device and becomes a grant issued by the server: entering the PIN gets a signed, time-limited permission that the cloud itself recognises. It lifts exactly two things — running a stock take and receiving Head Office transfers. Clearing or changing the PIN instantly kills every grant already out there.
decisions.why: The PIN as built was a hash comparison inside the browser, so it protected nothing against a tampered device, and it granted stock-take only — not the receive-transfer behaviour Kunal asked for. Making it a server grant is the only way the cloud can honour or refuse it.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the browser-only PIN check, and rules out letting a shop-floor account receive Head Office transfers without a PIN. Also rules out grants that outlive a cleared PIN (Kunal chose instant kill over letting them expire).

decisions.what: For offline login the device keeps a separate, deliberately slow-to-crack local check value (PBKDF2, 210,000 rounds, a random salt unique to that device). The real cloud password hash never leaves SharePoint. If the local value is deleted there is no fallback — you must be online to log in again — and it is stripped out of every backup file.
decisions.why: A stolen device or backup must not hand over anything that works against the cloud. A separate device-local value means the worst case is a slow, device-specific crack, not access to the account.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out storing the cloud password hash on the device, rules out a weaker 'just let them in' fallback when the local value is missing, and rules out backups carrying login material.

decisions.what: Chunk 9 was shipped ASLEEP: the two new cloud addresses are deliberately missing from the app's configuration, so the app still uses the old local login. But catalogue publishing and archiving ALREADY demand the new pass. So at switch-on, the app and the configuration must be flipped in the same moment.
decisions.why: Shipping it dormant meant nothing could break before it was proven. The catch is the half-and-half state: turn on one side without the other and catalogue publishing stops working.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out enabling either half on its own, and rules out treating the Chunk 9 switch-on as a low-risk config tweak.

decisions.what: Stock-take approval and discrepancy resolution should eventually happen ON THE SERVER, not in the browser. Kunal: 'I ultimately don't want anything in the browser that is not in the cloud.' Deferred out of Chunk 9, but recorded as a genuine commitment, not a nice-to-have.
decisions.why: Today a tampered device could in principle write the underlying approval rows itself. Moving the write server-side is the only real fix; it was too big for Chunk 9.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out closing this out as 'accepted risk' — Kunal explicitly asked for it to stay on the books.

decisions.what: Director-only stock actions (approving a stock take, resolving or cancelling a transfer, recording a delivery, making an adjustment) require INTERNET AT THE MOMENT you do them: the app gets a purpose-specific pass, attaches it to the resulting rows, and the cloud refuses those row types if the pass is missing or invalid. Ordinary store work is unaffected. NOT BUILT — the cloud never actually checks this today.
decisions.why: Kunal accepted the online-only cost for this small set of actions because it is the earliest way to stop a tampered device inventing Director-level records. It is a partial down-payment on the full server-side write commitment.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out Directors approving stock takes or resolving transfers offline. It does NOT yet rule anything out in practice, because the cloud-side check was never wired.

decisions.what: A pass never carries its own authority. When the cloud checks a pass it looks up the account's CURRENT role in SharePoint rather than believing the role written inside the pass, and the role named in a request is never trusted as permission. Related standing rules from the same audit round: the last remaining Director can never be deactivated or demoted, and a locked account stays locked even if the lock value is stored in an odd format.
decisions.why: If the pass could vouch for its own role, anyone who obtained one could keep acting as a Director after being demoted. The last-Director guard exists because deactivating the only Director would brick the admin screen with no way back in.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out role information travelling from client to server as authorisation, and rules out any 'trust the token's claims' shortcut in future server work.
decisions.whoDecided: Codex audit + internal deep audit, adopted

decisions.what: The very first Director account is created by a one-time seeding path that is then disabled, and a brand-new app install with no account list refuses all sensitive actions rather than allowing them.
decisions.why: You cannot create the first admin using the admin screen that requires an admin. The one-shot path solves it without leaving a permanent back door.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out leaving the seeding path permanently open, and rules out a fresh device 'failing open' before it has synced.

decisions.what: Which stores' data you can see is decided by the ACCOUNT you logged into, and that store list is fixed and held in the cloud. The server reads it only from the verified credential row — never from anything the app sends. Store account sees its one store; territory manager sees their stores; a franchisee sees their stores plus their franchise office; Head Office and Directors see everything. If the scope cannot be determined, the server sends NOTHING.
decisions.why: Kunal confirmed accounts are fixed identities tied to a place — nobody logs into another account 'inside' a store account, and a territory manager uses their own device. That single clarification collapsed a whole planned layer of device-versus-account intersection logic.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out cross-login (logging in as a different role on a store device), rules out the app telling the server which stores it wants, and rules out defaulting to 'send everything' when something is unclear.

decisions.what: Store isolation is not just about what you can READ — the cloud also REJECTS any attempt to WRITE a row for a store outside your account's list. The old rule ('your rows must match your one store') was widened to 'your rows must be inside your store list'.
decisions.why: Read-only isolation would still let a tampered device manufacture movements in another store's books. The old single-store rule had to be widened or a multi-store franchisee could not save anything at all — its rows belong to its member stores, not to the account itself.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating Chunk 10 as 'just a download filter'. Rules out the earlier absolute one-store write rule from Chunk 5.

decisions.what: A transfer between two stores is stored as two separate legs, each owned by one store. So plain store filtering already gives the receiving store its own leg — no special 'either end' logic is needed on the movement ledger. The 'either end' rule is only needed on the transfer PAPERWORK (the record steps), so a receiving store can see who sent what and when.
decisions.why: This was flagged as the hardest part of the design and was expected to need complicated rules. Building it revealed the data already worked that way, which made the whole thing simpler and safer.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out re-opening 'how does a receiver see an incoming transfer without seeing the sender's data' — it is settled. Rules out adding either-end logic to the ledger filter.

decisions.what: Minimum necessary sharing: a receiving store sees an incoming transfer's details (who sent it, what, when) but none of the sender's other movements; a store sees Head Office transfers to itself but not Head Office's stock; territory managers and franchisees see full individual movement detail for THEIR stores. Store NAMES stay visible to everybody — only DATA is scoped.
decisions.why: Franchisees pay for and trade their own stock, so they need full detail on their own stores and nothing beyond. Kunal judged the mere existence of other store names to be non-sensitive in a franchise chain — hiding them would have complicated the app for no real gain.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out scoping the store directory itself. Rules out giving a receiving store the sender's balances, costs or unrelated activity.

decisions.what: When the app does not yet know its store scope, it fails CLOSED: it falls back to the stores on the logged-in account, and if even that is unknown it treats nothing as allowed — no opening balances are seeded, and a backup import strips everything.
decisions.why: The first build failed OPEN in that window, which both auditors rated critical: a device could briefly hold and display another store's data before the first scope message arrived.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out any 'allow until we know better' behaviour in the scoping code.

decisions.what: The cloud builds its 'only these stores' database query by pasting in the account's store list, so that list is now validated with a strict allowlist: only ordinary letters, numbers, dash and underscore survive. Anything else — a quote, a bracket, a space — means NO stores, never a partial query.
decisions.why: An auditor showed the store list could in principle be crafted to break out of the query and widen it. Testing showed SharePoint happened to reject those attempts today, but the fix does not rely on that luck.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the earlier reasoning that 'it is safe because the owner sets the store names'. Rules out relying on the database to reject bad input.

decisions.what: When an account's store list changes, the device first pushes up anything it has not yet sent, then wipes out-of-scope data in one all-or-nothing operation, then re-downloads from scratch. If the wipe fails, a privacy lock is raised: backups are blocked, a warning shows, and it retries every cycle. The device never claims to be 'scoped and complete' until it really is.
decisions.why: Two separate dangers. Widening a scope would otherwise never deliver the new store's older records (the app only asks for records newer than the last one it saw). And a half-finished wipe would leave another store's data sitting on a franchise device while the app believed it was clean.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out an ordinary top-up sync after a scope change. Rules out purging before unsent work has been flushed — that used to lose offline entries and is now blocked outright.
decisions.whoDecided: Codex + Antigravity audit, adopted; the flush-first fix was Kunal-approved org W3 work
decisions.when: 2026-07-08 (decided) / fixed and extended 2026-07-13 in org wave 3

decisions.what: The trigger for that re-download is NOT the 'scope version' number originally specified. In practice the device compares the store list itself, plus a per-store ownership-era version the server sends with each download. That extra era signal exists because a store can change owner while its store list stays identical.
decisions.why: A franchise conversion leaves the shop-floor device pointed at the same one store, so a store-list comparison alone would never notice and the old owner's data would linger. The era version is what catches it.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out relying on a scopeVersion/scopeHash field — it was never built and nothing should be specified against it.
decisions.whoDecided: Auditor-driven (org-structure spec review), built by Claude
decisions.supersededBy: Org wave 3 store-list signature plus per-store topology (era) versions
decisions.source: sync.js:2178-2192; grep for scopeVersion/scopeHash returns zero client or Function code

decisions.what: Comparison reports mean 'compare within your own scope'. A single-store account has nothing to compare; a multi-store franchisee may compare among their own stores; territory managers, Head Office and Directors compare across theirs. Never beyond.
decisions.why: Kunal specifically did not want cross-store comparison to be a Head Office privilege only — a franchisee with several stores has a legitimate need to compare them.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out making comparison a Director/Head-Office-only feature, and rules out any report that reaches outside the viewer's stores.
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK10-SCOPE.md:86-89; implemented in the app at index.html:2950 and :3223 (store lists filtered to the account's stores)

decisions.what: A scoped account may pull ITS OWN stores' archived history — archive access is not restricted to Directors and Head Office forever. NOT BUILT: today the archive door is still Director/Head-Office only; the store filter is wired but not switched on.
decisions.why: Franchisees and managers need their own older data. The delivery mechanism was deferred so it could ship as part of the 'see older/archived data' permission toggle rather than as a separate one-off gate.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out designing archive access as permanently Director-only. Does not yet rule anything out in practice.
decisions.when: 2026-07-08 (decided); ownership moved to the Account Access chunk 2026-07-09

decisions.what: When a franchisee takes over a store that Head Office used to run, they do NOT get the store's history. They start from an opening stock balance as at the takeover date and see only what happens from then on, under their own costing. The Head Office era — especially anything carrying our costs — stays with us and is never sent to them. NOT BUILT. A normal scope widening (a franchisee already trading who gains visibility) still gets full history; only a takeover applies the cutoff.
decisions.why: Kunal: 'the franchisee's costs and our costs are different — I don't want the older data showing to a franchisee when they take over a store and see the costing of HO.'
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating a takeover as an ordinary scope widening. Rules out any 'give them everything and hide the cost column' approach.
decisions.when: 2026-07-08 (locked); enforcement assigned to the Account Access chunk 2026-07-09

decisions.what: Where a franchise store has no recorded takeover date, the cloud must serve NOTHING for the period in question, never everything. Granting a franchisee 'see older data' must be incapable of exposing pre-takeover corporate cost history, even before the tools that set takeover dates exist.
decisions.why: The archive door treats an empty store filter as 'no filter'. A literal, well-meaning implementation of the takeover cutoff would therefore have handed a brand-new franchisee the previous owner's entire trading history — the exact leak the rule exists to prevent.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out shipping the takeover cutoff as a filter that quietly does nothing when the date is missing. Rules out waiting for the org-structure chunk before enforcing it.

decisions.what: Remaining work is now ordered by RISK, not by chunk number. Staff are not technically inclined and are not treated as a hostile-user threat, so SECURITY HARDENING may follow release — but DATA LEAKS, LOGIC/MONEY defects and FEATURE GAPS may not be deferred. For this cluster that means store isolation (a leak) stays a launch blocker, while the remaining Account Access permission hardening (items 5-11) may land after release.
decisions.why: Kunal's judgement about who actually uses the app: a shared shop-floor account in a salon is not an attacker. What would genuinely hurt the business is a franchisee seeing another store's numbers, or a wrong invoice.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out blocking release on security hardening items. Equally, rules out deferring anything that leaks data across stores or gets money wrong.

decisions.what: Ardross and Bunbury are closed and are to be DELETED outright, not deactivated. In this cluster that means their seed entries and any store credential rows and store scopes carrying them go too.
decisions.why: The app has never been used, so there is no real trading history to preserve for those stores. Keeping them 'inactive' just leaves them in dropdowns and in credential scopes forever.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the usual soft-deactivate treatment for these two, and rules out keeping an ardross credential in staging.
decisions.source: index.html:602 and :604 (seed store list); HANDOVER.md:151-155 (staging still holds an ardross credential)

decisions.what: The Online Store is a real store — website and social-media sales, run by Head Office. It needs NO login or credential of its own for now, so it gets no account and no separate store scope; its movements ride Head Office's all-stores access.
decisions.why: Nobody works 'in' the online store as a separate location — Head Office fulfils it. Creating an account for it would be a credential to manage and rotate for no operational benefit.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out creating an online-store account or device credential, and rules out anyone outside Head Office recording online sales, since no other account's scope includes it.
decisions.source: index.html:609 (seeded as a store, type 'online'); no matching account in the seed list at index.html:613-628

decisions.what: The 16 accounts built into the app (both Directors, Head Office, six store accounts, six manager accounts and the Cockburn franchisee) carry throwaway demo passwords and PINs, not real credentials. No emergency deploy is needed — but they MUST be rotated before launch.
decisions.why: They were never real, so nothing is exposed today. They are, however, hard-coded into the shipped file, so leaving them in place at launch would mean the live app ships with known logins for the two Director accounts.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating this as a live incident, and equally rules out launching without rotation. Rotation belongs on the cutover checklist, which currently does not mention passwords at all.

decisions.what: The Cockburn Franchise Office is a deliberate, load-bearing part of the model, not a leftover: Head Office supplies the OFFICE, the office supplies the shop floor, and the OFFICE is what gets invoiced. In this cluster it is why a franchisee's access is 'their stores PLUS their franchise office' rather than just their shops.
decisions.why: Franchise billing runs through the office entity. If the office were treated as noise and removed, the franchisee's supply chain and their invoice would both lose their anchor.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out anyone 'tidying away' the franchise office as a duplicate store, and rules out a franchisee scope that omits the office.
decisions.source: index.html:616 (fran_cockburn seeded with cockburn_office in its store list); AZURE-CHUNK10-SCOPE.md:31-32

decisions.what: Who can do what is stored as an editable LIST OF PERMISSIONS (data), not written into the app's code. Adding a new permission later must be cheap — a data change, not a rebuild.
decisions.why: Kunal wants to change staff permissions himself without a developer. If permissions are baked into code, every 'can Booragoon do their own stock take?' question becomes a code change and an audit round.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out hard-coding role checks anywhere new; rules out 'just add an if-statement for this role'; rules out any code that assumes the role list is fixed.

decisions.what: The first version of the permission list was specified as the 15 existing permission gates plus 5 new 'what you can SEE' toggles (cost price, selling price, archived data, charts, comparison charts).
decisions.why: Kunal judged the existing set enough for v1 rather than designing a bigger scheme up front.
decisions.rulesOut: Nothing may still quote '5 view toggles' or '20 gates + 5' as the shipped list — two specs and one matrix row still do.
decisions.supersededBy: The seeCharts drop (AA-02, internal audit) — shipped set is 4 view toggles + editAccessPolicy = 20 capabilities

decisions.what: The 'can see charts' toggle was REMOVED before shipping. General charts sit all over the shared dashboard where staff also land, with no single place to guard them, so the switch could not actually be enforced. The cross-store COMPARISON report page is a real page and keeps its toggle.
decisions.why: A permission switch that does not actually stop anything is worse than no switch: the Director ticks it, believes staff can't see charts, and they can. Better to have no toggle than a lying one.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out re-adding a general 'see charts' switch without first creating a single enforceable guard point; rules out treating the spec's 5-toggle list as current.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude (internal deep audit), inside Kunal's D-AA-1
decisions.source: index.html:977-982 (code comment — the ONLY record); voids part of D-AA-1 and matrix row 19

decisions.what: An exception to the normal permissions is set on ONE SPECIFIC ACCOUNT — e.g. 'the Booragoon shop account may stock-take without the PIN'. There is no way to say 'all managers at store X'; you tick the individual accounts.
decisions.why: Kunal's own example was a single store. Group rules add a whole extra layer of 'which rule wins' arguments for a business with a handful of accounts. Because the list is data, group rules can be added later without a redesign.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out per-store overrides, per-role-per-store rules, and any group rule in v1; rules out using a store's ID to decide what someone may DO (store IDs only decide which rows their device receives).

decisions.what: The original wording said the order of precedence was: role default first, then the account's exception, then the 24-hour PIN.
decisions.why: First draft, written before an auditor walked through what happens when a Director has explicitly BANNED something and the person then types the PIN.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out any implementation that lets a PIN outrank a Director's explicit ban.
decisions.supersededBy: SR-7

decisions.what: Order of precedence, final: an explicit exception on the account WINS — whether it grants or bans. Only after that does the 24-hour PIN apply, and the PIN can only LIFT a restriction that came from the role default. Then the role default.
decisions.why: A Director banning one person from something must not be undone by that person typing the shop PIN. The PIN is a convenience to lift a general restriction, not a master key.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out PIN-as-override; rules out any second copy of this ordering logic — there is ONE algorithm, run in both the app and the cloud, with a test that proves they agree.
decisions.whoDecided: AGY audit finding, adopted by Claude/Kunal
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK-ACCOUNT-ACCESS-SCOPE.md:166-169; implemented accessPolicy.js resolveCapability (mirrored in client Auth.can, parity-tested)

decisions.what: By default the basic shop account needs the 24-hour PIN to do a stock take AND to receive a Head Office delivery. Receiving currently needs no PIN, so this is the one change staff will actually notice on day one.
decisions.why: Kunal wants receiving controlled the same way stock takes are, with the option to switch the PIN off for a store he trusts to run itself.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out shipping this quietly — it required a test written against the OLD behaviour first, then flipped. Still not live: it only bites once a policy is published AND the two ingest doors are switched on.

decisions.what: The app is built so brand-new account types can exist (the permission list works off role NAMES as data). The SCREEN for creating a new type is deliberately left for later.
decisions.why: The expensive half is making nothing in the code assume there are exactly six roles. Doing that now costs little; the create-a-role screen can wait until there is a real need.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out any new code that hard-codes the six current roles — a permanent standing constraint, not a one-off.

decisions.what: The org-structure tools (convert a store to a franchise, onboard a franchisee, add a store to an existing franchisee) were SPLIT OUT into their own separate piece of work, built straight after this one.
decisions.why: This chunk was already large, and the org tools are driven by a real deadline (a new franchisee around Sep-Oct 2026) with a manual fallback. Mixing them would have delayed both.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out building wizard/topology features inside the access chunk. Splits one rule in two: SETTING a franchise takeover cutoff belongs to the org chunk; ENFORCING it (never serving a franchisee the previous owner's history) stays here.

decisions.what: The list of actions that re-ask for the Director's password is ONE business-wide setting shared by both Directors, not a personal preference per Director. Day-to-day stock in/out starts OFF; publish, archive, user admin and backup start ON.
decisions.why: Kunal first said 'a setting in the Director's account', but one shared setting is simpler and safer — two Directors with different locks means nobody can say what the lock actually is.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out per-Director password policies; rules out treating the current hard-coded re-prompt list as fixed — it becomes an editable default. Extending re-prompts to non-Director roles was captured as a future idea, NOT built.

decisions.what: Editing the permission list itself ALWAYS asks for the Director's password, and that cannot be switched off. Same for editing the password-prompt list and adding/removing Directors.
decisions.why: The permission list IS the lock. If someone walks past an unlocked Director device, they must not be able to quietly grant themselves everything without re-typing the password.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out any 'convenience' setting that relaxes these; a saved policy that tries to relax them is REJECTED outright, not silently corrected.

decisions.what: The build went further than the spec: the always-ask-for-password protection covers ALL user administration, not only actions aimed at a Director.
decisions.why: Simpler and safer than picking apart which user operations are sensitive; a per-operation relaxation can be added later without changing anything structural.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out an auditor reading the spec and reporting the wider protection as a bug — but only if this is written down somewhere other than a code comment.
decisions.source: accessPolicy.js:33-38 (a code comment is the ONLY record); spec still says the narrower rule at AZURE-CHUNK-ACCOUNT-ACCESS-SCOPE.md:126-129

decisions.what: The cloud makes every permission decision from ITS OWN stored copy of the permission list. It never believes a copy or a claim sent up from a device. If the list is missing, unreadable or out of date, the answer is NO.
decisions.why: Anything a device sends can be edited by a determined person with browser tools. The device's copy exists only to show/hide things on screen.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out trusting a role name in a request; rules out fail-open ('if we can't read the rules, allow it'); rules out sending the policy up with the request to save a lookup.

decisions.what: Before building, every single permission had to be mapped to exactly where the cloud enforces it and what happens on failure. Permissions with no cloud enforcement are LABELLED as screen-only and honestly admitted to be bypassable.
decisions.why: Without that map it is impossible to tell a real lock from a hidden button. It also caught the concrete hole both auditors named: the PIN-to-receive rule had to be enforced in the cloud, not just in the app.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out describing any browser-side check as security; rules out adding a capability in future without a matrix row saying where it really bites.

decisions.what: Every edit to the permission list bumps a version number. When a permission is TAKEN AWAY, devices must delete the data they are no longer allowed to hold (cost figures, archived rows, cached reports) and block that screen until a clean re-download. Revoke means gone, not hidden.
decisions.why: Hiding a price on screen while the number is still sitting in the device's local database is not a revoke.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'just hide the column' as a revoke; rules out letting a backup export run while a purge is still pending.
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK-ACCOUNT-ACCESS-SCOPE.md:152-156; built as Sync._applyAccessPolicy + a purge-pending privacy lock wired into the backup export gate

decisions.what: Permission exceptions are looked up by ACCOUNT. Which stores' data a device receives is a completely separate question answered by the account's store list.
decisions.why: The original sketch mixed the two, which would have meant asking 'can this person do X at store Y' everywhere — twice the surface, and a store ID is not an identity.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a store ID ever identifying a permission exception; rules out re-introducing a per-store override without a redesign.

decisions.what: Every franchise store must have a record of WHEN its current owner took it over. Giving a franchisee the 'see older data' permission must be incapable of showing them the previous owner's trading history. No takeover record on file means serve NOTHING old for that store.
decisions.why: This is the exact disclosure the whole chunk exists to prevent. It has to hold before the franchise wizard exists, so the enforcement was pulled forward.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out relying on the org chunk to prevent the leak; rules out an empty filter meaning 'no restriction' (the live archive door behaves exactly that way, which is why this must be proven, not assumed). ⚠ The store_eras record it depends on HAS NEVER BEEN BUILT — zero code, zero cloud.

decisions.what: Every proof of identity is tied to the account and the device it was issued for, and the cloud always re-checks the CURRENT permission list rather than trusting a role name that arrived in the request. Old role checks in the cloud stay only as a second belt.
decisions.why: Once roles are data that a Director can edit, a hard-coded 'directors only' check in the cloud is either redundant or wrong — it must never be the real gate.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out role-allowlists in cloud workflows as the authority; rules out a proof minted for one device or purpose being reused for another.

decisions.what: When cost visibility became a switch, the cloud's default became STRIP THE COST. If the permission list is missing or unreadable, cost figures are removed.
decisions.why: A misconfiguration must fail private, not fail exposed. Cost price is the number Kunal least wants leaking to a franchisee.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the old 'strip cost only if the store is flagged as a franchise' logic being the sole gate.

decisions.what: Password re-prompts on purely LOCAL actions (like logging stock in or out) are cosmetic. So is the 'see selling price' switch. Both are written down as convenience, never called security.
decisions.why: There is no cloud step to check for a purely local action, and the selling price is already on every device as part of the public catalogue. Pretending otherwise would let a future audit call a known limitation a breach.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out marking these as security controls; rules out an auditor re-rating them as a critical leak (AGY did exactly that once — see AA-EXT-1). Server-withholding selling price would need per-account catalogue delivery, explicitly OUT of scope.

decisions.what: The CSV exports were made to honour the 'see selling price' switch too, so the toggle behaves the same way everywhere. The auditor's 'critical leak' rating was corrected down — the price is public catalogue data already on the device.
decisions.why: Cheap to fix and it makes the switch honest. But the severity had to be corrected, or the record would claim a data breach that did not happen.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out taking an auditor's severity at face value; rules out re-opening this as a data leak.

decisions.what: 'Clear PIN' is an INSTANT kill switch. The moment the Director clears or changes the shop PIN, every unlock already handed out stops working — nobody keeps working off yesterday's PIN for up to 24 hours.
decisions.why: The reason to clear a PIN is usually that someone should no longer have it. A revoke that takes a day is not a revoke. The grants also still expire on their own within 24 hours as a backstop.
decisions.rulesOut: ⚠ RESOLVED — THE REPO IS RIGHT, THE MEMORY INDEX AND HANDOVER ARE WRONG. This is decided AND built. It must come off HANDOVER.md:678 'Owner decisions waiting' and off the memory index. Rules out TTL-only expiry as the design.
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK-AA-LA-CHANGES.md:230-240; IMPLEMENTED and verified today at accessPolicy.js:105-114, :172-189, :226 (pinEpoch stamped on each grant, bumped only when the PIN is set or cleared)

decisions.what: PUBLISHING the permission list and TURNING ENFORCEMENT ON are two separate acts. Every cloud door reads ONE master switch and stays completely inert while that switch is absent or off — even after a permission list has been published.
decisions.why: Kunal's call, and it buys a rehearsal: publish the list, watch every door read it correctly, let it settle, then flip one switch. If anything misbehaves, flip the switch back and the published list survives. Under the old design the only undo was deleting the list you had just written. Cost is one tiny extra lookup per call — accepted.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'a policy exists, therefore enforce' anywhere; rules out arming doors one at a time (the switch is ONE row so both write doors arm together — a half-armed pair splits a stock-take approval). ⚠ Three doors (user admin, catalogue publish, the archive run) were specified with NO off-switch at all and would break their own working Director door the day they landed — all three still need this guard.

decisions.what: Originally, activation was one event: the Director publishes the default permission list, and that is the flag day.
decisions.why: It was the simplest model and avoided a drift window where devices disagreed. It was written before anyone noticed that two of the doors armed on publish while two armed on a separate flag.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out reading the wave review's activation section as current.
decisions.supersededBy: D-AA-A

decisions.what: When enforcement is switched on, only DIRECTORS see cost prices. Head Office is added afterwards by EDITING THE PERMISSION LIST — never by changing code or redeploying anything. If adding Head Office turns out to need a code change, the design has failed its own purpose and that is a defect to raise before switching on.
decisions.why: Today an unauthenticated Head Office device receives the whole cost list. Starting narrow and widening by a data edit is the safe direction, and it is also the acceptance test for whether the editable permission list actually works.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out seeding Head Office with cost access 'to avoid disruption'; rules out any future permission change that requires a deploy. ⚠ Contradicts the enforcement matrix row 16, which still seeds cost to 'director plus corporate Head Office' — the code follows this decision, the matrix is stale.

decisions.what: A client bug MUST be fixed before enforcement is switched on: the app fetches central cost updates once at start-up, BEFORE anyone has logged in, and quietly ignores a refusal. Once the person-level check is live, Director devices would silently sit on stale costs forever.
decisions.why: The failure is invisible — no error, no empty screen, just old numbers. Found by reading the code on 2026-07-30, not by any audit.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating this as part of a cloud apply — it is an app change with its own test and its own audit. It currently appears on no build list, no wave plan and no cutover checklist.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude (raised), Kunal (accepted as a pre-activation gate)

decisions.what: Two different kinds of failure at the cloud door: 'you are not allowed' is a permanent refusal, recorded and reported. 'Your proof of identity was missing or had timed out on the way' means TRY AGAIN — the record stays on the device and re-sends. A record is never permanently lost because a proof expired in transit.
decisions.why: Connectivity drops, retries and 5-minute proof lifetimes would otherwise quarantine perfectly legitimate stock movements by timing accident.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating any proof failure as a refusal; rules out silently dropping a batch. ⚠ A permanent refusal is DURABLE ON THE DEVICE — switching enforcement back off does NOT un-quarantine an already-refused record.

decisions.what: The 24-hour PIN is now checked by the cloud, not by the app on the device. Consequence Kunal accepted: a shop account needs internet AT THE MOMENT it types the PIN. The unlock then lasts until the PIN expires, offline or not.
decisions.why: A PIN checked on the device is a PIN a determined person can bypass with browser tools. Same trade-off Kunal already accepted for Director actions.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the old local hash check; rules out offline PIN entry. A PIN unlock can only lift TWO permissions — stock take and receive — and can never be minted with a password (accessPolicy.js:33-34).

decisions.what: A dedicated permission controls WHO may edit the permission list, and the cloud refuses to save any list that would remove that permission from Directors.
decisions.why: Any account can prove who it is with its own password — that alone does not make it a Director. The permission is what pins down who may use such a proof here. And a Director must never be able to save a list that locks all Directors out of the lock itself.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out relying on the Director device key alone; rules out a self-lockout. The very first save, when no list exists yet, falls back to requiring the proof's role to be director.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude (hole closed pre-emptively during build W4)

decisions.what: A known rough edge in saving the permission list (it writes three pieces one after another, and a failure part-way can temporarily block the Director from re-publishing until it is repaired) is NOT being fixed now. It fails SAFE — no bad list ships, devices keep the last good one.
decisions.why: The fix belongs with finalising the cloud write step; hand-fixing it now would change a workflow nobody is about to apply. Both the internal server audit and Codex independently found it and both rated it minor.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out re-raising it as a blocker. But it must be fixed BEFORE the cloud doors start reading the permission list (ITEM5-RESPEC:415).

decisions.what: The two doors every stock movement passes through get their new machinery installed SWITCHED OFF first (Stage 1, proven to change nothing), and turned on later by creating a single row of data (Stage 2). While off, anything unexpected — missing row, failed lookup, wrong list name — counts as OFF.
decisions.why: These two doors run on the same connection as the LIVE app. The previous version of this plan was reviewed clean three times and was still wrong three ways, because the reviews checked the design while the instructions had been written against a day-old picture of the actual machine. All three would have misbehaved on ordinary everyday traffic with nothing published at all.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'unknown means enforce' during Stage 1 (that hardening is deliberately a later, separately audited item); rules out applying these two doors first in the batch; rules out applying both halves in one sitting; rules out flipping with only one door armed.

decisions.what: The two ingest doors are PARKED and are applied LAST. Three audit rounds, three blocks, both auditors every time. They are not to be resumed until four specific preconditions are met — no partial credit.
decisions.why: Kunal's call: the earlier work does not depend on it, so it is not worth being the bottleneck. Resuming early is exactly what produced three rounds. The recurring defect was never a missing check — it was claiming something was covered or authoritative before it was.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out resuming on a partial edit set; rules out asserting coverage as an adjective ('authoritative', 'complete') instead of a measured number; rules out an off-switch design where an ABSENT switch row means ON — which is what the previous version actually did.

decisions.what: Account Access items 5-11 are SECURITY hardening, and security hardening may now follow release. They sit behind data leaks, money/logic defects and feature gaps in the queue.
decisions.why: Kunal's call today: staff are not technically inclined and are not a hostile-user threat, so the browser-to-cloud permission work can wait — but a franchisee seeing another store's figures, or a wrong number, cannot. This security work had been blocking a queue of money and data-leak defects that need none of it.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out resuming the Account Access cloud applies ahead of the Cockburn pricing and Southlands ownership work; does NOT rule out the data-leak parts of this chunk (the franchise history cutoff, SR-6), which are a leak, not hardening.

decisions.what: When 'see cost' is taken away, the device's OWN recorded cost history is not wiped — only the central cost figures it was sent. The cloud refuses all further cost lookups.
decisions.why: That history is data the device itself recorded; deleting it would destroy the store's own records to enforce a view setting.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out an auditor calling this a failed revoke. Note the coupling: granting 'see cost' also reveals the franchise-discount and price COLUMNS in the products table (editing them stays behind a separate permission).

decisions.what: A device that is completely offline keeps data it already downloaded until it reconnects. The delete-what-you-may-no-longer-see step fires on reconnect; until then the device cannot talk to the cloud at all.
decisions.why: Standard limitation of an app designed to work offline. Recorded openly so no future audit mistakes it for a hole.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out claiming an instant revoke reaches offline devices.

decisions.what: The existing password prompts for publishing, user administration and backup keep asking every time, even if the Director relaxes them in the settings. Only the NEW prompts (approve, resolve, delivery) honour a relaxed setting.
decisions.why: Deliberately conservative first version — these are the highest-consequence actions and nobody had asked for them to be relaxed.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out reading the settings screen as fully honoured today — a Director who un-ticks those three will still be prompted. Worth telling Kunal before he uses that screen.

decisions.what: A store's ownership is recorded as a dated HISTORY of who owned it and when ('eras'), not as a single 'this store changed hands on date X' field. Every change of hands closes the current era and opens a new one. Who is allowed to see which of a store's records is decided purely by which era those records fall into.
decisions.why: A single takeover date breaks the moment a store changes hands twice. Buy a store back and re-franchise it, and the new franchisee would inherit the previous franchisee's and Head Office's trading history. With eras, each owner sees only their own window, and the earlier takeover date simply becomes the first era boundary rather than a special case.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a single 'takeover cutoff date' field on the store. Rules out deciding visibility from the store's current franchise flags. Rules out any design where a new owner can be shown the previous owner's trading history.
decisions.whoDecided: auditor-driven (Codex R2-3), adopted by Kunal at the 2026-07-10 design session
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-STRUCTURE.md:48-52 (model) and :257-262 (the reasoning, from the Codex R2-3 spec review)

decisions.what: Two real, concrete situations drive this whole chunk and both must work properly: (A) an existing Head Office store becomes a franchise under a brand-new franchisee, and (B) a brand-new store joins a franchisee who already exists. Equal priority.
decisions.why: These are the actual business events coming up, not hypotheticals. Building to real cases keeps the design honest and stops it drifting into generic 'topology management'.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out building only the conversion path, or only the onboarding path. Rules out treating 'add a store to an existing franchisee' as a rare edge case.

decisions.what: When a Head Office store becomes a franchise: the store's own till/POS login STAYS the same (only who owns it changes). Personal logins tied to that store — staff, store manager, territory manager — lose that store. A person left with no stores at all is switched off; a territory manager who still covers other stores just loses this one and keeps working.
decisions.why: The physical shop keeps trading on the same device, so breaking its login would be pointless disruption. But the people are now the franchisee's responsibility, and the franchisee appoints their own. Switching off a territory manager's whole account because ONE of their five stores converted would be plainly wrong.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out cancelling the store's till login on conversion. Rules out blanket-deactivating every account that touched the store. Rules out leaving ex-Head-Office staff logins with access after the store has changed hands.
decisions.whoDecided: Kunal (rule), Claude (multi-store nuance, built and audited)
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-STRUCTURE.md:16-22 (decision + the nuance); AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-ENFORCEMENT-MATRIX.md:68 (the rule pinned); azure-functions/src/functions/topology.js:297 (built: deactivate only if zero stores left)

decisions.what: There is NO direct 'sell a store from one franchisee to another' path. It is always done in two steps: buy the store back to Head Office first, then hand it to the new franchisee.
decisions.why: The Head Office period sitting between the two franchise periods IS the clean boundary — it guarantees the incoming franchisee can never see the outgoing one's trading history. The ownership-era model then handles the whole thing for free, with no extra machinery.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out building a fifth wizard tool for franchisee-to-franchisee sale. Rules out any code path that re-owns a store whose current owner is not Head Office.
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-STRUCTURE.md:23-25; enforced in code at azure-functions/src/functions/topology.js:552 and :597 (rejects with DIRECT_TRANSFER_FORBIDDEN)

decisions.what: When a franchisee's last store leaves them, the app does NOT automatically switch off their office account. The Director switches it off by hand, once stock and money have been settled.
decisions.why: There may still be stock to transfer or accounts to settle after the store has gone. Automatically killing the login mid-settlement would be unhelpful and hard to undo.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out auto-deactivating an emptied office account. Rules out the reverse mistake too — a buy-back must never REACTIVATE an office the Director had already switched off.
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-STRUCTURE.md:26-29; refined by OS-SR-9 at :124-129; built at azure-functions/src/functions/topology.js:290-293 (an already-deactivated office is never silently switched back on)

decisions.what: An office account left switched on after its last store is gone has zero stores, and therefore sees nothing live at all. Settling up is done BEFORE the buy-back, or afterwards from the handover export — never by leaving them able to pull fresh data.
decisions.why: It resolves the apparent contradiction in D-OS-4: 'stays active for settlement' does not mean 'can still see the store's data'. It just means the login still exists until the Director tidies up.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out any 'historical read-only window' access for an ex-franchisee. Rules out settling up by letting them pull data after the buy-back.
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-STRUCTURE.md:124-129 (folded from the Codex R1 spec review)

decisions.what: At buy-back, the departing franchisee is given a DATA EXPORT of their period. Their live access ends immediately and their devices wipe.
