decisions.why: They have a legitimate accounting and tax need for their own trading records, but no ongoing business reason to see the store live. An export satisfies the first without any of the risk of the second — and it needs no special ongoing-access machinery.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out giving an ex-franchisee a lingering read-only login. Rules out building any 'historical access window' feature.

decisions.what: The buy-back export contains, for each product over the franchisee's ownership period: how much was used, what it cost them, and the retail profitability. Delivered as a CSV bundle, as a compulsory step inside the buy-back wizard.
decisions.why: It is an accounting and tax hand-off, so it must be the computed summary, not the raw movement log. Making it a wizard step means it cannot be forgotten in the rush of a handover.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out handing over the raw ledger. Rules out leaving the export as an optional afterwards-if-they-ask task.

decisions.what: The buy-back export is generated by the server and is strictly bounded to the franchisee's own closed period — both the start AND the end date. A record dated exactly at the end moment is excluded.
decisions.why: Without a hard upper bound, Head Office's trading after the buy-back would leak into the ex-franchisee's usage, cost and profit figures — a real number on a real settlement, computed wrong.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a client-side filtered export. Rules out a 'from this date onwards' export with no end date.

decisions.what: The buy-back settlement must be built from live records AND archived records together, and the engine refuses to produce a settlement at all if the records handed to it do not fully cover the period. Likewise an old franchise invoice must say 'older records need loading' rather than quietly printing a short one.
decisions.why: Old records get moved to an archive. A settlement built from an incomplete set would look perfectly normal while being short by whatever was archived — the worst kind of money error, because nobody would spot it.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out generating a settlement from the live table alone. Rules out any report that silently renders a partial invoice when its date range reaches past the local window.

decisions.what: The wizard's list of fields must be built as data, so more fields can be added later without redesigning the screen. It starts with store name, phone and type; franchise stores add the discount and the office login.
decisions.why: Kunal's own words were 'if there's anything else we can add that later'. Hard-coding the fields guarantees a rebuild the first time he wants one more box.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a hand-coded fixed form. NOTE: this rule governs Wave 5, which is NOT built — if this document is not re-read at wizard build time the rule is simply lost.

decisions.what: Before anything is committed, the wizard shows a plain-English summary of exactly what is about to change — 'moves Booragoon from Head Office to Franchisee X; X sees data from today; Head Office keeps the full history; the store till stays as-is; these 2 manager logins are cancelled' — and the Director confirms before the change fires.
decisions.why: These changes are irreversible in practice and touch several logins at once. A non-technical Director must be able to see, in words, what is going to happen before it happens.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a silent one-click commit. Rules out a technical/JSON preview.

decisions.what: A change of ownership is executed by ONE dedicated server job that writes a journal entry first ('pending'), then applies every sub-change one at a time in a way that is safe to repeat, then marks it complete. If it crashes halfway, a sweep resumes it. While a change is pending on a store, reads for that store are blocked rather than served half-changed data.
decisions.why: The underlying storage has no way to make several list updates succeed-or-fail together. Without a journal, a crash halfway through leaves the business in a split state — some logins moved, some not — with no way to know which. Blocking reads during the window is safer than serving a half-migrated picture.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the wizard making several separate writes from the browser. Rules out best-effort/no-journal application. Rules out serving reads for a store mid-change.
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-STRUCTURE.md:84-91; AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-LA-CHANGES.md:9-12 and the §1 route spec

decisions.what: The SERVER works out which logins are affected by an ownership change. The wizard's preview is for display only and its list is never trusted.
decisions.why: If the browser told the server which accounts to update, a tampered request could simply leave the outgoing owner off the list — and they would keep their access after the store had changed hands.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out sending a credential list from the client. Rules out treating the preview as the instruction — it is only a display of the server's own plan.

decisions.what: Ownership is recorded against a permanent franchisee identity, not against their login. Logins point at that identity.
decisions.why: Logins get deactivated, renamed and recreated. If history pointed at the login, deleting and recreating a franchisee's office account would orphan or misattribute their whole trading history.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out using the office account row or username as the owner key. Rules out reusing a username being harmless.

decisions.what: A device that belongs to a shop — the till and the store manager login — can only ever see the CURRENT owner's period. It follows whoever owns the store now and can never look back into a previous owner's trading.
decisions.why: The physical device stays in the shop through a handover. Without this rule the incoming franchisee's till would be sitting on the outgoing franchisee's full history.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out shop devices retaining prior-era data after a handover. Rules out treating shop devices like franchisee/Head Office accounts, which do map to specific periods.

decisions.what: Before a device wipes data it is no longer entitled to, it must first send up anything it recorded while offline. Nothing unsent is ever deleted — if the send fails, the wipe refuses and retries every cycle rather than losing the work.
decisions.why: Ground-truthed as a REAL live bug, not a theory: the sync code wiped by store, ignoring whether rows had been uploaded yet, so a staff member's offline stock entries could be destroyed the moment a store left their scope. This protects every scope change, not just ownership ones.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out wiping first and syncing later. Rules out a best-effort wipe that proceeds when the upload failed. IMPORTANT: also rules out re-reporting this as an open bug — it is fixed (see stale records).
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-STRUCTURE.md:107-112; the bug at AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-ENFORCEMENT-MATRIX.md:27-30; BUILT and audited at sync.js:2200-2203 (flush) and 2205-2215 (refuse-and-retry), build commit 7aa4733

decisions.what: A device must also reset itself when the OWNERSHIP of one of its stores changes, not just when its list of stores changes.
decisions.why: Discovered by reading the live code: the till keeps exactly the same single store through a conversion, so nothing looked different to it and it would have carried the old owner's data straight into the new ownership. The whole era model would have been silently defeated on the most important case.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out relying on the store-list signature alone as the reset trigger. Rules out a single global version number — it must be per store, or a change to one store is masked by another.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude (discovery sweep), folded into the build
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-ENFORCEMENT-MATRIX.md:31-36; AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-STRUCTURE.md build order :178; BUILT at sync.js:2177-2189 (per-store version map) and 2205 (targeted wipe)

decisions.what: The opening stock balance at a handover is calculated BY THE SERVER, at the exact moment the ownership boundary is set, as one operation.
decisions.why: A balance worked out on a device mid-trading-day drifts against whatever is still being pushed up. Then the new owner starts from a number that never existed.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a client-generated opening balance. Rules out taking the snapshot at any moment other than the era boundary.

decisions.what: A handover pauses first: the change stays 'pending' and the opening balance stays provisional until the shop's devices have finished sending up their old work, within a bounded waiting period. Anything that still turns up late is QUARANTINED and shown to the Director to settle by hand — never applied silently.
decisions.why: The two earlier rules collided. Accepting late offline rows (OS-SR-5) versus a finalised opening balance (OS-SR-7) meant a pre-handover entry arriving after the balance was struck would land in the old period and leave the new owner with phantom stock. Making it a visible reconciliation item instead is the honest answer.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out silently applying a late pre-handover row. Rules out finalising the opening balance before devices have drained. Note this is an example of the standing lesson: the FIX itself needed its own adversarial review, and that review found the race the fix introduced.

decisions.what: That final catch-up upload from a departing owner's device is authorised by a one-time, expiring permission issued by the server. A record's own claimed date is never enough on its own.
decisions.why: Dates on a record come from the device and can be set to anything. 'Accept it if the date falls in the old period' would let an ex-owner back-date entries into a closed period long after their access ended — directly affecting what they owe.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out trusting the record's timestamp as the authorisation. Rules out an open-ended grace period.

decisions.what: The franchise discount is kept as its own dated history, completely separate from who owned the store. Ownership periods decide WHOSE records you can see; the discount history decides WHAT RATE applies to a given record's date.
decisions.why: A discount can be renegotiated without the store changing hands, so one ownership period may span two different rates — meaning the rate cannot live on the ownership record. This also fixes a live latent bug that exists today: because only a single current rate is stored, changing it retroactively rewrites every past invoice.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out storing the rate on the ownership era record (which is what OS-SR-3 originally said). Rules out reading the store's current discount when pricing a historical line. Rules out one rate per ownership period.
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-STRUCTURE.md:150-157; the latent bug confirmed at AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-ENFORCEMENT-MATRIX.md:18-22

decisions.what: Money in reports must be worked out from the arrangement that was in force on that record's own date, never from the store's current franchise settings.
decisions.why: Reports read the store's live franchise flag and discount. Buying a store back — flipping that flag off — would therefore retroactively strip the franchise loading from every past franchise-era invoice.
decisions.rulesOut: The surviving rule still rules out reading the live store flag for historical money. Anyone implementing OS-SR-3 literally — putting the rate on the era record — would be building the wrong thing.
decisions.supersededBy: OS-SR-11 (and completed by OS-SR-12) — the principle survives, but the rate lives in a separate dated pricing history, NOT on the ownership era record as OS-SR-3 originally specified

decisions.what: Discount rates are append-only once anything has been invoiced against them. Changing a rate opens a NEW period from an effective date; it never edits an old one. Correcting a genuine past mistake requires a logged, visible adjustment — not a quiet overwrite.
decisions.why: Without this, a Director fixing a setup error ('that should have been 12%, not 10%') would silently rewrite every invoice already issued under the old rate. Past invoices need the same immutability as the movement ledger itself.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out an edit button on a closed rate period. Rules out back-dating a rate change over an already-invoiced window. The audited adjustment path itself is NOT built — see open questions.

decisions.what: The franchise rate for a given line is found by trying, in order: a rate set for that specific product for that specific franchisee, then a rate set for that product globally, then that franchisee's blanket rate. First match wins.
decisions.why: It preserves exactly how the app behaves today (product override beats office default) while making every tier date-aware, and it gives the global product-discount editor somewhere to write to — it has no franchisee context of its own.
decisions.rulesOut: Still rules out falling back to the stored current rate when a rate history exists — a broken rate configuration must fail loudly ('PRICING DATA ERROR'), never quietly use the old scalar.
decisions.whoDecided: auditor-driven (AGY R2-2), adopted; frozen in the W4.2 spec
decisions.supersededBy: Kunal's 2026-08-01 three-tier ruling, which inserts a PRODUCT TYPE tier this chain does not have

decisions.what: The franchise discount has THREE levels: a blanket rate for the store, overridden by a rate for a PRODUCT TYPE, overridden by a rate for an individual product. Setting the franchise discount must be possible at the moment you create a product type. Cockburn: retail 50%, professional about 25%; Cleaning and Stationery are partly supplied and need rates too.
decisions.why: It matches how the business actually prices — whole categories of product carry the same arrangement, so setting them one product at a time is unworkable.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the two-level product-override-beats-store-default model the app has today, and rules out the frozen three-tier chain as specified (franchisee-product, global-product, franchisee-blanket) — which contains no product-type level at all. Anyone implementing W4.2's chain as frozen will build the wrong thing.
decisions.source: Kunal, session of 2026-08-01 (not yet in any repo document). Conflicts with the frozen chain at AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-W4-SCOPE.md:33. The product-type creation form today has a Name field only: index.html:3533 (_savePT)

decisions.what: The Cockburn Franchise Office is a deliberate, load-bearing part of the structure, not a leftover to be tidied away. Head Office supplies the OFFICE, the office supplies the shop floor, and the OFFICE is what gets invoiced.
decisions.why: Everything about franchise billing hangs off it. Removing or 'cleaning up' the office entity would break the invoice.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating an office store as data debris. Rules out any design that bills the retail store directly and skips the office.
decisions.source: Kunal, session of 2026-08-01. Confirmed against the code: the franchise invoice bills each office store for Head-Office supply — AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-ENFORCEMENT-MATRIX.md:23-26, citing index.html:4710-4717

decisions.what: On every Head-Office-to-franchise supply line, both the selling price and the discount used are frozen onto the record at the moment it is committed. The invoice prefers those frozen figures and only calculates from history for older records.
decisions.why: Fixing the discount history alone left half the bug alive: the invoice still read the live selling price, so a price rise today still rewrote the dollar amounts on last month's invoices. Freezing both numbers per record is belt-and-braces alongside the rate history. Written at commit, never at draft, so nobody can sit on a draft through a price change.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out stamping at draft creation. Rules out relying on the pricing history alone for the dollar amounts.
decisions.whoDecided: Both auditors + Claude by convergence; confirmed by Kunal
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-W4-SCOPE.md:24 (W4-SR-7, promoted to core scope by convergence); Kunal confirmed 2026-07-13 — recorded in audit-artifacts/MASTER-DECISION-REGISTER.md:645-651 (ORG-3)

decisions.what: The franchise wizard is NOT part of the single big go-live. It ships afterwards as its own smaller, separately-audited release. The ~Sep–Oct 2026 franchisee no longer holds up launch.
decisions.why: It is a Director-only screen no staff member will ever open. The one-big-release rule exists to avoid a string of risky deploys, not to hold the entire launch behind a screen nobody using the app will touch.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating the September franchisee as a launch blocker. Rules out the earlier hard gate that no store device gets the app until every chunk is complete (CUT-4). CAUTION: the fallback it leans on — a scripted onboarding runbook — does not exist as a document (see open questions).

decisions.what: Buying a store back needs NO cost-boundary machinery. Because stock records only ever store quantities and movements, and money is worked out at the moment you look at a report, buying a store back simply means the franchise loading stops applying from that point. Nothing is stored, so nothing needs resetting.
decisions.why: Kunal spotted this and it was verified against the code. An auditor had raised 'cost contamination' as a concern, but that concern assumed franchise pricing was baked into stored records — which this app has never done.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a cost snapshot or reset mechanism at buy-back. Rules out baking franchise prices into stored records. NOTE: this does NOT remove the visibility curtain — the era records still control whose history a franchisee may see.
decisions.whoDecided: Kunal (insight), ground-truthed against the code and adopted

decisions.what: When a company store becomes a franchise, the new franchisee's cost visibility starts at an opening balance on the takeover date. They do not get the store's full corporate cost history.
decisions.why: The pre-takeover cost history is Head Office's commercial information and has nothing to do with the incoming franchisee's trading. Directors and Head Office keep full visibility throughout — this is a curtain on one side, not a deletion.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a full-history re-pull on a takeover. Rules out treating a takeover like an ordinary widening of someone's store list. Rules out any suggestion that Head Office loses history.
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-STRUCTURE.md:270-274 (carried in); AZURE-CHUNK10-SCOPE.md §D10-9; the era boundary IS this cutoff — AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-ENFORCEMENT-MATRIX.md:68

decisions.what: Wave 3 builds only the DEVICE half of the store-ownership safety work. The matching cloud changes (the switch that pauses a store during an ownership change, the one-off permission to flush old-era data, the quarantine of late arrivals) are deliberately left to the later staging-apply phase, and the wizard screens to W5.
decisions.why: W3 was the first org wave to touch the LIVE sync engine (sync.js and db.js). Keeping it client-only meant the change had to be safe against BOTH today's cloud and tomorrow's cloud, which is a much stronger test than building both halves together and letting them assume each other.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'build the Logic App and the client together in one wave'. Rules out any client change that only works once the cloud side lands — every W3 behaviour must degrade to today's behaviour when the cloud says nothing new.

decisions.what: When a store leaves a device's list, the device must first push everything it has not yet uploaded, and only then delete the local copy. If the push fails (no internet), it deletes NOTHING and tries again next cycle.
decisions.why: The old code deleted first and pushed afterwards, so a staff member's offline entries for a store that changed hands were destroyed before they were ever uploaded. This was ground-truthed as a real, live data-loss bug, not a theoretical one.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'purge now, push later'. Rules out accepting the loss as acceptable collateral of an ownership change. Rules out a partial purge that drops some rows and keeps others.
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-W3-SCOPE.md:63-79 (design W3-1); gap mapped at sync.js:1889 / db.js:381

decisions.what: The local clear-out runs as ONE single all-or-nothing database transaction — read, check, and rewrite happen inside one locked block.
decisions.why: The first attempted fix was proven wrong on re-audit: the app reads and rewrites in two separate database operations, so a write from a second browser tab landing in the gap was wiped out completely, and the safety re-check afterwards saw nothing wrong because the row was already gone. Only one atomic block excludes that window.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the 'refresh then persist' pattern and any check-then-act fix. Rules out a post-write re-check as a substitute for a lock — it cannot see a row that has already been deleted.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, from converged AGY + Codex re-audit

decisions.what: The out-of-scope detector lives at the DATABASE layer, and EVERY durable writer — including every one written in future — must call it. Nothing may rely on the obvious funnel points.
decisions.why: The obvious choke point (scheduleSync) is not the real one: draft-transfer writes go straight to the database and bypass it, so a stale draft screen could write a row for a store the device no longer owns with nothing to detect it. This is a standing rule on all future code, buried in a closed wave's spec.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out any future durable write path that skips the scope guard. Rules out 'we checked at the entry point' as an argument — the entry point was proven not to be the entry point.

decisions.what: When the cloud pauses a store mid-ownership-change it answers with a normal SUCCESS response carrying an empty result and a 'store update in progress' flag — never an error code, and never any extra fields.
decisions.why: Deliberately a success response so that today's already-deployed app treats it as a harmless empty sync and does no damage; new app versions read the flag and show a calm hold message. Extra fields were then explicitly banned because an older client seeing a position marker in an empty response would jump its bookmark forward and skip the withheld rows forever once the pause lifted.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out signalling the pause with an error status. Rules out including a position marker or store list in the pause response. Rules out a mocked test standing in for proof — the real Logic App must be shown to emit exactly this.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, from Codex-5 and Codex R3-2

decisions.what: Cost-visibility downgrades (taking away someone's ability to see cost prices) run FIRST and unconditionally on every sync, ahead of everything else.
decisions.why: Previously a stuck data clear-out could block them indefinitely, so a demoted user could keep seeing cost prices for days while offline. A permission removal must never be starved by an unrelated failure.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out ordering permission checks behind data-scope work. Rules out treating a permission downgrade as best-effort.

decisions.what: After six review rounds the single big W4 spec was SPLIT into four separate specs (planner, pricing lens, money stamps, buy-back export), each converging on its own. The original document became a frozen history record, and on any disagreement the sub-document wins.
decisions.why: Round 6 exposed design-level divergence inside one oversized document: parts that were already agreed kept getting reopened because they shared a file with parts that were still moving. Splitting let the settled parts freeze while only the disputed parts kept looping.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out reading AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-W4-SCOPE.md as the spec — it is history only. Rules out re-opening a frozen sub-spec without formally reopening that part's review.

decisions.what: Every franchise supply line gets BOTH its sell price and its discount permanently stamped onto it at the moment the stock is actually sent — not when a draft is created. Kunal confirmed this personally.
decisions.why: Freezing only the discount left half the bug alive: a catalogue PRICE change still silently rewrote the dollar amounts on old invoices. Stamping at commit rather than draft closes the obvious abuse — create a draft, wait for a price rise, then commit at the old numbers.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out stamps as an optional extra. Rules out fixing only the discount and calling the retroactive-invoice bug closed. Rules out stamping at draft creation.
decisions.whoDecided: Kunal (confirmed), recommended by Claude + both auditors

decisions.what: Prices and discounts are filed under the STORE, and a franchise office carries its own rate as a store in its own right. The earlier design that filed them under the franchisee (with a lookup table translating store to franchisee) was thrown out.
decisions.why: The franchisee-keyed design broke the ownership-timeline rule: a franchisee who owns store A since January and buys store B in July would have one January-rooted rate set overlapping B's January-to-July head-office period. Removing the translation layer also removed a whole class of bugs where the lookup table simply missed a key.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a franchiseeId-keyed pricing map and any store-to-franchisee resolver map. Rules out 'one franchisee, one rate set' as the storage model.
decisions.supersededBy: itself supersedes the R2 franchiseeId model
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-W4-SCOPE.md:47-60 (MODEL REVISION R4); supersedes W4-SR-4 at :21 and W4-SR-16 at :33

decisions.what: EARLIER RULING, NOW DEAD: pricing was to be filed under a stable franchisee id, with a lookup map covering the office and every retail store.
decisions.why: Adopted at review round 2 to solve invoices being billed to the office id while plans were keyed to the shop id. Recorded here so nobody re-proposes it.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules itself out — do not reintroduce the franchiseeId indirection to solve an office-vs-shop keying problem.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, from Codex-1 and AGY R2-2
decisions.supersededBy: The R4 Model Revision (store-keyed pricing), AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-W4-SCOPE.md:47-60

decisions.what: A line's discount is looked up in three steps, most specific first: a rate set for that exact product at that store, then a global rate for that product, then the store's general rate. Each rate has a date range, and each line is priced using the range covering ITS OWN date.
decisions.why: This is the fix for the live money defect: today a single current discount value silently recalculates every past invoice when it is changed. Dated ranges mean past lines keep resolving their own dates' rates and retroactive rewriting dies.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out storing a discount as a single current number. Rules out 'just remember to not change the rate'. NOTE: it also, today, rules out a PRODUCT TYPE tier — the chain has exactly three levels and no product-type concept exists anywhere in the W4 specs (see open questions).
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, converged with Codex + AGY (frozen at R13, both PASS)

decisions.what: Falling back to the old single discount number is allowed ONLY before the dated system is switched on. Once any dated pricing has been served, anything broken or missing shows a loud PRICING DATA ERROR at 0% — never a quietly-plausible old number. A pricing error at dispatch REJECTS the dispatch.
decisions.why: A silent fallback is the most dangerous failure mode here: it produces a believable invoice that is wrong, and nobody ever finds out. Refusing loudly forces a Director to fix the rate before stock moves, which is the only point where it is cheap to fix.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'use the last known good rate'. Rules out storing a zero or a null as if it were a real rate. Rules out letting a supply dispatch through with unresolved pricing.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, from Codex-2 / Codex R2-1 / Codex R3-4

decisions.what: The whole pricing file is validated before ANY rate is looked up. One bad entry anywhere invalidates the entire config.
decisions.why: Otherwise a corrupted specific rate is indistinguishable from a genuinely missing one, and the system quietly falls through to a valid but WRONG lower-level rate. Validating everything first means a null after validation genuinely means 'not set'.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out lazy or per-tier validation. Rules out 'skip the broken bit and carry on'.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, from converged AGY R3-3 + Codex R3-5

decisions.what: Two behaviours were formally adjudicated as NOT defects and recorded so they are not re-raised: (a) a failed sync cycle does not invalidate the device's pricing freshness; (b) anchoring 'as of' dates to UTC midnight rather than Perth time is deliberate.
decisions.why: Both were raised by auditors, both were ground-truthed, and both are correct as built — the calendar-day anchor exists precisely so the same date string produces the same number on every device. Without this record every future auditor re-raises them and burns a round each.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out adding a freshness expiry or per-cycle invalidation as a 'bug fix' — either would be a spec change that reopens W4.2's review. Rules out re-anchoring as-of dates to local time.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, adjudication accepted by both auditors

decisions.what: Onboarding a new franchisee creates their OFFICE as a real store in the same plan, and only onboarding accepts a rate from the caller. Adding a store to an existing franchisee, or converting a company store to a franchise, COPIES the office's current open rate instead.
decisions.why: If add and convert could carry their own rate, a caller could smuggle in a rate that disagrees with the office the invoice is actually billed to. Copying makes disagreement structurally impossible rather than merely checked for.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a rate parameter on add/convert operations. Rules out setting a store's franchise rate independently of its office at creation time.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, converged with Codex + AGY (frozen at R14, both PASS)

decisions.what: A franchise office is never a target of ordinary store operations — the system refuses. An office is created by onboarding and ended only by a manual deactivation. Buying back a retail store leaves the office and its rate open.
decisions.why: The office is a real, load-bearing entity in the money model (Head Office supplies the office, the office supplies the shop floor, and the OFFICE is what gets invoiced). Letting it be bought back or converted like a shop would silently orphan the billing chain.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating the Cockburn Franchise Office as leftover data to clean up. Rules out an automated 'close the office' path — closing an empty franchisee office is a deliberate manual act.

decisions.what: Two scoped amendments were made AFTER the spec was frozen and both auditors explicitly re-approved them: the office read must carry the id it was queried for, and a missing office rate surfaces as PRICING_ERA_MISALIGNED rather than the never-reachable NO_OFFICE_PRICING.
decisions.why: An empty read otherwise carries no identity, so the planner could schedule creation over an already-occupied id. The diagnostic re-pin exists because a promised error message that can never actually appear is a lie that future auditors will keep flagging.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating a frozen spec as unamendable — but the amendment route is scoped, written down, and re-approved by both auditors, not a silent edit.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, from Codex-5/-6, both auditors PASS at round 2

decisions.what: Every stamped line carries FOUR money-authority fields together or none at all, and separately records WHICH method valued it. A partly-stamped line is treated as corrupt and fails closed.
decisions.why: A half-set of authority fields is exactly what a tamper attempt looks like, and defaulting the missing ones would fabricate authority the system never had. Keeping the method flag separate was Codex's correction — a legitimately old line durably records 'valued by the dated lens' with no stamps at all, which the all-or-nothing rule would otherwise have called corrupt.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out filling in missing money fields with defaults. Rules out treating a partial stamp set as 'good enough'. Rules out folding the valuation-method flag into the atomic money tuple.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, from Codex (AGY initially objected, then fully retracted at R23)

decisions.what: Money stamps whose only source is a restored backup are marked UNTRUSTED and are never used to value an invoice. Those lines are valued by the server instead, through a gated lookup bound to the exact row, and until that answer arrives the invoice shows 'valuation pending' rather than a number.
decisions.why: A restored backup is client-supplied data. Trusting it would let a restored transfer quietly set its own price. Showing a pending state is honest; showing a locally-computed number would make the invoice disagree with the settlement.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out valuing a restored line from local live pricing. Rules out trusting stamps that arrived via a backup file.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, converged with both auditors at R22/R23

decisions.what: A pre-existing bug dating back to Chunk 4 was found and fixed during W4.3: two transfers that differed ONLY inside their item lines produced an identical fingerprint, so one silently overwrote the other; and a flagged disagreement stayed flagged forever.
decisions.why: Flagged KUNAL-VISIBLE because it is a real money-affecting bug that existed in the shipped design and was found by accident while building something else — $100 and $150 item stamps hashed identically.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the shortcut fingerprint method that ignored nested fields. Rules out assuming pre-Chunk-4 conflict handling was sound.

decisions.what: The buy-back settlement window includes the start moment and excludes the end moment, judged on the exact UTC time on the row — never the Perth calendar date. Deletion and correction records are exempt from the window and are matched by WHICH ROW they target instead.
decisions.why: An era boundary is an instant, but a date string is a whole day, so rows minutes apart would land on the same side. Corrections are exempt because a deletion made after the buy-back legitimately sits outside the window — excluding it would count a deleted row, and including it by date would be arbitrary.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out using the row's displayed date for settlement boundaries. Rules out guessing the boundary from the calendar day when the exact time is missing — that row makes the whole export refuse.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, from Codex R3-9 and W4-SR-115/123/124

decisions.what: A settlement is PROVISIONAL by default. It only becomes FINAL when all three of these are proven: the old owner's grace period has closed, every pending upload has been accounted for, and every row the departing device claimed to send is either present, covered by a deletion record, or sitting in the rejected queue.
decisions.why: A buy-back is rare and high-stakes. A row that is in none of those three states is indistinguishable from a mid-export escape, a lag, or genuine loss — all unsafe — so the engine refuses to call the number final rather than guess.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a settlement that looks final because nothing obviously failed. Rules out inferring completeness from the rows you happen to have received.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, converged with both auditors at R25

decisions.what: Kunal's ruling: any settlement containing even one row whose quantity cannot be independently verified is HELD for manual review, not auto-finalised. This reversed the engineer's earlier position that a hard block was disproportionate.
decisions.why: Kunal's reasoning: a buy-back is rare and high-stakes, so an unverifiable quantity must never quietly become a final number someone pays. It fails safe and the settlement can be regenerated once the server-side row signature ships.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the earlier adjudication that a hard block would be disproportionate because it would hold every settlement containing a common direct-log line. Rules out surfacing an unverifiable row as a warning while still finalising.

decisions.what: Kunal's business rules on returns: stock a franchisee sends BACK to Head Office is NOT credited against their supply bill — it is treated as fresh Head Office stock, because it was already billed. Customer refunds ARE deducted from retail revenue, at the frozen price.
decisions.why: Kunal's own rule, given as a rare case: once supply has been billed to the franchisee, sending it back does not un-bill it. Customer refunds are different — that money genuinely never was revenue.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out netting HO returns off the supply bill. Rules out ignoring customer refunds in retail-profit.

decisions.what: The engine refuses to pay item-level stamps that came from an unverified source step — going BEYOND what the frozen spec requires.
decisions.why: The spec required server verification of row-level stamps only. Paying item stamps from an unverified step would reopen exactly the same forgery hole one level down. This is an engineering extension, not a spec pin, so every auditor reading only the spec flags it as unjustified unless told.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out narrowing the engine back to the spec's literal wording. Any future auditor brief must say this is deliberate.

decisions.what: Kunal FROZE the buy-back settlement engine on 2026-07-22 after seven parallel audit rounds and 29 real bugs fixed — deliberately stopping while auditors were still finding real issues, and switching to server-side work instead.
decisions.why: Every one of the last three rounds reduced to ONE root cause: the engine is checking a set of rows a franchisee could edit, with no server signature on them. Each round bound one more field and the next found the adjacent one. That class cannot be closed inside a pure engine — it needs the server to sign each row at the moment it is synced. Continuing the loop was diminishing returns.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out more engine-only audit rounds against the same class. Rules out reading the freeze as 'the engine is finished' (see the standing marker).

decisions.what: THE STANDING MARKER — the freeze does NOT mean finished. Auditors were still finding real bugs when Kunal froze it, and three classes of finding (rounds 5, 6 and 7) are only HELD as manual-review, not fixed. Once the server contracts land, the engine and server MUST be re-audited together in full. Kunal's firm marker: money-critical, never skip.
decisions.why: Without this marker the freeze reads as a clean finish, and a future session ships a settlement engine that is quietly holding three unresolved classes of tampering. The marker exists to stop that specific misreading.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out shipping any buy-back settlement without the return re-audit. Rules out treating 'engine frozen, gates green' as certification. NOTE: what the marker actually REQUIRES is still contested — see open questions.

decisions.what: On 2026-07-30 the return re-audit was formally NARROWED: it covers the engine plus Contract 1 only, at a zero-corrections baseline, and the auditor pack must say so explicitly. It must also build the signature test family FIRST, and the verdict must be written so nobody can read it as covering corrections.
decisions.why: Contract 2 was parked on 2026-07-29, so the old checklist step 'Land Contract 2' became impossible. Left unamended, an auditor flags the absent correction route as a gap and a whole round is burned. Building the test family first is the mutation-testing rule: a gate never seen to fail is not a gate — the current 170-probe suite has ZERO signature coverage.
decisions.rulesOut: Supersedes the original re-audit checklist that made 'Land Contract 2' step 2. Rules out an auditor brief that presents the correction lane as in scope. Rules out a verdict phrased as 'engine re-audited, clean'.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, as carried obligation 1 of Kunal's C2 parking decision

decisions.what: DO NOT ship Contract 1's engine change on its own. Applied by itself it is a net SAFETY REGRESSION — it was run, and it turned a deleted-movement case from held-for-review into FINAL owed 675, silently billing it. The compensating deletion guard must ship in the same batch.
decisions.why: Recorded because it was demonstrated by running it, not reasoned about. This is the single most dangerous instruction in the cluster: the change looks like a pure improvement on paper.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out applying the C1 design §4 item 1 verbatim as a standalone step.

decisions.what: Kunal's three Contract 1 rulings: (1) sign MORE fields than the minimum — approved; (2) if signing fails at upload, the whole batch is refused and retried, so a row is NEVER stored unsigned; (3) customer SALE prices are not signed, so the retail-profit figure stays informational and does not affect what is owed.
decisions.why: Signing more costs nothing and closes splice attacks. Fail-closed was chosen because unlike the existing money route there is no client-side backstop for a missing signature — devices already queue and retry, so refusing is cheap. Sale prices have no server-side record to sign against, and the payable is anchored on Head Office supply cost, not sales.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a minimum-fields signature. Rules out storing an unsigned row and signing it later. Rules out treating retail profit as an amount payable.

decisions.what: The signature itself IS the row's proof — the separately-planned plain 'this row was checked' marker was dropped. Two more fields were pulled into the signature at audit: the free-text Reason, and the four price/discount authority fields.
decisions.why: A plain marker is forgeable by exactly the same person who could tamper with the row, so it proves nothing. Reason had to be covered because when a row has no structured source the engine falls back to reading the words 'head office' out of it — editing that flips how the row is billed. The price fields had to be covered because otherwise a valid signature from another row's price could be transplanted in.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a plain server-set 'attested' column as sufficient. Rules out leaving any field the engine reads outside the signature — a full inventory was done and pinned.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, from AGY-1, AGY-2 and Codex-1 (converged), both PASS at R2

decisions.what: Each signature names the key that made it, and the server accepts any key still configured. Rotating a key means adding the new one and switching over; old signatures keep verifying. DELETING a retired key silently invalidates every signature ever made with it — and those rows then fail closed.
decisions.why: Rotation without mass re-signing was both auditors' suggestion. The deletion warning is recorded because it is a one-line Azure setting change with catastrophic, non-obvious consequences, and it exists in exactly ONE place in the whole repo.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out mass re-signing as routine (reserved for active compromise). Rules out storing signing keys anywhere but Azure Function settings — never SharePoint, never the client, never the repo. Rules out sharing the login-password key.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, merging both auditors' Q3 suggestions

decisions.what: Two more Contract 1 rulings: no blanket back-signing of old rows (pre-contract rows keep the manual-review path), and signing happens in ONE batched call per upload, with a per-row identity cross-check before each insert.
decisions.why: Back-signing would attest to rows nobody actually verified — the signature would be a lie. Batching was adjudicated in AGY's favour over Codex's 'per-row is fine' because a Monday morning offline flush can be hundreds of rows, and per-row calls multiply cost, latency and throttling risk. The identity cross-check exists so a mismatched response can never attach one row's signature to another row.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a backfill script for historic rows. Rules out per-row signing calls.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, adjudicating a split between AGY and Codex

decisions.what: Contract 1 is COMPLETE as of 2026-07-23 — spec and build both dual-audited to PASS, applied to staging, and proven through a real archive run 17 out of 17. A latent Chunk-8 bug was found and fixed on the way: the archive list stored a timestamp as text while the source stored it as a number.
decisions.why: Recorded so it is not re-litigated as outstanding work. The archive-carry piece mattered because an archived row that loses its signature is indistinguishable from a tampered one — and the upload key had NEVER been carried to the archive before.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out re-opening Contract 1 as unfinished work. Note: the ENGINE side of Contract 1 (the predicate change) is deliberately NOT done — it waits for the return re-audit, batched with its guard.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, both auditors PASS first round

decisions.what: When the re-audit was narrowed, one money hole was deliberately MOVED onto Contract 2's list rather than dropped: a published correction record's quantity or price can be edited directly in SharePoint, pass the current check, and settle FINAL at 3.75 instead of 375. It was reproduced by running it.
decisions.why: Narrowing the re-audit without re-homing this item would leave it owned by nobody — it would fall through the gap between the two lists. Kunal's note flags this as the one not to lose.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out closing the return re-audit as covering the corrections lane. Rules out fixing the related colon-id defect by loosening the id validator — it must be fixed by minting ids without colons, because the whole server phase leans on that validator.

decisions.what: The correction route — the feature that lets a director fix a mistake in a past stock record — is PARKED. It will not ride the single big end-of-phase cutover. It ships later, on its own, with its own separate audit, exactly like the franchise wizard.
decisions.why: It is the least-finished thing in the whole project: 17 confirmed defects and 7 blocking gaps on its delivery path, never deployed, never run once — while everything else is built and audited. Holding the launch behind it would risk everything that IS ready. Parking was checked first and found safe: the coupling inventory came back empty, nothing already on staging depends on the correction route existing, and there is no correction screen in the app, so no user loses a capability they already had.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out putting Contract 2 back into the single-cutover deploy; rules out re-arguing whether parking it is safe (the coupling check was run and came back empty); rules out treating the six carried obligations as optional — parking is only safe because they were written down.

decisions.what: When the correction route IS eventually built, a director's correction must reach the shop floor — the number staff see on their own device has to change. It is not allowed to be a books-only fix that only corrects reports and settlements.
decisions.why: Kunal's explicit direction. The alternative on the table was 'the server books are right, the shop floor stays stale' — which the design's own honest notes H7/H13 had accepted. That trade turned out to be worse than written: the archive job that was supposed to eventually fold the correction in is completely correction-blind, so the staleness would never expire on its own. A stale shelf number is what a stock take reads as its system count, so it can become a permanent, director-approved wrong adjustment.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the books-only / 'directors are simply told a correction fixes reports' option; rules out shipping C2 as a small route-only job — Option A makes it BIGGER, which is itself a further reason not to build it under time pressure.

decisions.what: The accepted price of parking: with the correction route parked, the business cannot produce ANY buy-back settlement at all — the figure you would owe a departing franchisee. That is fine for alpha, but it must have a slot before the ~Sep–Oct 2026 franchisee.
decisions.why: The buy-back export route is itself unbuilt and depends on Contract 2's control/tombstone assembly contract. Stating the cost openly stops a future session assuming parking was free and quietly discovering at franchisee time that no settlement can be calculated.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out claiming settlements are 'available but untested'; rules out parking C2 indefinitely without a date — it and the export route need a slot before the Sep–Oct franchisee.

decisions.what: Carried obligation 1: the return engine re-audit was formally narrowed IN WRITING to cover the money engine plus Contract 1 only. The correction lane is deliberately excluded and the engine is audited at a 'no corrections exist anywhere' baseline. This is DONE — the checklist was amended on 2026-07-30.
decisions.why: The re-audit checklist still listed 'Land Contract 2' as step 2. Left alone, an auditor would flag the missing correction route as a gap and a whole paid round would be burned arguing about something deliberately parked.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out auditors treating the absent correction route as a finding; rules out anyone re-adding Contract 2 to that checklist without re-opening the parking decision.

decisions.what: Carried obligation 2 — the one flagged 'DO NOT LOSE THIS': responsibility for making the money engine check the tamper-seals on correction records was MOVED onto Contract 2's own list. It has been physically moved out of the re-audit checklist, so it is now owned by C2 and cannot fall between the two.
decisions.why: It is a proven money hole, not a theory. The published record of a correction is bound only by its name and version number, so someone editing the quantity directly in SharePoint sails past the check. Reproduced against the real frozen engine: a settlement that should have paid 375 settled FINAL at 3.75. Narrowing the re-audit (obligation 1) without re-homing this would have left it owned by nobody.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'the engine was re-audited and came back clean' being read as covering tampered correction records; rules out fixing it inside the re-audit scope — it is C2's now.

decisions.what: Carried obligation 3: Contract 1's rule change about which stock rows the engine trusts must NEVER ship on its own. The compensating guard for deleted movements ships in the same batch.
decisions.why: Applied by itself, exactly as written, it turned a deleted-movement case from 'held for a human to look at' into FINAL owed 675 — silently billing for something that had been deleted. That is a net SAFETY REGRESSION. The guard was built and RUN and works; they only make sense together.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out splitting the predicate change out as a quick standalone win; rules out anyone reading the C1 design §4 item 1 as a self-contained instruction.

decisions.what: Carried obligation 4: before the engine re-audit runs, the test suite must be given real coverage of the new row-level tamper seal, and the three known unfixed problem cases must be made to FAIL at the verification step rather than merely be held for manual review.
decisions.why: The engine's 170-check suite has ZERO coverage of the new seal today — it still runs on the older, weaker marker. The project's own standing rule applies: a gate you have never seen fail is not a gate. Paying for an audit with nothing mechanical to bite on is not worth the money.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out booking the re-audit before the probes exist; rules out counting 170/170 green as evidence the seal works.

decisions.what: Carried obligation 5: the re-audit's verdict must be written so it cannot be over-read. It has to say in plain words that the correction lane was NOT certified.
decisions.why: The engine is being certified for a world with zero corrections in it. Without that sentence, a reader six months later takes 'engine re-audited, clean' as covering corrections — which it does not.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a bare PASS/clean verdict on the re-audit; rules out later citing the re-audit as evidence the correction path is safe.

decisions.what: Carried obligation 6: the 'never skip the engine re-audit' marker must be collapsed into ONE list in ONE place. It currently says different things in at least three places — the handover mentions it with no contents at all, the memory note lists three items, and the C2 design lists five.
decisions.why: Until it is one list, every new session re-litigates what the marker actually requires, and items quietly drop off. This has been identified as the single most important thing in the whole register to collapse.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating any one of the three (or four) versions as authoritative; rules out starting the re-audit before the list is unified.

decisions.what: The 'colon' defect is banked onto Contract 2 and must be fixed there, by giving correction records names that contain no colons. It must NOT be fixed by loosening the rule about what characters an id may contain.
decisions.why: The correction code names its records things like 'ctl:op-0001'. The settlement engine's id rule bans the colon, so the FIRST correction ever made against a store would abort that store's entire buy-back export. Proven by running it: swap the colon for a dash and the identical correction sails through. Loosening the id rule instead would weaken a validator the whole server phase leans on — and the colon is currently also an accidental safety net, the only thing stopping a correction row being sucked into the app as a phantom stock movement.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out widening the id pattern (reqId / ID_RE) as the fix; rules out treating this as an engine bug — the engine's correction machinery works fine.

decisions.what: The 'deleted movement still gets billed' problem is banked onto Contract 2 and ships with C2's tombstone-adoption piece and the buy-back export route — not fixed anywhere else, not fixed earlier.
decisions.why: Measured today: when a staff member deletes a stock movement in the app, the settlement engine skips the deletion silently and still bills the original — 375 owed, marked FINAL, with nothing surfaced to say anything was wrong. Making a staff deletion something the engine honours needs C2's registry, adoption and published manifest; there is no smaller fix.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out patching this in the engine or the export route separately; rules out claiming deletions are handled today.

decisions.what: Delivering Option A (corrections reaching the shop floor) is scoped as nine identified gaps, seven of which block arming the feature at all. They are banked onto C2 and must be treated as one package.
decisions.why: Each gap was reproduced by running the real code, not by reading it. The headline ones: an ordinary recent correction publishes a change of exactly zero and the archive job that was meant to apply it later knows nothing about corrections; a correction against an already-archived record writes the wrong column names into the archive table and fails its own self-check AFTER it has already signed and saved a row, leaving a sealed orphan every single time; the filter that was supposed to keep correction rows off staff devices exists in no deployed definition; and the app itself has literally zero code that understands what a correction row is.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'fixing delivery' as a quick win — making corrections arrive without teaching the app to read them would make a corrected item count TWICE, worse than the original mistake; rules out fixing the timestamp gap first, and rules out fixing the archive column names in isolation.

decisions.what: 'Rolled back' becomes a real, written state on a correction's progress record. An abandoned correction is treated as SETTLED, and a fresh attempt must use a brand-new operation id.
decisions.why: Two parts of the code already filter on that state and nothing has ever written it. So an abandoned correction is indistinguishable from one still in flight, and the recovery sweep re-picks dead work forever. Kunal's ruling: abandoned means settled.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out leaving abandoned corrections in limbo; rules out re-using the same operation id to retry.

decisions.what: The dangerous half of the rolled_back rule: a correction may be marked rolled back ONLY when the route can prove the change never landed AND can undo everything durable it already wrote. 'Publish may have landed' means ATTEMPTED, not failed. 'Probably didn't land' is not proof, and 'the record looks tidy now' is not undone.
decisions.why: There is a trap lane where the recovery logic positively reports 'safe to roll back', so it reads as the one post-publish case that is provably clean. It is not — by that point a sign-out row and a signed correction record have already been written and the route contains ZERO delete operations, so settling there strands the record and makes that transaction permanently uncorrectable by anyone, with no journal left for recovery to find.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out marking rolled_back anywhere downstream of the publish attempt; rules out scoping the rollback work to the emergency handler alone (the pre-commit refusal lanes bypass it entirely and would keep leaking orphans).
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, ground-truthed by running the artifact's own expressions

decisions.what: Banked contract for code nobody has written yet: the correction screen must mint a FRESH operation id for every attempt.
decisions.why: Once the rolled_back work lands, re-sending the same id returns a permanent 'already settled, failed' answer and never re-attempts. A 'try again' button that reuses the id would give the director a dead end with no way forward. Decide it now, before the screen is built — the client half of the correction route does not exist at all today.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a retry button that reuses the id; rules out discovering this after the screen is built.

decisions.what: Six known holes in the automated safety checks are recorded as a PINNED expected-to-fail baseline rather than deleted or silenced. They print loudly on every run, but they do not fail the whole local gate.
decisions.why: Deleting a failing test to make a suite green is the exact reflex that file exists to prevent. But failing the whole gate on a defect the owner consciously deferred trains everyone to ignore a red run, which costs more than it buys. The fix for all six was batch 1 of the C2 plan, and batch 1 parks with C2. One case (S-WALK-3b) is deliberately NOT parked: it is the A/B anchor proving a future fix targets the real problem rather than taking a shortcut.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out deleting the six mutations; rules out reading a green mutation run as a clean bill of health for C2; rules out un-parking S-WALK-3b.

decisions.what: If the system cannot work out the correct prices to attach to a corrected record, the correction is REJECTED with a clear reason and waits, until the dated pricing-history feature ships. It never guesses.
decisions.why: Fail closed. Guessing a price on a correction puts a wrong number straight into money that gets invoiced.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out inventing or inheriting prices for a correction; rules out shipping the correction route ahead of dated pricing history and hoping.

decisions.what: All data that exists before the server phase goes live is TRIAL data. At go-live the app starts with fresh real data.
decisions.why: Kunal's own ground truth about his business, and it de-risks two whole lanes of the design: the awkward cases around records that pre-date the new rules become defence-in-depth rather than live business paths. It is also why an unauthenticated legacy shortcut is acceptable on staging but can never be exercised in production (production cuts over on an empty archive).
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out designing migration/backfill machinery for historical trial data; rules out treating pre-epoch edge cases as production-critical. Note: a production cutover that finds a NON-empty archive must HALT and come back to Kunal, never proceed silently.

decisions.what: Deletions go through the same director correction route as replacements — one route handles both 'this record is wrong, here is the right one' and 'this record should not exist'.
decisions.why: Kunal's ruling. One adjudicated path means one place where money-affecting changes are authorised, sealed and published.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a separate delete-only mechanism; rules out a raw deletion that skips the approval route.

decisions.what: Only one job may touch the books at a time, governed by a single shared five-state 'who has the lock' record. Every state has a defined way to take over from a crashed holder, and recovery TAKES OWNERSHIP and drops a marker so a stalled worker that wakes up later can never finish its half-done job.
decisions.why: A stalled worker could otherwise wake up after recovery had already cleaned up after it and publish a change pointing at a record that no longer exists. The design also fixed the opposite failure: an unconditional 'release the lock' could let a stalled worker clobber a live successor's lock. And no state may strand the machine on a crashed holder — every one has a takeover rule.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out unconditional lock releases anywhere (including the archive job's); rules out recovery acting on a worker that is still alive; rules out any state with no takeover path.
decisions.whoDecided: auditor-driven (AGY F1/F1b, Codex 4a/4b), folded by Claude

decisions.what: After any attempt to publish a change, the route decides what actually happened by RE-READING the data — never by trusting the success/failure reply it got back. It only undoes work after positively reading proof the change did not land.
decisions.why: The classic lost-acknowledgement problem: the change applies, the reply gets lost, and a naive route then rolls back a correction that had genuinely gone through. If the answer is ambiguous or unreadable, the job stays open for recovery rather than guessing.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out deciding rollback on an HTTP error; rules out any silent rollback of a possibly-published correction.

decisions.what: The 'sign this record out for work' step was moved DOWN to the last possible moment before the point of no return — and the fix was that move, not adding clean-up deletes. Its position is now pinned by an automated rule, not by memory.
decisions.why: Arming the route armed a trap. The sign-out book refuses duplicates and the route has no delete anywhere, and there were five refusal lanes BELOW the sign-out step. So a single refused correction would have made its target permanently uncorrectable by anyone, forever.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out solving it with compensating deletes at each refusal lane; rules out anyone moving the step back up on the basis that 'it reads better there' — a mechanical reachability rule now blocks that.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude (raised against the 46-edit wave before it shipped)

decisions.what: For the correction record's tamper seal only, 'empty' and 'not there at all' are now treated as the same thing. This deliberately NARROWS a previously converged rule and was flagged to the auditors as a rule change, not a routine fix.
decisions.why: The seal could not survive its own storage. A deletion-type correction is built with twelve fields absent; the database hands them back present-but-empty. Under the strict rule every deletion correction would be rejected by its own self-check — and no future verifier could ever reproduce the seal either. The narrowing is scoped to that one seal format on purpose; the equivalent format used by the archive run records deliberately keeps the strict distinction.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out applying the collapse to the other seal formats; rules out treating this as a quiet fold — it changes a rule both auditors had already passed.
decisions.whoDecided: Claude, flagged to auditors as QZ1

decisions.what: The workflow that runs a correction contains no decision-making of its own. All the arithmetic and all the 'is this allowed?' rules live in one testable function; the workflow only executes what that function returns.
decisions.why: An audit round found the workflow had drifted into doing the balance arithmetic and the legality checks itself, in workflow expressions — which cannot be unit-tested, cannot be probed, and were exactly where errors hid. Two new compute operations were added so that zero arithmetic and zero legality conditions remain in the workflow.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out adding 'just one small condition' to the workflow later; rules out testing the route by reading the workflow.

decisions.what: Correction records are never sent down to staff devices, and the buy-back export's ordinary row queries exclude them too — a correction reaches the engine only inside its proper correction envelope.
decisions.why: Correction records live in the same ledger table as ordinary movements. Without the filter, the engine would see the replacement twice and refuse the whole export, and a replacement row would land on a staff device as a phantom extra stock movement — a double count.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out letting devices read correction rows as a shortcut to Option A delivery; rules out fixing device visibility without also teaching the app what a correction IS.

decisions.what: If the system ever detects that its core safety rule has been broken, archives and exports stop for the WHOLE business, not just one store, until a director resolves it. The loud full stop is deliberate.
decisions.why: There is one shared coordination record and one shared snapshot, so the blast radius is global by construction anyway. Quietly carrying on in part of the business over a broken invariant is exactly how money goes silently wrong. Reaching this state requires a should-never-happen violation in the first place.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a per-store degradation mode; rules out auto-recovering from this state without a person.

decisions.what: A deletion made on a store device now reaches OTHER devices only after the server has accepted it — in practice one sync round-trip later, seconds to minutes. The deleting device still sees it instantly.
decisions.why: That small delay is what guarantees a deletion that loses a race against a director's correction can never reach the other devices at all. Before this, a losing deletion could permanently remove the original record on every device with no way back. The accepted deletion is then sent out as a fresh row through the ordinary sync path, because the earlier design flipped the original row in place — which devices that had already synced past it would never have seen.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out publishing a device deletion straight to peers; rules out flipping an existing row's state in place as the delivery mechanism.

decisions.what: No backfill of historical deletions into the new register. Instead, when the route trips over an existing untracked deletion it registers it on the spot.
decisions.why: Backfilling old records is a large, risky, one-shot migration for a lane that is defence-in-depth on trial data anyway (see D-C2-2). The on-the-spot registration is the compensating control and is deliberately documented as such.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out proposing a registry backfill migration; rules out treating an unregistered old deletion as a blocker.

decisions.what: The correction route's DESIGN is converged — both auditors passed the identical revision after 25 rounds and roughly 110 real findings, every one ground-truthed. But design convergence explicitly does NOT mean the built thing is signed off: three specific proofs were named as things that must be demonstrated at the staging test, not assumed.
decisions.why: Written into the design's own header so nobody later cites 'converged, both PASS' as clearance to deploy. The three named proofs are about completeness of checks, retrying rather than assuming 'absent' when a read is inconclusive, and the order two recovery steps must run in.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out reading 'SPEC CONVERGED, both auditors PASS' as build sign-off; rules out skipping the staging end-to-end and crash drill.
decisions.whoDecided: Codex R25 PASS + AGY R24/R25 confirm, recorded by Claude

decisions.what: The built-but-never-deployed artifacts carry 17 confirmed defects with an ordered eight-batch fix plan, gate repairs BEFORE product fixes. Five of them are capabilities the spec asked for that were simply never built. This whole plan parks with C2.
decisions.why: All four automated gates were GREEN on every one of these defects, so the fixes have to land behind repaired detectors or they cannot be trusted. Three of the six repair types fail 100% of the time today; a correction that fails partway leaves a stuck record and a signed orphan forever; and the tamper-seal check before the point of no return was proven blind — a forged seal and a completely stripped seal both compared as 'identical'.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out cherry-picking the small batches and deferring the big ones to 'after alpha' (that ships a correction feature that looks maintained and cannot correct anything); rules out landing the mode/target fix before the reservation fix — on its own it is strictly WORSE than today and permanently burns a slot; rules out presenting a green gate run as evidence the spec is implemented.
decisions.whoDecided: auditor-driven (Codex R12 5/5 + AGY R12 4/4 confirmed) + internal, ground-truthed by Claude

decisions.what: Today's re-sort of the backlog by RISK explicitly names the correction route as SECURITY work, and therefore as something that MAY follow release.
decisions.why: Kunal ruled that staff are not technically inclined and are not a hostile-user threat — six salons, known people, internal use only. Security hardening had been blocking a queue of money and data-leak defects that need none of it. Data leaks, money/logic defects and feature gaps may NOT be deferred.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out resuming C2 ahead of the Cockburn pricing-history fix, the Southlands ownership-era record, and the pull-hardening install. See the open question below — this classification sits awkwardly against C2 also parking all buy-back settlements and the deleted-movement over-bill, both of which are money.

decisions.what: Remaining work is now sorted by RISK, not by chunk order. Because staff are known people at six salons, not technically inclined and not a threat, SECURITY hardening (moving permission checks from the browser into the cloud) MAY ship after release. But DATA LEAKS (one store or franchisee seeing another's figures, or a prior owner's history), LOGIC/MONEY defects and FEATURE GAPS may NOT be deferred.
decisions.why: The app has spent about a month on security hardening (Account Access items 5-11, the correction route) while a queue of money and data-leak defects that need none of it sat behind them. The threat the hardening protects against is a hostile insider with developer tools — which is not the risk this business actually faces. The risks that ARE real have dates on them: Cockburn's franchise discount is wrong today, Southlands may convert around Sep-Oct.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out resuming Account Access items 5-11, Item 5 or the correction route ahead of the pricing-history and ownership-era work. Rules out the old 'finish the chunks in order' sequencing. Also rules out the opposite over-read — it does NOT license deferring anything that leaks data, computes money wrongly, or leaves a promised feature missing.

decisions.what: Ardross and Bunbury are closed stores and are to be DELETED outright from the app, not kept as inactive records.
decisions.why: The app has never been used in production, so there is no genuine trading history attached to either store that needs preserving. Keeping dead stores as inactive rows only exists to protect real history; with none to protect, they are just clutter that shows up in dropdowns, reports and test fixtures and makes every store list wrong.
decisions.rulesOut: Supersedes the earlier ruling that Ardross be kept as an inactive store with its history preserved. Rules out 'deactivate and hide' as the treatment for these two. Does NOT set a precedent for stores that HAVE traded — once the app is live, closing a store must still mean deactivate, never delete.
decisions.source: Kunal, 2026-08-01 (verbal, not yet in any file). Live code still has them: index.html:602 ardross active:true, index.html:604 bunbury active:true

decisions.what: The Online Store is a real selling location — website and social-media sales — operated by Head Office. It needs no login or credential of its own for now.
decisions.why: Sales genuinely happen through it, so stock has to move out of it and be reported against it; treating it as a fiction would put those sales nowhere. But nobody sits at an 'online store' device — Head Office staff record those sales — so giving it a credential would create an account with no user, which is a security liability for no benefit.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out deleting the Online Store as a leftover test row. Rules out minting a store credential / device key for it in the cutover credential set, and rules out counting it when sizing the account list.
decisions.source: Kunal, 2026-08-01 (verbal). Entity exists in live code: index.html:609 { id:'online', name:'Online Store', type:'online', active:true }

decisions.what: The franchise discount is THREE tiers, most specific wins: a universal store-wide rate, overridden by a PRODUCT TYPE rate, overridden by a per-product rate. Setting the franchise discount must be possible at the moment a product type is created. Cockburn's real rates: Retail 50%, professional roughly 25%; Cleaning and Stationery are partly supplied and need rates too.
decisions.why: One flat percentage per store cannot express how the business actually supplies a franchisee — retail product and professional product carry genuinely different margins, and some categories are only partly supplied. Without a middle tier, every product in a category has to be set individually, which guarantees somebody misses one and a line gets invoiced at the wrong rate.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the current two-tier product-then-store fallback as sufficient. Rules out hard-coding Cockburn at a single 25%. Rules out a product-type screen that cannot set a rate. Does NOT change the separate ruling that a franchisee's own cost is franchisee-entered and is never BOB's cost.
decisions.source: Kunal, 2026-08-01 (verbal). Today the app has only TWO tiers: index.html:3418 discPct = per-product franchiseDiscount ?? store franchiseDiscount; index.html:603-604 Cockburn + Cockburn Office both flat 25%

decisions.what: The 16 seeded account passwords and PINs shipped in the app file are throwaway demo values, not real credentials. They must still be rotated before launch, but this is not an emergency and needs no unplanned deploy.
decisions.why: They were placed there to make the demo usable, not to protect anything, and the app is not in use, so nothing real is behind them. But they are named after real people (both directors included) and the file is publicly served from the live address, so anyone who found them could pre-compute the answers and be waiting on launch day. Rotating at cutover, with the other secrets, is the right trust boundary.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating this as a live security incident requiring an out-of-band deploy. Rules out ALSO forgetting it — it must be a named line on the cutover checklist, which today contains no mention of seed accounts or passwords at all.
decisions.source: Kunal, 2026-08-01 (verbal). Verified present: 16 seeded accounts carrying password hashes in index.html (count only; values <redacted>) — on this branch AND on main, which is what is live

decisions.what: A single living FEATURE + DECISION REGISTER is to be built and kept current, and it doubles as training material for staff and Head Office. It is being built BEFORE the Cockburn pricing work and the Southlands ownership work.
decisions.why: There are around a hundred documents at the repo root, each a snapshot of a past moment and none a record of current truth. Decisions get silently re-argued because the reasoning behind them lives in a file nobody opens. Kunal is not a developer and should not have to personally remember rulings made months ago. Building it first also means the pricing and ownership work gets recorded properly as it happens instead of adding two more snapshots.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the sequencing where Cockburn pricing goes first. Rules out leaving the register in audit-artifacts/ (gitignored — it would vanish with the machine). Rules out a developer-facing document: it must read as plain English because staff will be trained from it.
decisions.source: Kunal, 2026-08-01 (verbal). Partial prior attempt exists at audit-artifacts/MASTER-DECISION-REGISTER.md (built 2026-07-30) — but that path is gitignored, so it does not survive this machine

decisions.what: The Cockburn Franchise Office is a deliberate, load-bearing part of the business model, not a leftover test record. Head Office supplies the OFFICE; the office supplies the shop floor; and the OFFICE is what gets invoiced.
decisions.why: A franchisee is run as a miniature version of the business that BOB both supplies and tracks. Stock leaving Head Office to the franchise office is a genuine wholesale sale and is what BOB bills; what moves from the office to the Cockburn shop floor is the franchisee's own internal transfer and is none of BOB's billing. Collapsing the two would either bill the franchisee twice or bill them for the wrong movement.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out deleting cockburn_office in any store-list cleanup (it sits next to Ardross and Bunbury, which ARE being deleted — do not sweep it up with them). Rules out billing the franchise invoice off franchise-STORE receipts, which is what the current code targets and which is a known defect.
decisions.source: Kunal, 2026-08-01 (verbal), confirming the model at audit-artifacts/WAVE-K-TIER4-SCOPE.md §C. Entity live at index.html:604 { id:'cockburn_office', isFranchiseOffice:true }

decisions.what: The franchise wizard (the Director screen that creates stores, onboards franchisees, converts a company store to a franchise and buys one back) is NOT part of the single launch deploy. It ships afterwards as its own smaller, separately-audited release. If it is not ready when the new franchisee arrives around Sep-Oct 2026, a written step-by-step manual onboarding routine covers that franchisee instead.
decisions.why: The one-cutover rule exists to avoid a string of risky deploys before launch — it was never meant to hold the entire launch behind a screen that only a director ever opens and no staff member will ever touch.
