Holding staff back for months for something none of them will use is the wrong trade. The manual routine already exists on paper and is safe, so the wizard serves the NEXT onboarding, which is the one that actually saves time.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the absolute 'nothing ships until every chunk is built and audited' gate. Rules out the Sep-Oct franchisee being treated as a launch blocker. Does NOT relax the one-cutover rule for anything else — everything except the wizard and the correction route still lands in one deploy.

decisions.what: No store device, franchisee stores included, receives the app until ALL chunks are built and audited.
decisions.why: Written as a hard rollout gate so that no store could end up running a half-finished permission model.
decisions.rulesOut: It is still written in capitals as a hard gate in three separate files, so a future reader could reasonably refuse to launch on the strength of it. It no longer holds: the org-structure chunk is deliberately NOT built at launch, and the correction route is parked.
decisions.supersededBy: CUT-2 (franchise wizard split out, 2026-07-29) and CUT-3 (Contract 2 parked, 2026-07-29)

decisions.what: Contract 2 — the correction route that lets a director fix a mistake in a stock record — is PARKED. It ships later as its own separately-audited deploy. When it IS built, corrections must reach the shop floor, not just the books (Option A).
decisions.why: It is the least-finished thing in the project — 17 confirmed defects plus blocking gaps on its delivery path, never deployed, never run — while everything else is built and audited. Parking was checked to be safe: nothing already applied depends on it and there is no correction screen in the app, so no user loses something they had. The cost, stated plainly: it also parks the ability to produce any buy-back settlement figure.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out building the correction route under launch time pressure. Rules out a books-only correction that leaves the shop floor showing the old number. Rules out producing a franchise buy-back settlement before it lands — which matters for the Sep-Oct franchisee. Parking is only safe if six written obligations are honoured (HANDOVER.md:424-470), one of which is a run-demonstrated money hole where a settlement came out at 3.75 instead of 375.

decisions.what: Item 5 (the ingest validation edits) is PARKED as of 2026-08-01. Sessions 1-6 of the staging apply proceed without it; it is applied last. It may not be resumed until FOUR preconditions are all met, no partial credit: (1) the edits file is complete at 58 of 58 actions with real definitions and the replacement values for every existing edit; (2) the four validator blind spots are closed, each with a self-test seen to actually fire; (3) coverage is stated as a measured number, never as an adjective like 'authoritative'; (4) the enforcement switch is re-derived so that an ABSENT switch row means OFF.
decisions.why: Three audit rounds, three BLOCKs, both auditors every time — and the recurring cause was never a missing check, it was claiming something was covered or authoritative before it was. Round 3 found the 'authoritative' file actually broke the safety property it existed to guarantee: with no switch row present, enforcement turned ON, the exact inverse of what was intended, and all four checks passed it. Since nothing in sessions 1-6 depends on Item 5, letting it be the bottleneck buys nothing.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out resuming Item 5 on a partial fix — resuming early is precisely what produced three wasted rounds. Rules out sending it to auditors again with prose corrections hand-patched into the document; the machine-checkable half must be data with a validator. Under the 2026-08-01 risk re-sort it is security work anyway, so it sits behind the money and data-leak queue.

decisions.what: 'Clear PIN' is an instant kill switch — clearing it immediately revokes unlock grants already handed out, rather than letting them run out on their own timer.
decisions.why: A director clears a PIN because something has gone wrong right now; a revocation that takes hours to take effect is not a revocation.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the time-to-live design. IMPORTANT STALE RECORD: HANDOVER.md:672-674 still files this under 'Owner decisions waiting' and the project memory index still lists it open — it is decided, built and tested, and both open lists should drop it. A separate question it does NOT answer is still genuinely open (see open questions: what happens to counts a staff member already took).

decisions.what: ONE master enforcement switch governs the whole Account Access chunk. Every gated cloud step reads a single switch record and stays completely inert while that record is absent — including after a permission policy has been published. Publishing and enforcing are two separate acts.
decisions.why: It buys a rehearsal: publish the policy, confirm every door actually reads it, then flip the switch. Undo is flipping it back, and the policy survives. It exists because three of the cloud changes had no activation branch at all and, applied literally, each would have broken its own working director door the instant it landed.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the earlier design where the cost door and the archive door armed themselves the moment a policy was published. Rules out any gated step being written without an activation branch. Note the switch record, its writer and its nine readers do not exist in the cloud yet — this is unbuilt, not merely unflipped.

decisions.what: When Account Access is switched on, seeing what products COST is directors only. Head Office is added later by editing the policy, not by changing code.
decisions.why: 'Added later by editing the policy' was written as an acceptance test in its own right — if adding Head Office turned out to need a code change, the whole configurable-permissions design would have failed its purpose.
decisions.rulesOut: Contradicts the enforcement matrix, which still seeds cost visibility as 'director plus corporate Head Office' — the code follows this decision, not the matrix. Practical effect: today a Head Office computer with nobody logged in receives the full cost list; after activation it will not. Carries a companion defect that must be fixed BEFORE activation: the app fetches costs at start-up before anyone logs in and silently swallows the refusal, so director devices would sit on stale costs forever (sync.js:815).

decisions.what: When a company store converts to a franchise, the store's own till/POS login STAYS (same login, only who owns it changes), but the personal accounts tied to that store — staff, store manager, territory manager — are cancelled, and the franchisee sets up their own people.
decisions.why: The store keeps operating through the same physical till on the same day; forcing a new login at the moment of handover creates an outage for no reason. The people, though, are BOB's employees, not the franchisee's, so their personal access must end at the boundary.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out reissuing the store login at conversion. Rules out leaving BOB staff accounts pointed at a store BOB no longer owns. Carries an explicit open nuance about territory managers — see open questions.

decisions.what: There is no direct franchisee-to-franchisee sale. If a store moves between franchisees it is done in two steps: buy it back to Head Office first, then reassign it out to the new franchisee.
decisions.why: The two-step route reuses paths that already exist, so no new tool is needed. More importantly it puts a clean Head Office period between the two franchise periods, which is exactly what stops the incoming franchisee ever being able to see the outgoing one's trading history.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out building a fifth wizard tool for direct transfers. Rules out any design that would have to reason about two consecutive franchise owners with no gap between them.

decisions.what: When a franchisee's last store leaves them, the wizard does NOT touch their office account. It is left active and a director switches it off by hand once stock and money are settled.
decisions.why: There is usually still stock to move and money to settle after the store itself changes hands. Automatically cutting off their office account at the moment of buy-back would lock them out mid-settlement.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out automatic deactivation of an emptied franchise office. THIS IS THE 'EX-FRANCHISEE OFFICE ACCOUNT' QUESTION — it is answered, but HANDOVER.md:675 still lists it as an owner decision waiting, and AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-STRUCTURE.md:237 also still asks it as 'still open' 200 lines after answering it. Both should become links to this ruling.

decisions.what: An outgoing franchisee gets a DATA EXPORT of their own ownership period at buy-back — not continuing live access to the app. The export is a spreadsheet bundle produced as a step inside the wizard, covering, per product: what they used, what it cost them, and their retail profitability. Not the raw movement list — the computed summary.
decisions.why: They need their records for tax and accounting, which an export satisfies completely. Leaving them logged in instead would mean building and maintaining a whole 'historical read-only window' mechanism, and would leave a former business partner holding live access. Making it a step inside the wizard is what stops it being forgotten on the day.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out lingering read-only access for an ex-franchisee. Rules out handing over the raw ledger. NOTE THE UNRESOLVED TENSION: the 'retail profitability' line in this export is the only profit figure left in the product after the 2026-06-16 no-profitability ruling — see open questions.

decisions.what: Before any store or ownership change is committed, the wizard shows a plain-English summary of exactly what is about to change — for example 'moves Booragoon from Head Office to Franchisee X; X sees data from today onward; Head Office keeps the full history; the store till login stays; these 2 manager logins are cancelled' — and the director confirms that before anything is written.
decisions.why: These operations rewrite who can see what across several accounts at once and cannot be sensibly undone. A director should be able to read, in ordinary words, what is about to happen before it happens.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a silent 'save' button on any topology change. Sets the standard that the confirmation is written for a business owner, not a developer.

decisions.what: When a company store converts to a franchise, the new franchisee starts from an opening balance as at the takeover date. They do not get a full re-pull of the store's history, and the pre-takeover cost history stays with Head Office.
decisions.why: The store's trading history before the handover is BOB's commercial information, including what BOB paid for stock. Handing it to the incoming franchisee along with the store would be a real disclosure, not a technicality.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating a takeover as an ordinary widening of someone's access (which DOES re-pull everything). NOT BUILT, and dangerous: the ownership record this depends on has never existed anywhere, and because the archive service treats 'no filter specified' as 'send everything', a naive build of this would hand the new franchisee the previous owner's ENTIRE trading history — the exact opposite of the intent. This is risk #2 on the 2026-08-01 work queue, with a Sep-Oct date on it.
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK10-SCOPE.md:141-157 (locked by Kunal 2026-07-08); carried to AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-STRUCTURE.md:272-276

decisions.what: Buying a franchised store back under Head Office is IN SCOPE, not a hypothetical edge case — it really happened last year. And the money side needs no special machinery: the records only ever store quantities, with prices and franchise discounts applied at the moment a report is viewed, so buying a store back simply means the franchise discount stops being applied.
decisions.why: Kunal's own insight, then checked against the code and confirmed: the franchise loading is never baked into stored rows. So there is no cost snapshot to take, nothing to reset, and no contamination to clean up — flip the flag off and the numbers are simply right from then on. An auditor's concern about cost contamination assumed baked-in pricing the app does not do.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out building cost-boundary machinery for buy-back. Rules out treating buy-back as a parked edge case. Does NOT remove the need for ownership periods — those still govern WHOSE history a franchisee may see; this ruling only covers which prices are applied.

decisions.what: The app is a stock and costing tool, not an accounting system. There is NO profitability, margin or profit-and-loss anywhere: the computed profit and margin figures are dropped and the Margin Report is removed. Reports show two honest numbers — Gross Sales and Total Cost — and let the reader see the gap themselves.
decisions.why: Kunal's direct words: 'the app is a stock + costing tool, not accounting.' It also removes a whole class of risk — every computed profit figure is another live money number that can be wrong in a way nobody notices.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out re-adding any margin or profit column, including the broken store-comparison profit column — that becomes a removal, not a fix. DIRECTLY IN TENSION with the ex-franchisee buy-back export, which is specified to produce a retail-profit summary — see open questions. Also carries its own unanswered micro-confirmation (that 'Total Cost' means cost of goods sold, not the value of stock sitting on the shelf).
decisions.source: audit-artifacts/WAVE-K-TIER4-SCOPE.md:168 (FOLLOW-UP DECISIONS, 2026-06-16) and the CONSOLIDATED FINAL PLAN below it

decisions.what: The franchise invoice bills ONLY genuine supply from Head Office to the franchise — never returns and never adjustments. Locked.
decisions.why: Returns and adjustments are corrections to what was already supplied, not new supply. Billing them would charge the franchisee twice for the same goods.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out any billing rule derived from total stock movement. Note the current code bills off the wrong side of the transaction (franchise-store receipts rather than Head-Office-to-franchise-office supply) — a known, unfixed defect.

decisions.what: Stock a franchisee returns to Head Office is NOT credited against their supply bill — it is treated as fresh Head Office stock arriving, because it was already billed to them. Customer refunds, by contrast, ARE netted off: a refund reverses the sale and reduces recorded revenue at the price at the time.
decisions.why: Kunal's rule, and it turns on who already paid. The franchisee has already been invoiced for supply, and the case is rare, so re-opening the invoice is not worth it. A customer refund is different — the sale genuinely did not happen, so leaving it in revenue would overstate sales.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out crediting franchise returns against the supply bill. Rules out leaving refunded sales in the sales total. NOTE: this resolves two PARTS of note N9 — the third part, the retail-profit formula itself, is still unanswered.
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-W44-AUDIT-RESPONSE.md:106 ('N9 RESOLVED by Kunal 2026-07-20'); built, proofs 133 to 135

decisions.what: Official transfer policy: a franchisee ranks at territory-manager level (both run multiple locations); a store manager is local-store only and CANNOT send transfers. Creating/sending and cancelling a transfer is for franchisees, territory managers, Head Office and directors, with franchisees and territory managers limited to stores they actually control. Receiving is any staff member at the receiving store. Resolving a discrepancy or writing stock off is DIRECTOR ONLY.
decisions.why: It matches how the business actually works: the people who run multiple locations move stock between them; a store manager runs one shop and receives what is sent. Writing stock off is a money decision, so it stops with a director.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out implementing this as a simple seniority ladder — the code's internal role order puts franchisee BELOW store manager, which contradicts the business hierarchy, so it must be written as explicit lists of roles. That constraint is live-relevant right now because the Account Access work makes roles data-driven and could quietly reintroduce a ladder.

decisions.what: Two known weaknesses accepted for the small trusted alpha, to be hardened before wider use: (a) the high-impact operations (creating users, changing roles, deleting, seeing cost) are hidden in the browser rather than actually enforced, so a logged-in staff member with developer tools could promote themselves; (b) the backup export file contains the user table including password and PIN hashes.
decisions.why: The alpha is director-only backups and a handful of known staff. Both are real, both were written down rather than glossed over, and both were given a beta deadline rather than being closed at the time.
decisions.rulesOut: Half (b) is now closed — the backup export scrubs the secrets (index.html:3910). Half (a) is still open in substance and is exactly the class the 2026-08-01 risk re-sort says MAY follow release. But the same hole has since re-opened on the IMPORT side, which is NOT the same acceptance: the backup import validates products, stores, money and quantities hard but checks the users list only for being a list, so a shared or crafted backup can add a director account with a password the sender knows. That is not covered by this acceptance.

decisions.what: Accounts are per ROLE AND LOCATION, not per person. There are no individual staff logins — roughly two accounts per store (a basic store account and a store manager), about 15-40 in total. Staff still type their name on each movement, as a label, not as a login.
decisions.why: Six salons with shared tills; individual logins would mean dozens of accounts to create, reset and revoke for no gain, because the till is shared anyway. Keeping the name as a label preserves who-did-what on the record without pretending it is authentication.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out per-person logins in this generation of the app. Rules out treating the typed staff name as proof of identity in any report or audit statement — the standing honest-language rule is that no report may ever claim 'person X personally did it'.

decisions.what: Kunal sets and keeps everyone's passwords. No self-service reset, no forced-change-on-first-login. Minimum 8 characters, 10 for director accounts. Auditors are to treat 'the director knows every password' as an accepted business trust model, not a finding.
decisions.why: Six salons of known people with shared tills; a self-service reset flow is machinery for a problem this business does not have, and the director is the one who onboards and offboards staff anyway.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out building password self-service. Rules out an auditor reporting shared-password knowledge as a defect. Its corollary is the honest-audit-language rule above.

decisions.what: Approving a stock take and resolving a transfer discrepancy move fully into the cloud. Kunal: 'I ultimately don't want anything in the browser that is not in the cloud.' Targeted at the first server wave after launch, but tracked as a real commitment, not an aspiration.
decisions.why: These are the two director-only actions where the check today happens in the browser, which means it is a display rule rather than an enforced one. What protects the business meanwhile is that the movement history is append-only, so everything leaves a trail.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out closing this out as 'good enough' because the browser hides the button. Under the 2026-08-01 risk re-sort this is security work and MAY follow release — but it is a commitment with a named target, not an open question. The document it lives in is headed 'Status: OPEN' and is otherwise almost entirely superseded, so readers skim past it.

decisions.what: There is a third class of credential — the DIRECTOR key — held by Kunal and Shahin on four personal devices. It works from any store and gates adjustments, delivery records, stock-take approvals, transfer resolution and cancellation, and anything that changes cost.
decisions.why: Kunal explicitly rejected the cheaper approximation that 'a Head Office device is close enough to a director'. Directors act from any store on their own phones, and the actions above are the ones that move money; tying them to a location would either block real work or hand a location director powers.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out folding director rights into the Head Office device class. Carries an accepted caveat in writing: a leaked director key means write control over every store until it is rotated.

decisions.what: All secret rotation and relocation happens AT the launch cutover, not months early.
decisions.why: Rotate at the boundary you are actually protecting. Rotating early just means rotating twice, and the intervening period is no safer.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out emergency rotations for known-and-accepted items — which is why the 16 demo passwords (K-2026-08-01-E) need no unplanned deploy, and why the deployment token sitting in plain text in the workflow file is knowingly left until cutover. It does NOT rule out rotating something actually exposed.

decisions.what: Leave the read-only auditor cloud login and the wide tenant-level app permissions in place for now; tear them down before beta.
decisions.why: The app is not in use and the auditor credential is still needed for the outstanding settlement-engine re-audit. This is the one part of the security checklist that was actually checked against the live cloud on the day it was written.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out tearing it down now and having to re-mint it for the engine re-audit. Two facts qualify it: the auditor app has TWO secrets, not one, and the second runs to 2027-01-22 — so 'just let it lapse' leaves outside read access live for six more months. And a separate app registration holds tenant-wide control over the ENTIRE Microsoft 365 tenant (HR, finance, contracts) with a secret valid to 2028, referenced by no code at all.

decisions.what: External auditors must RUN the checks themselves every wave, not accept a reported result. They report findings only and never edit files. Both auditors always get the SAME complete brief — questions are never split by which auditor is thought to be stronger.
decisions.why: A static read misses runtime bugs, and the harness needs no credentials so there is no excuse. The both-auditors rule earned itself immediately: on the Item 5 spec review one auditor passed a question outright while the other found a counter-example to it, so splitting the questions would have shipped the defect.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out accepting a reported test run. Rules out using an agent that edits files as an auditor. Rules out sending auditor A the 'hard' questions and auditor B the rest, even to save time or credits.
decisions.source: AZURE-CHUNK-PROCESS.md:42-46; HANDOVER.md:104-110; commit 05fe86a ('Process: both auditors always get the SAME complete brief (Kunal 2026-07-31)')

decisions.what: For the big final blind audit, auditors will DELIBERATELY be given live cloud access — specific callback addresses, a staging director key, a function key and scoped write access to a test area — minted at audit time and revoked afterwards. Separately, an unauthenticated pass-through service was deleted in July with a standing rule never to recreate one; mint a properly scoped credential instead.
decisions.why: An earlier blind audit degenerated into a code-only read because the auditors could not touch anything, which is precisely the failure mode the audits exist to avoid.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a credential-free final audit. Rules out recreating an open proxy as a shortcut — which matters right now, because the service being deliberately KEPT for seeding (bob-stock-tmp-c9) is the same shape of object.

decisions.what: 'Adopt' (the director action that formally accepts a shop-floor deletion) should join the existing update lane rather than being treated as a separate design question. Kunal explicitly required this be PROVEN by actually running it before anything was built on top of it.
decisions.why: Kunal's standing preference for a demonstrated result over a plausible argument.
decisions.rulesOut: THE PROOF WAS RUN AND IT REFUTED THE REASONING. Both independent attempts refuted the central mechanism at high confidence: the assumption that the record already has a registry line before adopt runs is not true, there is a reachable path where adopt creates a line and never closes it, and — the blocker — adopt as written in the specification carries no record identifier at all, so it is rejected at the door and cannot be invoked in its specified form today. The conclusion (adopt must not create a reservation) survives; the stated reason did not. HANDOVER still says 'do not treat as settled until that verification is recorded here' and the verification is NOT recorded there — it lives only in a gitignored file. Kunal's requirement is met but the answer never came back to him.

decisions.what: Remaining work is now sorted by RISK, not by chunk order. Because staff are known, non-technical people and not a hostile-user threat, SECURITY hardening (moving permission checks from the browser to the cloud) may follow release — but DATA LEAKS, LOGIC/MONEY defects and FEATURE GAPS may not be deferred.
decisions.why: Six salons, internal use, no public sign-up. The old order put a month of security work in front of money and data-leak defects that need none of it. Risk to the business, not chunk numbering, decides what gets built first.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out resuming Account Access items 5-11, the correction route, or any other security-hardening work ahead of the money/leak queue. Also rules out the old blanket rule 'client-side auth must move server-side BEFORE beta' as an absolute launch gate — it becomes a post-release item.

decisions.what: Ardross and Bunbury are closed and are to be DELETED outright from the system, not deactivated. The real store list is Booragoon, Claremont, Karrinyup, Whitfords, Southlands, Cockburn (already franchised) plus Head Office.
decisions.why: The app was never actually used at those two sites, so there is no real trading history worth preserving. Keeping dead stores as 'inactive' clutters every picker and every report for no benefit.
decisions.rulesOut: Overturns the earlier 2026-06-16 ruling 'Ardross = CLOSED, keep inactive with history preserved'. Rules out any future proposal to soft-deactivate them. Also rules out trusting the store list in CLAUDE.md section 1, which still names Ardross as an operating location.
decisions.source: HANDOVER.md:145-161; commit fba1962; supersedes audit-artifacts/WAVE-K-TIER4-SCOPE.md follow-up decisions

decisions.what: The Online Store is a real selling location (website plus social media), run by Head Office. It needs no login or credential of its own for now.
decisions.why: Head Office staff already have accounts and are the only people who fulfil online orders, so a separate credential would add an account to manage with nothing extra to protect.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating the Online Store as a data-entry error or an unmodelled channel, and rules out minting it a store key at cutover.
decisions.source: 2026-08-01 session (Kunal, verbal — not yet in any repo file)

decisions.what: The franchise discount has THREE tiers, most specific wins: a universal store rate, overridden by a PRODUCT TYPE rate, overridden by a per-product rate. Setting the franchise discount must be available at the moment a product type is created. Cockburn today: retail 50%, professional about 25%; Cleaning and Stationery are partly supplied and need their own rates.
decisions.why: A single store-wide percentage cannot express the real commercial arrangement — retail stock and professional stock are supplied on different terms, and some categories are only partly supplied. Without the product-type tier the discount has to be typed onto every product one at a time.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a single flat per-store discount as the model. Note: the code today implements only TWO tiers (store default '*' and per-product) at index.html:1233-1241 — the product-type tier does not exist yet and is new work, not a documentation fix.

decisions.what: The 16 account passwords and PINs shipped inside the app file are throwaway demo values, not real credentials. They still must be rotated before launch. No emergency deploy is needed.
decisions.why: Nobody uses those logins; they were seeded to make the app usable during building. Treating them as a live breach would trigger a panic deploy of unaudited work, which is a bigger risk than the exposure itself. Rotating at cutover, with everything else, is the right moment.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out an emergency out-of-band deploy. Also rules out ignoring it: the rotation must appear as an actual line item on the cutover checklist, which today contains the word 'password' zero times. Verified: index.html still contains 16 seeded SHA-256 password hashes, on this branch and on main.
decisions.source: index.html (16 matches for a 64-hex password literal); AZURE-CUTOVER-SECURITY-CHECKLIST.md (zero mentions of 'password')

decisions.what: The Cockburn Franchise Office is a deliberate, load-bearing entity, not leftover test data. Head Office supplies the OFFICE, the office supplies the shop floor, and the OFFICE is what gets invoiced.
decisions.why: The franchisee's legal entity, not the shop, is the party being billed. Modelling the office as its own location is what makes the invoice come out addressed to the right party and keeps shop-floor stock separate from what the franchisee has bought.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out deleting or merging the Franchise Office as a duplicate of the Cockburn store, and rules out billing rules that assume Head Office supplies the shop floor directly.
decisions.source: 2026-08-01 session (Kunal); office/store split already modelled at index.html:4897-4936

decisions.what: CORRECTION — dated franchise pricing IS built. Three documents claim there is 'zero effectiveFrom / asOf / rate-history in the client or the Functions'. That is FALSE and must not be inherited by the new register.
decisions.why: The claim was produced by searching for the words 'effectiveFrom' and 'asOf', which this project never used as names. The real feature is called something else: the client has a full dated-pricing engine (Pricing, with from/to intervals, as-of resolution, fail-closed error states and a staleness horizon) and the server has the matching validators and resolver, with a proof file exercising them. What is genuinely missing is (a) the write endpoint that saves a new dated rate — the client calls a pricingChangeUrl that no deployed function answers — and (b) any published pricing data, so today's numbers still come from the old single-value field. So the risk to Cockburn's money is real, but the fix is 'finish and switch on', not 'design and build from scratch'.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out re-specifying and rebuilding a dated-pricing model from zero — which is what the false claim would cause the next session to do. Rules out repeating the claim in the new register. The three documents that carry it must all be corrected together: HANDOVER.md:31, HANDOVER.md:160, HANDOVER.md:171 (plus the softer restatements at HANDOVER.md:667, audit-artifacts/PENDING-ROADMAP-2026-07-29.md:197, audit-artifacts/MASTER-DECISION-REGISTER.md:641, and AZURE-CHUNK-ORG-STRUCTURE.md:150 which says 'ground-truthed: no rate history today').

decisions.what: Every secret is rotated and relocated AT the single live cutover, not months early — you rotate at the boundary you are protecting, which is the moment the app stops being one owner's and starts being staff's.
decisions.why: Rotating early means doing it twice and leaves a window where the new secret is also stale. The exposure being protected against (staff, beta users, a wider audience) does not exist until cutover.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating the plaintext deployment token committed in .github/workflows/deploy-swa.yml:14 as an emergency — it is a knowingly accepted, private-repo exposure until cutover. Verified still present today.

decisions.what: The read-only auditor Microsoft credential and the tenant-wide app permissions stay in place for now; the teardown happens before beta, not today.
decisions.why: The app is not in use, and the auditor credential is still earning its keep for the pending settlement-engine re-audit. Removing it now would just have to be re-minted.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'just let the credential lapse' — the auditor app has TWO secrets, not one, and the second runs to 2027-01-22, so lapsing leaves outside read access live for another six months. Both must be deleted explicitly.

decisions.what: For the app registration named 'BOB Stock App', REMOVE its two tenant-wide SharePoint permissions rather than deleting the app.
decisions.why: Removing the permissions is reversible and anything that secretly depended on the app fails loudly and immediately; deleting it fails silently and cannot be undone. This grant reaches the entire Microsoft 365 tenant — HR, finance, contracts — not just stock, and its secret is valid to 2028.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out deleting the app as the first move. Note the register's claim that this is the ONLY record of a tenant-wide grant is WRONG — a second app (BOB-Stock-SP-Automation) was created the same way in June, was correctly scoped down, but still holds a live secret to 2026-12-19 with no teardown line item anywhere.
decisions.whoDecided: Kunal / verified against the live tenant

decisions.what: Never delete a cloud resource because its name looks temporary. Assert what the thing actually IS before deleting it. Specifically: bob-stock-tmp-c9 is the still-needed seeding path despite the 'tmp' in its name, and bobstockfnval2607 is the STORAGE ACCOUNT the whole money and login backend runs on — deleting it would destroy every server route.
decisions.why: Two name-based guesses in this one section were each proved wrong within a day. That is an observed failure rate, not cautious drafting. Of the 36 Logic Apps, roughly 16 look like leftovers and at least six of those are live deliverables or cutover tooling.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out bulk deletion by name pattern, permanently. Rules out following AZURE-CHUNK9-WAVE-REVIEW.md:86, which still instructs 'Delete bob-stock-tmp-c9' — verified still present and still wrong.

decisions.what: All the server work ships as ONE single deploy at the end of the phase, with Kunal's explicit go-ahead, never a string of small deploys.
decisions.why: Each deploy to the live app is a risk event. Batching them into one audited cutover means one risk event instead of thirty, and the owner runs every cloud change himself.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out per-fix deploys and rules out the instruction at AZURE-PULL-HARDENING-CUTOVER-RUNBOOK.md:24-26 to 'merge to main and deploy' — following that today would ship 305 commits of unaudited work to the live app. The governing process document, AZURE-CHUNK-PROCESS.md:90, still states the rule unqualified and does not know about either exception, in breach of its own rule that process changes get written down.
decisions.supersededBy: CUT-2 (franchise wizard split out, 2026-07-29) and CUT-3 (correction route parked, 2026-07-29). The one-cutover rule still governs everything else.

decisions.what: ROLLOUT GATE: no store device, including franchise stores, gets the app until ALL chunks are finished and audited.
decisions.why: Written when the plan assumed everything shipped together. It was meant to stop a half-built permission model reaching a store.
decisions.rulesOut: Dangerous if inherited: it is written in capitals as a hard gate in three places, so a future reader could reasonably block the entire launch on it. It must be marked superseded at each site, not just here.
decisions.supersededBy: CUT-2 / CUT-3 (2026-07-29) — the org-structure chunk is explicitly NOT built at launch, and Contract 2 is parked

decisions.what: The pending settlement-engine re-audit was formally re-scoped to cover the engine and Contract 1 only, with the correction lane deliberately excluded and tested at an empty baseline.
decisions.why: Contract 2 is parked, so an auditor reading the old instruction would flag the missing correction route as a gap and burn an entire audit round on it.
decisions.rulesOut: CORRECTION TO THE EXISTING REGISTER: audit-artifacts/MASTER-DECISION-REGISTER.md:475 states this obligation is 'verified NOT DONE' and that the contracts file 'still reads Land Contract 2 as step 2'. That is now STALE — the phrase no longer appears anywhere in the file and the section carries an explicit 'It is now done' marker.

decisions.what: The ten-stage per-chunk process is the governing process, and any change to it gets edited into the process document itself, not merely agreed in conversation.
decisions.why: A process that lives in chat is a process nobody can find. The stages exist because each one caught something the previous one missed.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out re-deriving the workflow each session. The rule has already been broken twice (the wizard split and the Contract 2 parking were agreed in chat and never written into AZURE-CHUNK-PROCESS.md), which is the cheapest outstanding fix in the repo.

decisions.what: External auditors must RUN the test harness themselves every wave, not read a reported result. It needs no credentials, so there is no excuse. Auditors report findings only and never edit files.
decisions.why: A static read misses bugs that only appear when the code actually executes. And an auditor that edits files has trampled uncommitted work before.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out accepting a pasted pass/fail summary. BUT the ledger auditors are pointed at still tells them to expect 153 of 153 — the real figures are 277 sentinels and 322 mutations, so an auditor following it reports a mismatch against a perfectly healthy suite.

decisions.what: Gemini is retired as an auditor. The auditors are GPT/Codex and Antigravity. No full blind audit happens before the final one.
decisions.why: Gemini fabricated findings, including an invented security advisory and two hallucinated critical issues. An early full audit would only re-flag items already known to be open, at full cost.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out sending work to Gemini for review. CLAUDE.md section 7 still contains the obsolete rule 'every significant step must go to Gemini' underneath a supersession banner — the banner is doing all the work and the body should be deleted.

decisions.what: The blind audit method: six AI auditors were each given the app with NO framework, NO 'already fixed' list and NO context, and NOTHING was fixed until all six reports were in.
decisions.why: A primed auditor confirms your fixes instead of attacking them. The single most-confirmed bug of the whole exercise — offline deletes never syncing — sat in code one auditor had previously called clean, and every primed reviewer agreed with that verdict rather than testing it.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out fixing findings as they arrive (it biases the later auditors) and rules out telling auditors what has already been fixed. Banked as standing principle P-17.

decisions.what: Every auditor finding is triaged against the real code before it is believed: genuinely new, plausible-needs-repro, already known, or verifiably false. About 14 of roughly 75 findings were provably wrong.
decisions.why: Auditors assert things confidently that the code disproves in seconds — one claimed the app never asks the browser for persistent storage when it does, another claimed a cross-site-scripting hole in a view that escapes everything.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out acting on an auditor's severity rating without reproducing it. This is the direct ancestor of the current standing rule to ground-truth every finding.

decisions.what: The 'rewrite the whole thing / switch database library' recommendation was rejected. It is an opinion, not a finding.
decisions.why: It ignores a working, three-times-audited core and the deliberately accepted alpha constraints. The value in that report was the specific bugs, not the architecture verdict.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out re-proposing a rewrite or a database-layer swap on the strength of an auditor's architectural opinion.

decisions.what: The single biggest architectural gap found by four independent auditors: transfers, deliveries and stock takes did not sync between devices — only the stock movements did — making the whole multi-store feature effectively single-device.
decisions.why: The receiving store could see the stock arrive but never see the transfer record to receive it. Four auditors found it independently, which is the strongest signal in the whole audit.
decisions.rulesOut: Must NOT be inherited as open. REMAINING-WORK.md still lists it as 'the #1 blocker' at line 27, and that file is still linked from HANDOVER as somewhere to look.
decisions.supersededBy: Built as the record-steps sync (Chunk 4) — the recordsteps-push and recordsteps-pull endpoints are deployed and referenced throughout the cutover checklist

decisions.what: Accepted for alpha and recorded, not forgotten: browser-side permission checks are convenience rather than security; passwords and PINs are hashed without salt, with no lockout and a default PIN; the sync web addresses can be extracted with developer tools; and small rounding drift on money is accepted.
decisions.why: A trusted internal alpha with one owner, no customer data and no payments. Closing these properly needs a server, which is what the whole Azure phase was for.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out an auditor rating browser-side price hiding as a critical leak — that is a mis-rating under the standing principle. But the acceptance as written UNDERSTATES the exposure: it does not record that the live app on main ships 16 unsalted password and PIN hashes for real named accounts including both directors, downloadable by anyone who can reach the public address.
decisions.supersededBy: Partly by the 2026-08-01 risk re-sort (security hardening may now follow release) and partly by Chunk 9, which built the server-side login. The rounding acceptance and the browser-checks-are-not-security principle both remain in force.

decisions.what: Stop hand-writing counts, commit references and file sizes into documents. A guard script should generate them, and the guard itself must be mutation-tested — deliberately broken inputs must make it fail before it is trusted.
decisions.why: A number typed into prose is stale the moment the file changes. The same probe count is stated as 51, 54 and 61 across six documents when the file actually holds 67; the smoke count is given as both 239 and 238 inside one document. And a gate nobody has ever seen fail is just another document nobody reads.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out 'just correct the numbers this once' — the register's own corrections went stale in two days: it states HEAD 4ab135c and far ahead of `main` (run `git rev-list --count main..HEAD` for the current number); today it is 4529b90 and 305 ahead. Eleven guard scripts now exist under audit-artifacts/ (check-docs.js, check-name-collisions.js, check-edit-premise.js, check-expr-safety.js and others), so this is partly built.
decisions.source: audit-artifacts/MASTER-DECISION-REGISTER.md:173-263; verified git rev-parse (HEAD 4529b90, 305 ahead, index.html 6637 lines)

decisions.what: The register's own headline finding, verified and still true: 285 recorded decision mentions collapse to about 61 real ones. The other 220 are the same ruling restated in different files, which is exactly how they drift apart.
decisions.why: Every restatement is a chance for one copy to be edited and the others not. The engine re-audit marker now says three different things in three places (in fact four, in four); the catalogue publish authority is recorded as both decided and open inside a single file, twelve lines apart.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out the new register carrying a decision in more than one place. Every other mention must become a link, and any second copy of a marker's contents is a defect. Verified still live: AZURE-CHUNK6-SCOPE.md:109 records the publish authority as decided while :139 calls it 'the one OPEN decision for Kunal'.

decisions.what: The most dangerous facts in this project live in exactly one place each, and several of those places are in a folder excluded from version control — they would vanish with this machine.
decisions.why: Three of the project's known money-critical or data-loss facts existed only in ignored files. Two owner decisions from 2026-07-30 existed in one file each plus a commit message.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out citing anything under audit-artifacts/ as the authority for a load-bearing fact. Note the permanent security rule in CLAUDE.md itself points at a backlog file by a path that does not exist — the real file is in the ignored folder.

decisions.what: AA-20 ('Clear PIN' revokes access instantly rather than letting it time out) is DECIDED and BUILT, not open.
decisions.why: An instant kill switch is what a manager expects when they clear a PIN; a grant that survives for hours afterwards would surprise them. The code carries it: a cleared PIN bumps a counter that makes every already-issued grant dead on arrival.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out re-asking the question. It is still listed as an open owner decision in HANDOVER.md:672-674 and in the memory index — both must be corrected. Verified in code.
decisions.source: azure-functions/src/functions/accessPolicy.js:110-118 (pinEpoch check — a stale epoch kills the grant); AZURE-CHUNK-AA-LA-CHANGES.md:155 vs HANDOVER.md:672-674

decisions.what: Store isolation fails CLOSED: if the app does not yet know which stores a device is allowed to see, it shows nothing rather than everything.
decisions.why: The opposite — showing everything until told otherwise — was found by an auditor as a critical privacy hole on a fresh device that had never synced.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out any 'show all until scope arrives' fallback. Verified in code. AZURE-CHUNK10-WAVE-REVIEW.md contains BOTH statements — the correct fail-closed one at line 20 and the stale fail-open one at line 88 — as descriptions of current security behaviour, 68 lines apart in one file.
decisions.source: index.html:1370-1375 ('Fail-CLOSED: unknown scope … -> false'); AZURE-CHUNK10-WAVE-REVIEW.md:20 vs :88

decisions.what: Archiving is triggered by the ledger reaching about 5,000 rows OR six months passing, whichever comes first, and archived rows move to a separate list rather than being flagged in place.
decisions.why: The 5,000 figure is not arbitrary — the archive job reads the whole ledger in a single request and Microsoft refuses beyond that size. Relaxing the cadence silently breaks the archive run, and only one sentence in one wave review says so.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out relaxing the archive cadence without first building paging, which was documented but never implemented. Also note the growth projection that motivated urgency is void — the app is not in use and nothing is filling the ledger.

decisions.what: The archival cutoff is a running record number, not a business date. A movement entered late or backdated from offline still gets a higher record number, so it lands after the cutoff and is counted rather than silently lost.
decisions.why: If the cutoff were a date, a movement dated last month but entered today would fall on the wrong side of the line and disappear from both the archive and the live totals. The business date is kept for reporting only.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out any date-based archival cutoff, permanently. This is the single decision most likely to be re-proposed by someone who finds date-based cutoffs more intuitive.

decisions.what: Head Office cost prices are left out of the shared product catalogue entirely. Cost is served by a separate, permission-gated endpoint that a franchisee's key is refused. A franchisee's own entered costs are never overwritten.
decisions.why: Kunal's business rule is that a franchisee's cost is not BOB's cost. Both auditors rejected the original design — which sent the cost and asked the app not to display it — as an actual leak rather than a display preference.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out any 'send it and hide it in the interface' approach to cost. This is a genuine privacy boundary and is enforced on the server, unlike selling price, which is public catalogue information and only hidden as a view preference.

decisions.what: Categories and product types can never be hard-deleted — deleting one deactivates it instead. Inactive ones disappear from pickers but keep their label on historical records, and the server refuses to attach a new or edited product to an inactive one.
decisions.why: Hard deletion orphans every historical record that referenced the deleted item, so old reports start showing blanks.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out a real delete button for categories and product types.

decisions.what: There is ONE master on/off switch for the whole Account Access permission system. Every gated cloud step reads a single setting and stays completely inert while it is absent — including after a permission policy has been published. Publishing and enforcing are two separate acts.
decisions.why: It buys a rehearsal: publish the policy, confirm every door reads it, then flip the switch. Undoing is flipping it back, and the policy survives. It exists because three of the cloud changes had no such switch and, applied as written, would have broken their own working director access the instant they landed.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out arming enforcement as a side effect of publishing a policy — which two parts of the design previously did. Rules out applying the user-admin, catalogue-write and archive changes without adding the guard first.

decisions.what: When the Account Access system is switched on, cost figures are visible to DIRECTORS ONLY. Head Office is added later by editing the policy, never by changing code.
decisions.why: Start tight and widen. Written as an acceptance test in its own right: if adding Head Office turns out to need a code change, the design has failed its purpose.
decisions.rulesOut: Contradicts the governing permission matrix, which still seeds cost visibility as 'director plus corporate Head Office'. The code agrees with this decision, not the matrix. Practical effect: today an unauthenticated Head Office device receives the full cost list; after activation it will not.

decisions.what: THE CUTOVER CHECKLIST DECLARES ITSELF INCOMPLETE. Its own banner says the body predates the Account Access work, the franchise work and both July server contracts, and that cutover obligations still live only in HANDOVER sections 5a and 6, in REMAINING-WORK.md and in the memory ledger. All four sources must be folded into it before cutover, after which only it is followed.
decisions.why: At cutover you follow one list, under time pressure, and anything not on it does not happen. The document is otherwise the best-maintained in the repo, which makes the gaps more dangerous, not less.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating AZURE-CUTOVER-SECURITY-CHECKLIST.md as the whole cutover list today. The reconciliation has NOT been done — see the six confirmed missing items in the open questions below.

decisions.what: Cockburn franchise discount rates are settled: Retail products 50% off, and Treatment (professional), Cleaning and Stationery all 25% off. In practice that means ONE universal rate of 25% for the store, with a single product-type override of 50% for Retail.
decisions.why: Kunal confirmed Cleaning and Stationery are partly supplied to Cockburn and carry the same 25% as professional products. Because only Retail differs, the three-tier model collapses to a simple, low-risk shape: one store rate plus one type override — 1 exception instead of 20 per-product overrides, and a new Retail product automatically inherits 50% instead of being silently under-discounted.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out tagging the 20 retail products individually (the approach that leaks money whenever a new retail product is added). Rules out needing per-product overrides at all for Cockburn today, though the per-product tier still exists for future exceptions.
decisions.source: chat 2026-08-01/02; implements the three-tier model; current code has only two tiers (index.html:1234-1237)

decisions.what: Expiry and Batch Tracking is BACK IN SCOPE and is to be built now. Specified 2026-06-16: shelf life per product, expiry entered per delivery line at receipt, dead stock defined as past 50% of time-to-expiry, a separate expired list, and route-to-store / sell-direct-from-HO / destroy-to-wastage actions.
decisions.why: Kunal specified it in full in June, it was sequenced as step 2 of three, and steps 1 and 3 were built while step 2 was skipped entirely. It appears on no backlog or roadmap and was invisible until the register found it. Under the 2026-08-01 risk ruling, FEATURE GAPS may not be deferred, and this is the largest one in the project.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out treating it as post-launch. It also rules out slipping it in late: it needs per-batch identity on top of a ledger that today keeps one running total per product, so the data-model decision has to come first.

decisions.what: When a company-owned store converts to a franchise, a territory manager who also covers OTHER stores keeps their account and keeps those other stores. They lose only the converted store. The converted store becomes a franchise store, and in Southlands case a franchise office is created alongside it.
decisions.why: Kunal ruling. Cancelling a territory managers whole account because one of their stores changed hands would lock a working employee out of every other store they run, on the day of a handover — the worst possible moment. This settles open question D-OS-2.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out deactivating a territory manager on conversion when they still cover at least one other store. Deactivation applies only when the converted store was their LAST remaining store.

decisions.what: Stock on hand is valued AT COST on every screen that reports its value. If a retail-value figure is wanted as well, it must carry a visibly different label (e.g. "Retail Value of Stock"), never the same words as the cost figure.
decisions.why: Kunal ruling. "Total Stock Value" currently appears on the Dashboard valued at RETAIL and on Reports > Overview valued at COST — two numbers differing by two to three times under an identical label. Cost is the money actually tied up in the shelf and is the figure an accountant expects. Separately confirmed: the "Total Cost" figure on Store Comparison is NOT part of this problem — it is correctly labelled "stock used, at cost" and means cost of goods consumed in the period.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out leaving two screens showing different numbers under one label, and rules out silently switching the Dashboard to cost without relabelling anything that still shows retail.

decisions.what: FRANCHISE PRICING MUST STAY FULLY FLEXIBLE AND OWNER-CHANGEABLE. All three tiers — the store-wide rate, the per-product-type rate, and the per-product override — must be editable by Kunal from inside the app at any time, for any store and any future franchise, with no code change and no developer. The fact that Cockburn today needs only 25% plus a Retail override describes the DATA, never the design.
decisions.why: Kunal stressed this explicitly and repeatedly. The risk is that the current simple shape (one universal rate plus one type override) gets hard-coded as a special case, leaving him unable to change a rate without asking for a code change — which is exactly the position the app is in TODAY, where Cockburn 25% is a hard-coded seed value with no editing screen anywhere. This constraint also connects the two halves of the pricing work: because every rate change must open a NEW dated period rather than overwrite the old one, flexibility and the fix for retroactively-rewritten invoices are the same piece of work.
decisions.rulesOut: Rules out hard-coding any rate, any tier, or any store-specific assumption. Rules out shipping the pricing fix without editing screens for all three tiers, including on the product-type screen. Rules out a design where adding a future franchise store requires a developer. Acceptance test: Kunal can add a new franchise store and set its rates end-to-end without anyone touching code.

decisions.rulesOut: Rules out any further speculation about these column types, and rules out citing diag-c1-insert.js as evidence of the live schema.
